questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy, was discharged after drain removal on the first postoperative day, but returned on the second day with abdominal pain and fever. Ultrasound reveals a fluid collection in the subhepatic space. What is the most likely cause of this collection?
questions.explanation: The acute presentation of fever, increasing abdominal pain, and a localized subhepatic fluid collection shortly after a cholecystectomy is highly suspicious for a Bile leak (Option C). Post-laparoscopic bile leaks often result from a dislodged clip on the cystic duct or a minor injury to the common bile duct. The leaked bile causes localized chemical peritonitis and fluid accumulation (biloma). General infection (Option A) would not typically present with a large organized collection this rapidly without an underlying leak. Surgical site pain (Option B) would not cause a large ultrasound collection and fever. Retained stones (Option D) usually cause jaundice and biliary colic rather than a large subhepatic fluid pocket. Therefore, because a biloma is the most common reason for a large, acute postoperative collection in this specific space, bile leak is the definitively probable cause. Management involves ERCP and stenting to decompress the biliary system
questions.learning: The acute presentation of fever, increasing abdominal pain, and a localized subhepatic fluid collection shortly after a cholecystectomy is highly suspicious for a Bile leak (Option C).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Morbidity of a disease is on the rise. Which of the following statements is correct with respect to this?
options: Incidence will increase and prevalence will decrease
Incidence and prevalence are not related to it
Incidence will decrease and prevalence will increase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Incidence and prevalence will increase

The incidence and prevalence will increase when the morbidity increases.

Morbidity refers to any deviation, whether subjective or objective, from a state of physical well-being. It encompasses conditions such as sickness, illness, and disability. Morbidity is typically measured by morbidity rates or ratios, which include frequency, duration, and severity. Disease frequency is indicated by incidence and prevalence rates.

Incidence refers to the number of new cases of a disease that occur in a population during a specific time period, while prevalence represents the total number of cases, both new and existing, in a population at a given time. Additionally, the average duration of illness, represented by the disability rate, and the severity of illnesses, indicated by the case fatality rate, are also used as measures.

As morbidity increases in a population, both incidence and prevalence rates tend to rise. This is because a higher morbidity indicates a greater number of people experiencing illness (increased incidence) and a larger number of existing cases (increased prevalence). The increased duration of illness (disability days) and the severity of conditions also contribute to the overall morbidity burden.

Pearl PF0231: Mortality and morbidity indicators in epidemiology

Crude death rate = ( Number of deaths during the year/Mid year population ) x 1000

Age specific death rate = ( Number of deaths in specific age groups/Mid year population of that age group ) x 1000

Sex specific death rate = ( Number of deaths per year of that sex/Mid year population of that sex ) x 1000

Case fatality rate = ( Total number of deaths due to a particular disease/Total number of cases due to same disease ) x 100

Proportional mortality from a particular disease = ( Number of deaths from a specific disease in a year/ Total deaths from all causes in a year ) x 100

Under 5 mortality rate = ( Number of deaths under 5 yrs of age in a year/Total live birth in that year ) x 1000

Survival rate = ( Total number of patients alive after 5 yrs /Total number of patients diagnosed or treated ) x 100

Mortality Indicators

Morbidity Indicators

1. Crude Death Rate
2. Life Expectancy
3. Age-specific Death Rates
4. Infant Mortality Rate
5. Child Death Rate
6. Under 5 Proportionate Mortality Rate
7. Adult Mortality Rate
8. Maternal Mortality Rate
9. Disease-Specific Mortality Rate
10. Proportional Mortality Rate
11. Case fatality rate
12. Years of Potential Life Lost

1. Incidence and Prevalence
2. Notification Rates
3. Attendance Rates at OPD
4. Admission, Discharge & Readmission Rates
5. Duration of Stay in Hospital
6. Spells of Sickness or absence from work or school
questions.learning: Incidence and prevalence will increase — The incidence and prevalence will increase when the morbidity increases. Morbidity refers to any deviation, whether subjective or objective, from a state of physical well-being.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A person has the false belief that he owns a lot of property and is wealthy, and that someone he knows wants to kill him to take it away. He appears depressed and physically unwell. What is seen here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Delusion of grandeur and persecution

This scenario where he has lots of property and somebody wants to kill him points towards diagnosis of delusion of grandeur and persecution.

A person has the false belief that he possesses vast property and is very rich, which represents a delusion of grandeur, characterized by an exaggerated sense of self-importance, wealth, exceptional abilities, or fame. He also believes that someone wants to kill him and take away his property, which corresponds to a delusion of persecution, the most common type of delusion. Thus, both delusions of grandeur and persecution are present in this case.

A delusion is a false, firm, fixed belief that is not in keeping with the patient’s socio-cultural and educational background.

Delusions are of two types based on their origin:

Primary: Delusions that do not occur in response to another psychopathological form such as mood disorder.
Secondary: Delusions that are secondary to other morbid psychological conditions like depressive moods and hallucinations. They are understandable when a detailed psychiatric history and examination are available.

DSM-5 criteria for diagnosis of delusional disorder:

The presence of one (or more) delusions with a duration of 1 month or longer.

* Criteria for schizophrenia have never been met.

* Functioning is not markedly impaired, and behavior is not obviously bizarre or odd.

* If manic or major depressive episodes have occurred, these have been brief relative to the duration of the delusional periods.

* Not attributable to substance abuse, another medical condition, or another mental disorder.

Other options:

* Delusion of reference means delusion in which events, objects, or other persons in one’s immediate environment have a particular and unusual significance in reference to the person experiencing the delusion.
Examples : A feeling that people on television or radio are talking about or talking directly to them
Believing that headlines or stories in newspapers are written especially for them.

* Delusion of Nihilism seen in cotard’s syndrome is a false belief that self, body parts or world do not exist.

Pearl PF1258: Types of delusions

THE TYPES OF DELUSIONS

Delusion of control

False belief that a person’s will, thoughts, or feelings are being controlled by external forces.

Delusion of grandeur or Megalomania

Exaggerated conception of one’s importance, power, or identity.

Delusion of infidelity or morbid jealousy or Othello syndrome

False belief that one’s lover is unfaithful. Sometimes called pathological jealousy.

Delusion of love or erotomania

False belief that another person is in love with them. In De Clerambault syndrome, the woman believes that a man, frequently older and of higher status, is in love with her.

Delusion of misidentification

Capgras syndrome: Belief that a familiar person has been replaced by an exact double i.e. an impostor.

Fregoli syndrome: Person holds a delusional belief that different people are in fact a single person who changes his or her appearance or is in disguise.

Nihilistic delusion

False belief that oneself, others or the world, is non-existent or about to end. When nihilistic delusion is accompanied by ideas concerning bodily function failure e.g. putrefaction of intestine etc, it is called Cotard syndrome.

Delusion of infestation

False belief that one is infested with small but visible organisms. As a monosymptomatic delusional disorder, this is called Ekbom syndrome.

Delusion of persecution

The most common delusion. False belief of being harassed or persecuted.

Delusion of poverty

The person strongly believes they are financially incapacitated.

Delusion of reference

False belief that the behavior of others has a particular and unusual significance, usually of a negative nature. The person may falsely feel that others are talking about them (e.g. the people on television are talking to or about the person).

Delusion of self-accusation

False feeling of remorse and guilt. Seen in depression with psychotic features.
questions.learning: Delusion of grandeur and persecution — This scenario where he has lots of property and somebody wants to kill him points towards diagnosis of delusion of grandeur and persecution.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs were not given for hypertension in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Enalapril is an ACE inhibitor and is strictly contraindicated during all stages of pregnancy. These drugs are highly teratogenic and can cause severe fetal complications, including renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia, and intrauterine growth restriction. Methyldopa (Option A) is a centrally acting alpha-2 agonist and has historically been the gold standard for long-term management due to its proven safety profile. Labetalol (Option C) is a combined alpha and beta-blocker frequently used as first-line therapy for acute severe hypertension in pregnancy. Nifedipine (Option D) is a calcium channel blocker considered safe and effective for controlling blood pressure without affecting uterine blood flow. Because ACE inhibitors like Enalapril interfere with the vital fetal renin-angiotensin system, they must be discontinued immediately upon the recognition of pregnancy in favor of the safer alternatives mentioned

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient came to the casualty with acute bronchial asthma after treatment for glaucoma. Which of the following is most probable causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Timolol

Timolol is a non-selective beta-blocker that is used in glaucoma. Non-selective beta-blockers can cause precipitation of bronchial asthma in susceptible individuals (beta-2 block on bronchi).

Ocular beta-blockers reduce Intraocular pressure by decreasing aqueous formation by blockade of β2 receptors. The most commonly prescribed non‐selective beta‐blocker eye drops is timolol and eye drops significantly affect lung function and increase asthma morbidity.

Betaxolol is a beta 1 selective blocker that is used in glaucoma and has a lower propensity to precipitate bronchial asthma. (option B)

Latanoprost and bimatoprost are prostaglandin (PGF2 alpha) analogs and does not precipitate bronchial asthma. (option C and D)
questions.learning: Timolol Timolol is a non-selective beta-blocker that is used in glaucoma. Non-selective beta-blockers can cause precipitation of bronchial asthma in susceptible individuals (beta-2 block on bronchi).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: The following findings were noted during the autopsy of a patient with a gunshot injury. What is the likely range of the gunshot?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Close range

The likely range of the gunshot injury shown above is close range, characterized by a circular wound with blackening and tattooing.

To determine the range of firing, the following parameters are used:

• The entry wound size and shape
• Blast effect – Muzzle end imprint and edge eversion
• Blackening, Tattooing, Singeing of hair, Abrasion collar, and Grease collar
• Hair should be preserved to determine the range of firing which can be examined for carbonization/desiccation in close range, also from lead deposition around the wound to assess the range of firing.

Blackening occurs due to the deposit of smoke and can be removed with a wet cloth. This can be seen up to around 15 cm of firing. Whereas, tattooing occurs due to the deposition of unburnt powder particles and are difficult to remove. They are also called stippling or peppering. This is seen up to 50 cm of firing.

Abrasion collar: Gyroscopic movement of the bullet, the skin's elasticity, and the grease and dirt particles on the bullet's surface are the major causative factors of abrasion and grease collar. They are seen on the skin around the wound of entry at all ranges. Depending on the angle of entry made by the bullet, i.e.

• A perpendicular entry of the bullet develops the abrasion collar of a rounded shape.
• An acute angular entry of the bullet develops the abrasion collar of an oblique or oval shape.
• Some contusion present in the abraded collar is known as contusion collar

Grease collar: Mostly seen on the clothing and is seen as a black deposit, sharply outlined as if printed (better seen on light colour clothes and fair-skinned individuals). Its medicolegal importance is that it helps derive information such as entry wound and direction of firing.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 6 month-old girl has developed seborrheic skin eruptions over the past 3 months. She has had recurrent upper respiratory and middle ear infections with streptococcus pneumoniae for the past year. Physical examination indicates that she also has hepatosplenomegaly and generalized lymphadenopathy. Her hearing is reduced in the right ear. A skull radiograph shows an expansile, 2 cm lytic lesion involving the right temporal bone. Laboratory studies show no anemia, thrombocytopenia, or leukopenia. The mass is curetted. Which of the following is most likely to be seen on microscopic examination of this mass?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Histocytes with Birbeck granules

Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) is characterized by clonal proliferation of Langerhans cells that form lytic bone lesions, especially in the skull and temporal bone, often causing recurrent ear infections and hearing loss.

• Seborrheic dermatitis–like rash
• Hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy
• Usually normal blood counts early

Langerhans cells containing Birbeck granules (tennis-racket shaped organelles) on electron microscopy. Immunopositive for CD1a and S-100

Why not others:

• CD3 lymphoblasts → T-cell ALL
• Plasma cells with Russell bodies → multiple myeloma
• Reed–Sternberg cells → Hodgkin lymphoma

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A middle-aged man was brought to the ER after an assault with a sharp axe. Identify the type of wound?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chop wound

The given wound caused by an axe, is likely to be a chop wound.

Chop wounds are so-called because of the action in which they are produced. Depending on the type of instrument, they may resemble an incised or a lacerated wound. The shape of the wound may give clues to the type of weapon. It would be a deep, well-margined wound, gaping with limited damage to the surrounding skin.

For example, in the given image, the wound resembles an injury produced by a sharp axe. Such wounds may be inflicted with homicidal intent on the skull/scalp.
questions.learning: Chop wound — The given wound caused by an axe, is likely to be a chop wound. Chop wounds are so-called because of the action in which they are produced.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with fatigue, loss of appetite, constipation, recurrent kidney stone–related urinary symptoms, and polyuria, along with a history of psychiatric illness, raising suspicion of hyperparathyroidism. Which investigation would be most helpful in confirming this diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This patient presents with multi-system symptoms of hypercalcemia: fatigue, constipation, and renal stones ("Stones, Groans, and Psychic Moans"), strongly suggesting Primary Hyperparathyroidism. This condition is most commonly caused by a benign parathyroid adenoma. Once the diagnosis is biochemically established (elevated PTH and Calcium), imaging is required to localize the abnormal gland for surgery. The Tc-99m Sestamibi scan (Option A) is the gold standard functional imaging prioritized for this purpose. It is highly effective at detecting overactive parathyroid tissue due to its high mitochondrial content, which retains the tracer longer than normal thyroid tissue. USG neck (Option B) is an excellent structural adjunct but may miss ectopic glands. CT neck (Option C) and PET scan (Option D) are much less sensitive or specific as initial localization tools compared to Sestamibi. Therefore, the Sestamibi scan is the most beneficial diagnostic imaging step for pre-operative planning. **************
questions.learning: This patient presents with multi-system symptoms of hypercalcemia: fatigue, constipation, and renal stones ("Stones, Groans, and Psychic Moans"), strongly suggesting Primary Hyperparathyroidism.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following criteria is used for diagnosing abdominal pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Studdiford's criteria

Studdiford's criteria is used in the diagnosis of primary abdominal pregnancy. It includes:

• Presence of normal tubes and ovaries with no evidence of recent or past injury/pregnancy.
• Absence of uteroperitoneal fistula.
• Presence of a pregnancy related exclusively to the peritoneal surface and early enough to eliminate the possibility of secondary implantation after primary tubal nidation.

Other options:

Option A: Spiegelberg’s criteria is used in the diagnosis of ovarian pregnancy:

• Tube on the affected side must be intact.
• The gestation sac must be in the position of the ovary.
• The gestation sac is connected to the uterus by the ovarian ligament.
• Ovarian tissue must be found on its wall on histological examination.

Option B: Rubin's criteria is used in the diagnosis of cervical pregnancy:

• Soft, enlarged cervix equal to or larger than the fundus.
• Uterine bleeding following amenorrhea, without cramping pain.
• Products of conception are entirely confined within and firmly attached to endocervix.
• A closed internal cervical os and a partially opened external os.

Option D:Godin's sonographic criteria is used for the diagnosis of a cesarean scar pregnancy:

• Empty uterine cavity
• Empty cervical canal
• A gestational sac in the anterior part of the uterine isthmus
• Absence of healthy myometrium between the bladder and gestational sac

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: On the 5th postoperative day post CABG, the patient develops tachypnea and hypotension. What is the most probable cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute respiratory failure

The clinical presentation of tachypnoea and hypotension in a post-op day 5 patient who underwent coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) points towards lung collapse (atelectasis) - type 3 respiratory failure.

Atelectasis is the most common respiratory complication in a post-operative patient.

The factors predisposing to atelectasis are general anesthesia, upper abdominal surgery, and thoracic surgery. They commonly present with tachypnoea and decreased oxygen saturation. On examination, the breath sounds are bronchial in nature and reduced in intensity.

Lung atelectasis can be reversed (within 24h-48h) with early mobilization, deep breathing (5 sequential breaths for 5s), incentive spirometry, and chest physiotherapy.

Other postoperative systemic complications include:

1. Pneumonia and myocardial infarction : First few days after surgery
2. Venous thromboembolism, kidney failure, and urinary tract infection: Days 4 to 7
3. Superficial and deep surgical site infections: 2nd post-op week

Other options:

Option A: For a diagnosis of sepsis, SEPSIS 3 criteria needs to be satisfied:

• A documented infection
• An acute increase in >2 SOFA points

Option B: Acute kidney failure is defined as a decrease in urine output (<0.5 mL/kg/h for 6-12h) and a rise in serum creatinine values ( >1.5x baseline or >0.3 mg/dL).

Option D: Acute cardiac failure has features of hypotension and tachycardia, with peripheral signs of hypoperfusion characterized by cold clammy extremities.
questions.learning: Acute respiratory failure — The clinical presentation of tachypnoea and hypotension in a post-op day 5 patient who underwent coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) points towards lung collapse (atelectasis) - type 3 respiratory failure.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: SARS-CoV-2 can be detected by all except ______.
options: Real-time PCR to detect viral mRNA
Rapid antigen test to detect spike proteins
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Southern blotting

SARS-CoV-2 can be detected by all except Southern blotting.

Southern blotting cannot be used to detect SARS-CoV-2 because there is usually not enough DNA in the collected sample to obtain a pattern on gel electrophoresis.

Real-time PCR uses nasopharyngeal secretions to detect viral genomic RNA or DNA in respiratory secretions. It is the most sensitive and specific test available.

Rapid-antigen test detects spike proteins in nasopharyngeal secretions.

Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) against spike protein is also found to be sensitive and specific for SARS-CoV-2.
questions.learning: Southern blotting SARS-CoV-2 can be detected by all except Southern blotting. Southern blotting cannot be used to detect SARS-CoV-2 because there is usually not enough DNA in the collected sample to obtain a pattern on gel electrophoresis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following antidiabetic drugs is associated with the development of lactic acidosis?
questions.explanation: Metformin, a biguanide, is the first-line medication for Type 2 Diabetes. Its most feared, though rare, side effect is lactic acidosis. This occurs because Metformin inhibits mitochondrial respiration and gluconeogenesis, which can lead to an accumulation of lactate. This risk is significantly increased in patients with renal impairment, as Metformin is renally excreted; if it builds up, the metabolic shift toward lactic acid production becomes dangerous. Tolbutamide (Option A) and Glipizide (Option B) are sulfonylureas, which primarily cause hypoglycemia. Pioglitazone (Option C) is a thiazolidinedione associated with weight gain and fluid retention. Clinicians must monitor renal function (Creatinine/eGFR) closely and hold Metformin during acute illnesses or before radiocontrast procedures to prevent this complication. Because lactic acidosis is the classic metabolic adverse event associated with the biguanide class, Metformin is the correct choice for this diabetic complication
questions.learning: Metformin, a biguanide, is the first-line medication for Type 2 Diabetes. Its most feared, though rare, side effect is lactic acidosis.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A farmer presents with a painful snakebite on his right foot, showing two distinct fang marks along with swelling and bleeding at the site. What should be the first step in the management of this patient?
options: Sling or splint leading to immobilization
See the snake brought by a relative
questions.explanation: The first step in the immediate management of a snakebite in the field or upon arrival at a clinic is the immobilization of the affected limb using a sling or splint. This is critical to slow the systemic absorption of venom through the lymphatic system, which is accelerated by muscle movement. The patient should be kept calm and moved as little as possible. Polyvalent Anti-Snake Venom (ASV) (Option A) is the definitive treatment but is only administered once signs of systemic envenomation or severe local effects are confirmed. Venom suction (Option C), cutting the wound, or applying a tourniquet are obsolete and harmful practices that increase local tissue damage. Trying to see or identify the snake (Option D) often leads to dangerous delays or additional bites. Immobilization is the most effective first-aid measure to prevent the rapid spread of toxins until life-saving ASV can be safely administered
questions.learning: The first step in the immediate management of a snakebite in the field or upon arrival at a clinic is the immobilization of the affected limb using a sling or splint.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A middle-aged man presents with the following lesion on his face. He has a history of acne rosacea. The condition is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rhinophyma

The image above shows an exophytic, pink, lobulated mass over the nose with superficial vascular dilation suggesting a diagnosis of phymatous rosacea or rhinophyma

Phymatous rosacea is a subtype of acne rosacea characterized by thickened skin and prominent follicular openings. There is marked nasal distortion with an increase in size and a bulbous tip. Rhinophyma is the most common type of phymatous rosacea.

Rhinophyma (potato tumour/elephantiasis of the nose) is due to hypertrophy of the sebaceous gland. It is associated with long-standing cases of acne rosacea.  It is mostly seen in middle-aged men involving the tip of the nose causing unsightly appearance and obstruction to breathing and vision.

Treatment of rhinophyma

* First-line

* Topical skin‐peeling agent if there are large occluded follicles

* Electrocautery or laser for telangiectases

* Second-line - Low‐dose isotretinoin therapy

* Third line - Ablation of phymatous tissue with carbon dioxide laser • Surgical remodelling of the nose.

Other options:

Option B: Rhinoscleroma is a chronic granulomatous disease caused by gram-negative bacillus Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis. It presents with chronic granulomatous inflammation of the nasal cavity, causing nasal obstruction, discharge, crusting, and eventual nasal deformity.

Option C: Rhinosporidiosis is a chronic granulomatous disease caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi. It presents with painless, friable, polypoidal masses in the nasal cavity, often causing nasal obstruction and bleeding.

Option D: Scleroderma causes rashes on the face but has no association with long-standing acne rosacea. It is characterized by skin thickening, tightening, Raynaud's phenomenon, and internal organ involvement such as the lungs, heart, and gastrointestinal tract.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Affinity maturation is due to:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Somatic hypermutation

Affinity maturation is due to somatic hypermutation.

Affinity maturation is the process by which antibodies gain increased affinity, avidity, and anti-pathogen activity. It is a result of somatic hypermutation (SHM) of immunoglobulin genes in B cells, coupled to selection for antigen binding.

This process occurs in the germinal centers and proceeds for weeks after acute infection or vaccination, or for many cycles during chronic infection. The resulting antibodies can be highly mutated from their germline-encoded counterparts, with increases of several orders of magnitude in affinity for antigen compared to the corresponding naïve B cell receptors (BCRs).

Other options:

Option A: Isotype switching, also known as class switch recombination, is a process where the constant region of the antibody heavy chain is changed, leading to a switch in the antibody isotype (e.g., from IgM to IgG). This process is crucial for the functional properties of antibodies but is not directly involved in affinity maturation.

Option C: mRNA splicing is a cellular process that involves the removal of introns and the joining of exons to generate mature mRNA. While this process is essential for the production of functional antibodies, it is not specifically associated with affinity maturation. Affinity maturation primarily occurs through somatic hypermutation.

Option D: VDJ rearrangement is the process by which the variable regions of immunoglobulin genes are assembled from gene segments (V, D, and J segments). This process contributes to the diversity of antibodies but is distinct from affinity maturation. Affinity maturation occurs after VDJ rearrangement and is driven by somatic hypermutation in the variable regions.
questions.learning: Somatic hypermutation Affinity maturation is due to somatic hypermutation. Affinity maturation is the process by which antibodies gain increased affinity, avidity, and anti-pathogen activity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In the context of mitral stenosis, which clinical feature is typically observed?
questions.explanation: A loud, snapping first heart sound (S1) is a hallmark of mitral stenosis. This occurs because the mitral leaflets are thickened but still mobile, and the high pressure gradient in the left atrium causes them to slam shut forcefully at the start of systole. An absent S1 (Option B) is more characteristic of severe mitral regurgitation where the leaflets fail to coapt. An S3 gallop (Option C) is associated with volume overload and heart failure, which is not typical for the restricted filling of mitral stenosis. Muffled heart sounds (Option D) suggest pericardial effusion or severe obesity. Other classic findings of mitral stenosis include an opening snap and a mid-diastolic rumbling murmur best heard at the apex with the patient in the left lateral position
questions.learning: A loud, snapping first heart sound (S1) is a hallmark of mitral stenosis. This occurs because the mitral leaflets are thickened but still mobile, and the high pressure gradient in the left atrium causes them to slam shut forcefully at the start of systole.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Blood cholesterol shown as mg/ml value is in which scale?
questions.explanation: Data in biostatistics is classified into different scales based on its nature. Blood cholesterol levels, measured as specific numerical values (e.g., in mg/ml or mg/dL), are an example of continuous data. Continuous data can take any value within a given range and can be measured with any degree of precision (including fractions or decimals). Nominal data (Option B) involves categories without an inherent order, like gender or blood group. Ordinal data (Option A) involves categories with a meaningful rank or order, such as stages of cancer or socio-economic status. Discrete data (Option C) involves whole number counts, such as the number of hospital beds or the number of children in a family. Understanding these scales is fundamental for choosing the correct statistical tests for data analysis. Continuous variables like cholesterol, blood pressure, and height are typically summarized using means and standard deviations and are analyzed using parametric tests like the t-test or ANOVA
questions.learning: Data in biostatistics is classified into different scales based on its nature. Blood cholesterol levels, measured as specific numerical values (e.g., in mg/ml or mg/dL), are an example of continuous data.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient came to the medical OPD with complaints of polyuria. He has a history of undergoing total hypophysectomy. His Na+ levels are found to be 155 mEq/L, urine osmolality was 200 mOsm/L. What is the definitive management?
options: DDAVP for 2 weeks and then discontinue
Upsetting of receptors so no treatment is required
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. DDAVP supplementation for lifelong

Total hypophysectomy causes central diabetes insipidus due to permanent ADH deficiency.

ADH normally acts on kidney collecting ducts

⬇

Inserts aquaporin channels

⬇

Water reabsorption

⬇

Concentrated urine

| Parameter | Finding | Meaning

| --------- | ------- | -------

| Serum Na⁺ | 155 | Water loss (hypernatremia)

| Urine osmolality | 200 | Dilute urine

| History | Hypophysectomy | Central cause

Hypernatremia with low urine osmolality confirms inability to concentrate urine. Definitive therapy is lifelong desmopressin (DDAVP) replacement to restore water reabsorption.

Temporary therapy or thiazides are used in nephrogenic DI, not central DI.

| Feature | Central DI | Nephrogenic DI

| ------- | ---------- | --------------

| ADH | ↓ | Normal

| Cause | Pituitary damage | Kidney resistance

| Treatment | ⭐ Desmopressin | Thiazides

| Response to ADH | Yes | No

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and intermittent palpitations. She has a history of recurrent sore throats during childhood. On cardiac auscultation, there is a loud first heart sound (S1) followed by a high-pitched sound shortly after the second heart sound (S2), preceding a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumbling murmur heard best at the cardiac apex. The additional heart sound described is most commonly associated with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mitral stenosis

An opening snap (OS) is a high-frequency early diastolic sound produced by the abrupt opening of a stenotic but still mobile mitral valve. It is a classic auscultatory finding in rheumatic mitral stenosis.

• The sequence is: S2 → Opening Snap → Mid-diastolic rumbling murmur.
• A shorter A2–OS interval indicates more severe mitral stenosis because elevated left atrial pressure forces the valve open earlier.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Aortic stenosis: Produces an ejection click (if valve is mobile) and an ejection systolic murmur, not an opening snap.
• C. Mitral regurgitation: Causes a pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla; no opening snap.
• D. Aortic regurgitation: Causes an early diastolic decrescendo murmur and may have an Austin Flint murmur, but not an opening snap.
questions.learning: Mitral stenosis — An opening snap (OS) is a high-frequency early diastolic sound produced by the abrupt opening of a stenotic but still mobile mitral valve.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A person was bought to the emergency department with facial swelling, itching, and hypotension following a bee sting. The mentioned clinical features are due to the increase in which immunoglobulin? IgA- Immunoglobulin A IgE- Immunoglobulin E IgM- Immunoglobulin M IgG- Immunoglobulin G
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IgE

The given clinical features suggest Type 1 hypersensitivity reaction and are mediated by immunoglobulin E (IgE)

Immediate (Type I) Hypersensitivity is also called allergic reactions or allergies

It is a rapid immunologic reaction that is triggered by the binding of an antigen to IgE antibody on the surface of mast cells. It occurs in a previously sensitized individual. These reactions are induced by environmental antigens (allergens) that stimulate strong TH2 responses and IgE production in genetically susceptible individuals. Activation of TH2 cells is mediated by IL-4 and in turn, TH2 cells produce IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13. These cytokines act on B cells to stimulate IgE and activation of eosinophils. IgE coats mast cells by binding to the Fcεg receptor. Re-exposure to the allergen leads to cross-linking of the IgE and FcεRI which in turn causes activation of mast cells releasing powerful mediators. The principal mediators are histamine, proteases, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, cytokines like TNF, IL-1, and chemokines. The clinical manifestations may be local or systemic and range from mildly annoying rhinitis to fatal anaphylaxis.

It occurs in two phases:

* Immediate phase is characterized by vasodilation, vascular leakage, smooth muscle spasm (in asthma), or glandular secretions. These changes occur within minutes after exposure to an allergen and subside in a few hours.

* Late-phase reaction is characterized by infiltration of tissues with eosinophils, neutrophils, basophils, monocytes, and CD4+ T cells leading to mucosal epithelial cell damage and tissue destruction. Late-phase reaction sets in 2 to 24 hours later and may last for several days.

Image: Sequence of events in immediate(type 1) hypersensitivity

Pearl PF0858: Disorders Caused by Immediate Hypersensitivity

Clinical Syndrome

Clinical and Pathologic Manifestations

Anaphylaxis (may be caused by drugs, bee sting, food)

Fall in blood pressure (shock) caused by vascular dilation; airway obstruction due to laryngeal edema

Bronchial asthma

Airway obstruction caused by bronchial smooth muscle hyperactivity; inflammation and tissue injury caused by late-phase reaction

Allergic rhinitis, sinusitis (hay fever)

Increased mucus secretion; inflammation of upper airways, sinuses

Food allergies

Increased peristalsis due to contraction of intestinal muscles

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A man is brought to the emergency department after falling from a height with his hand outstretched. X-ray shows a clavicular fracture. Which part of the clavicle is most likely to be fractured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Junction of medial 2/3rd and lateral 1/3rd

The junction of medial 2/3rd and lateral 1/3rd (middle third) of the clavicle is most likely to be fractured.

The middle third of the clavicle is the narrowest and has the least amount of surrounding soft tissue structures. Therefore, most fractures (~80%) are seen in the middle third.

Fall on the shoulder (direct impact) and fall on the outstretched hand are the most common causes of clavicle fracture.

The patient will be presented with the flexed elbow as the arm will be held to the chest to prevent movement. It is divided into three based on the location of the fractures:

* Group I – middle-third fractures

* Group II – lateral-third fractures

* Group III – medial-third fractures
questions.learning: Junction of medial 2/3rd and lateral 1/3rd — The junction of medial 2/3rd and lateral 1/3rd (middle third) of the clavicle is most likely to be fractured.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient with a humerus fracture is scheduled for orthopaedic surgery. Regional anaesthesia is planned, and a brachial plexus block is performed. Through which approach is the brachial plexus most commonly accessed for this procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Supraclavicular

The supraclavicular approach to the brachial plexus provides the most complete and reliable anesthesia of the upper limb below the shoulder. Because the plexus is densely packed at the level of the trunks/divisions, it is commonly used for orthopedic procedures involving the humerus, elbow, forearm, and hand.

The patient requires orthopedic surgery for a humerus fracture. A supraclavicular brachial plexus block offers:

• Rapid onset
• Dense sensory and motor blockade
• Excellent anesthesia for surgery involving the upper extremity below the shoulder

Why not the other options?

• B. Infraclavicular: Primarily blocks the cords; useful for elbow, forearm, and hand surgery but less commonly used for proximal humeral procedures.
• C. Interscalene: Best for shoulder and proximal humerus surgery, but often spares the ulnar nerve (C8–T1) and is not ideal for surgery involving the distal upper limb.
• D. Axillary: Suitable for forearm and hand surgery; does not reliably anesthetize the musculocutaneous nerve unless blocked separately and is inadequate for humeral fractures.
questions.learning: Supraclavicular — The supraclavicular approach to the brachial plexus provides the most complete and reliable anesthesia of the upper limb below the shoulder.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which is the first organ to putrefy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Brain

Among the given options, the first organ to putrefy is the brain.

The order of organ putrefaction (from first to last):

1. Larynx and trachea
2. Stomach, intestine, spleen
3. Liver and lungs
4. Brain
5. Heart
6. Kidney and the bladder
7. Prostate and uterus
8. Skin, muscle, tendons
9. Bones
questions.learning: Brain Among the given options, the first organ to putrefy is the brain. The order of organ putrefaction (from first to last): 1.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a village, it is observed that several farmers have crossed gait and use a stick for support to stand up and walk. Due to poor yield from farms, they consume meals containing rice and pulses only. Supplementing their diet with which of the following vitamins could have prevented this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vitamin C

The clinical picture describes lathyrism, seen in famine-affected villages where people consume Kesari dal (Lathyrus sativus) along with rice. The neurotoxin β-ODAP causes spastic paraparesis with scissoring (crossed) gait, forcing patients to use a stick for walking. Vitamin C supplementation reduces the neurotoxicity of the toxin and helps prevent lathyrism.
questions.learning: Vitamin C — The clinical picture describes lathyrism, seen in famine-affected villages where people consume Kesari dal (Lathyrus sativus) along with rice.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is part of the complete syndrome triad associated with Anterior Choroidal Artery Syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Contralateral hemisensory loss

Anterior choroidal artery syndrome classically presents with a triad due to infarction of structures supplied by the anterior choroidal artery, a branch of the internal carotid artery.

Classic triad:

1. Contralateral hemiplegia → due to involvement of the posterior limb of internal capsule (corticospinal tract).
2. Contralateral hemisensory loss → due to involvement of thalamocortical sensory fibers.
3. Contralateral homonymous hemianopia → due to damage to the optic tract or lateral geniculate body.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Bilateral hemiplegia: Not typical; the deficit is contralateral and unilateral.

C. Bitemporal hemianopia: Occurs with optic chiasm lesions (e.g., pituitary tumors).

D. Ipsilateral homonymous hemianopia: Visual field loss is contralateral to the lesion.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is given to prevent neural tube defects in pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Folic Acid

Folic acid (Vitamin B9) is given to prevent the incidence of neural tube defects.

Folic acid deficiency is implicated in neural tube defects like spina bifida, encephalocele, and anencephaly.

* Supplementation of folic acid, in doses of 400 μg/day, prior to conception has been shown to cause a significant reduction in the incidence of spina bifida and other neural tube defects.

* Reduced activity of the enzyme 5,10-methylene-THF reductase (MTHFR) caused by a common C677T polymorphism in the MTHFR gene is one of the causes of Neural tube defects in Folate deficiency.

As per the Anemia Mukt Bharat Program, during the period of pre-conception up to the first trimester, women are advised to have 400 mcg of folic acid tablets daily to reduce the incidence of neural tube defects in the fetus.

Note that, non-pregnant, non-lactating women of reproductive age (20–49 years) who are not actively planning a pregnancy in the near term should receive 1 iron and folic acid tablet containing 60 mg elemental iron + 500 mcg folic acid.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is a mitochondrial matrix enzyme?
questions.explanation: The mitochondrial matrix is the site for several major metabolic pathways, including the TCA (Krebs) cycle and beta-oxidation. Citrate synthase is a key TCA cycle enzyme located within the matrix that catalyzes the condensation of oxaloacetate and acetyl-CoA to form citrate. Monoamine oxidase (Option B) is an enzyme located on the outer mitochondrial membrane. ATP synthase (Option C) is a complex structure embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane, although its catalytic head projects into the matrix. Catalase (Option D) is primarily located in peroxisomes, where it breaks down hydrogen peroxide, not the mitochondria. Other matrix enzymes include pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and those of the urea cycle (CPS-I and ornithine transcarbamoylase). Sub-cellular localization of enzymes is essential for coordinating metabolic flux; the matrix provides the concentrated environment necessary for the efficient cycling of the TCA pathway and the generation of reduced electron carriers for the electron transport chain

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with complications after undergoing an illegal attempt to terminate her pregnancy. Which of the following methods used for inducing abortion is considered abnormal and unlawful?
questions.explanation: Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act in India, abortion must be performed by a registered medical practitioner using approved medical or surgical methods. Standard, legal methods include pharmacological agents like Mifepristone (Option B) and surgical procedures such as vacuum aspiration (Option D) or dilatation and curettage (Option A). An abortion stick (Option C) is a traditional, highly dangerous, and unlawful method used by unauthorized persons ("quacks"). It involves inserting a wooden or bamboo stick coated with an irritant paste (like marking nut or arsenic) into the cervix to induce uterine contractions or local necrosis. This method is "abnormal" as it carries an extreme risk of sepsis, uterine perforation, and death. Therefore, because it is an improvised, non-medical device specifically associated with criminal abortion, the abortion stick is the correct answer
questions.learning: Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act in India, abortion must be performed by a registered medical practitioner using approved medical or surgical methods.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with a linear, branching corneal ulcer as shown in the image, decreased corneal sensation, along with loss of corneal sensation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Viral Keratitis

Herpes simplex viral keratitis presents with a dendritic (branching) corneal ulcer and reduced corneal sensation.

• Linear, branching ulcer with terminal bulbs (seen on fluorescein staining)
• Decreased corneal sensation (important clue)
• Pain, redness, photophobia

Pathophysiology:

• HSV infects corneal epithelium → dendritic epithelial ulcer

Why not others:

• Pseudomonas → rapidly progressive suppurative ulcer
• Acanthamoeba → severe pain, ring infiltrate
• Fungal → feathery margins, satellite lesions

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 68-year-old patient with a known history of lung cancer presents with progressively worsening shortness of breath. On physical examination, bronchial breath sounds and a dull note on percussion are detected in the left infrascapular area. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s history of lung cancer and increasing dyspnea suggests a common complication like fluid accumulation. The clinical findings of a dull percussion note and bronchial breathing (which occurs just above the fluid level) in the left base are hallmark signs of a Pleural Effusion. The provided chest X-ray provides definitive radiological confirmation, showing a homogenous opacification of the left lung base with a classic meniscus sign (concave upper border). Cardiac tamponade (Option A) and pericarditis (Option B) would present with heart-specific signs like muffled sounds and JVP changes. Pulmonary embolism (Option C) typically presents with a normal chest X-ray or non-specific wedge shadows. Therefore, given the specific combination of lung malignancy, pathognomonic physical signs, and clear radiographic meniscus, a left-sided pleural effusion is the definitive diagnosis

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 68-year-old woman is diagnosed with a diabetic cataract that has developed over the past three months. Which substance is responsible for the formation of this type of cataract?
questions.explanation: The pathophysiology of diabetic cataracts is primarily linked to the polyol pathway. In a state of chronic hyperglycemia, the enzyme aldose reductase becomes active in the crystalline lens. This enzyme converts excess intracellular glucose into sorbitol. Because sorbitol is a sugar alcohol that does not easily diffuse out of the lens cells and is only slowly metabolized by sorbitol dehydrogenase into fructose, it accumulates significantly. This accumulation creates a high osmotic gradient, drawing water into the lens fibers, leading to swelling, hydropic degeneration, and eventually permanent lenticular opacification. While glucose (Option A) is the starting substrate and fructose (Option B) is the final product, it is the combination of the osmotic effect of sorbitol and its subsequent conversion to fructose that drives the structural damage. Lactose (Option C) is relevant to galactosemic cataracts but not diabetic ones. Therefore, the accumulation of sorbitol and fructose is the critical metabolic event leading to the rapid development of cataracts in patients with poorly controlled diabetes
questions.learning: The pathophysiology of diabetic cataracts is primarily linked to the polyol pathway. In a state of chronic hyperglycemia, the enzyme aldose reductase becomes active in the crystalline lens.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which receptor contributes to static 2 point discrimination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Merkel cell

Merkel cell contributes to static 2 point discrimination.

Merkel cells are responsible for static two-point discrimination. These cells are specialized for detecting pressure and texture and are involved in the detection of fine touch. They provide information about the spatial resolution of tactile stimuli, which is essential for static two-point discrimination, where the ability to differentiate between two distinct points of touch is tested.

Merkel cells are expanded dendritic endings in the epidermis of glabrous (non-hairy) skin. They respond to sustained pressure and touch. They are slowly adapting receptors.

Static vs. Dynamic Two-Point Discrimination
Static: Measures the ability to distinguish stationary points; mediated by Merkel cells (slow-adapting receptors).
Dynamic: Measures the ability to distinguish moving points; mediated by Meissner corpuscles (fast-adapting receptors).

Other options:

Option B: Meissner corpuscle: Meissner corpuscles are dendrites encapsulated in the connective tissue beneath the epidermis of glabrous (non-hairy) skin. They respond to tap and flutter (low-frequency vibration - 5-40Hz). They are rapidly adapting receptors.

Option C: Pacinian corpuscle: Pacinian corpuscles are the largest cutaneous mechanoreceptor. They are present in the dermis of glabrous (non-hairy) and hairy skin. A Pacinian corpuscle consists of a nerve ending encapsulated by concentric layers of connective tissue, giving it an onion-like appearance. They respond to fast vibration (60-500Hz) and deep pressure. They are rapidly adapting receptors.
questions.learning: Merkel cell Merkel cell contributes to static 2 point discrimination. Merkel cells are responsible for static two-point discrimination.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presents with a linear depressed lesion over the forehead extending into the scalp, associated with localized alopecia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. En coup de sabre

En coup de sabre is a form of linear localized scleroderma (linear morphea) characterized by a linear, depressed, scar-like lesion on the forehead or scalp, often associated with scarring alopecia.

The patient has:

• Linear depressed forehead lesion
• Extension into the scalp
• Localized alopecia

These findings are classic for En coup de sabre.

Why not the other options?

• A. Linear lichen planus: Violaceous, pruritic papules; does not produce depressed scar-like lesions.
• C. Alopecia areata: Non-scarring alopecia without skin atrophy.
• D. DLE: Causes scarring alopecia but presents with erythematous discoid plaques, not a linear scar.
questions.learning: En coup de sabre En coup de sabre is a form of linear localized scleroderma (linear morphea) characterized by a linear, depressed, scar-like lesion on the forehead or scalp, often associated with scarring alopecia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In a triage setting, which of the following categories requires the highest priority intervention?
questions.explanation: In disaster medicine and emergency departments, triage is used to prioritize patients based on the severity of their condition. The Red category (Priority I) is reserved for patients with life-threatening injuries who have a high chance of survival if given immediate intervention. Examples include tension pneumothorax or major airway obstruction. The Yellow category (Priority II) includes patients with serious but not immediately life-threatening injuries who can wait for a few hours (e.g., stable large fractures). The Green category (Option C, Priority III) includes the "walking wounded" with minor injuries. The Black category (Option D, Priority 0) is for those who are already deceased or have injuries so catastrophic that survival is unlikely even with care. Therefore, "Red" always receives the absolute highest priority. Efficient triage is essential to maximize the number of lives saved when medical resources are limited during a mass casualty incident

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is occipitomental view with open mouth also known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Water's view

Occipitomental view is called Water's view. Water's view with an open mouth is known as Pierre's view. Among the given options, Water's view is the best answer.

In Water's view, the patient’s head is positioned such that the nose and the chin touch the film while the X-rays are projected from backward. The mouth is usually kept open, which allows visualizing the sphenoid sinus.

Structures seen in Water’s view are:

• Maxillary sinuses (seen best)
• Frontal sinuses
• Sphenoid sinus (if the film is taken with an open mouth)
• Zygoma
• Zygomatic arch
• Nasal bone
• Frontal process of the maxilla
• Superior orbital fissure
• Infratemporal fossa

Other options:

Option B: Towne's view is an angled anteroposterior radiograph of the skull. Structures seen are the petrous part of the pyramids, arcuate eminence, superior semicircular canal, mastoid antrum, internal auditory canal, tympanic cavity, cochlea, and external auditory canal. This view is taken for acoustic neuroma and apical petrositis.

Option C: Law's view is a lateral oblique X-ray view of the mastoid. Structures seen are the external auditory canal, mastoid air cells, tegmen, lateral sinus plate, and temporomandibular joint.

Option D: Stenver's view is an X-ray view of the skull where the long axis of the petrous bone is parallel to the film. Structures seen are the entire petrous pyramid, arcuate eminence, internal auditory meatus, labyrinth with its vestibule, cochlea, and mastoid antrum.
questions.learning: Water's view Occipitomental view is called Water's view. Water's view with an open mouth is known as Pierre's view.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which nerve innervates the muscle responsible for the movement shown below?
questions.explanation: The image depicts a person shrugging their shoulders, an action primarily performed by the trapezius muscle. The spinal accessory nerve (Cranial Nerve XI) provides motor innervation to the trapezius and the sternocleidomastoid muscles. Shrugging tests the upper fibers of the trapezius. The long thoracic nerve (Option B) supplies the serratus anterior muscle; damage to this nerve leads to "winging of the scapula". The axillary nerve (Option C) supplies the deltoid and teres minor muscles. The radial nerve (Option D) innervates the triceps brachii and the extensor muscles of the forearm. Clinically, injury to the spinal accessory nerve—often occurring during neck surgeries like lymph node biopsies—leads to shoulder droop and the inability to shrug the shoulder on the affected side. Patients may also experience difficulty in rotating their head to the opposite side due to involvement of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Precise anatomical knowledge of this nerve is essential for both neurologists and surgeons
questions.learning: The image depicts a person shrugging their shoulders, an action primarily performed by the trapezius muscle. The spinal accessory nerve (Cranial Nerve XI) provides motor innervation to the trapezius and the sternocleidomastoid muscles.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 36-year-old woman presents with bleeding per rectum that coincides with her menstrual cycles. On per rectal examination, a nodule is palpated anteriorly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endometriosis

Deep infiltrating endometriosis (DIE) should be suspected in women with cyclical bleeding per rectum, dyschezia, or painful defecation during menstruation. A tender nodule on the anterior rectal wall on per rectal examination is characteristic of rectovaginal septum or bowel endometriosis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Colorectal cancer: Causes persistent, non-cyclical rectal bleeding, often associated with weight loss or altered bowel habits.
• C. Hemorrhoids: Cause painless bright red bleeding during defecation and are not related to the menstrual cycle.
• D. Inflammatory bowel disease: Produces chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, and rectal bleeding independent of menstruation.
questions.learning: Endometriosis Deep infiltrating endometriosis (DIE) should be suspected in women with cyclical bleeding per rectum, dyschezia, or painful defecation during menstruation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An adult man presents to the outpatient department with painful scrotal swelling and fever. The swelling involves the tunica vaginalis and is associated with fluid accumulation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A hydrocele is defined as an abnormal collection of serous fluid within the layers of the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis. While often painless, an acute or infected hydrocele (pyocele) can present with pain and fever. The characteristic "fluid accumulation" within the tunica vaginalis is the hallmark of this condition. A varicocele (Option A) involves the dilation of the pampiniform plexus of veins, often described as a "bag of worms," and does not typically involve fluid accumulation in the tunica. A cystocele (Option B) is the herniation of the bladder into the vagina, which is anatomically impossible in this male patient. Torsion of the testis (Option D) is a surgical emergency presenting with sudden, severe pain and a high-riding testis, but it is primarily a vascular compromise rather than a fluid collection in the tunica vaginalis. Given the specific description of fluid within the tunica vaginalis, hydrocele is the most accurate diagnosis
questions.learning: A hydrocele is defined as an abnormal collection of serous fluid within the layers of the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis. While often painless, an acute or infected hydrocele (pyocele) can present with pain and fever.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old female presents with headache, fever, and nuchal rigidity. Lumbar puncture was done, and CSF analysis shows abundant lymphocytes with normal glucose and elevated proteins. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Viral meningitis

The given clinical picture of headache, fever, and nuchal rigidity, and CSF examination findings of abundant lymphocytes with normal sugar and elevated proteins are suggestive of viral meningitis.

The CSF findings in viral meningitis are usually pleocytosis, normal or mildly elevated protein (20-80 mg/dL), normal glucose levels, and slightly elevated opening pressure. The total CSF cell count usually ranges from 25 to 500 cells/microliter, predominantly lymphocytes.

The classic clinical triad of fever, headache, and neck rigidity is suggestive of meningitis. Other common complaints are nausea, vomiting, and photophobia. Nuchal rigidity (“stiff neck”) is the pathognomonic sign of meningitis. Hip and knee flexion on passive flexion of the neck is called Brudzinsky's sign. Raised intracranial pressure (ICP) is a complication that presents as papilledema, disorientation, or dilated, poorly reactive pupils.

Other options:

Option A: In bacterial meningitis, classic CSF abnormalities include polymorphonuclear (PMN) leukocytosis (>100 cells/μL in 90% of cases), decreased glucose concentration (<40 mg/dL), elevated protein concentration (>45 mg/dL in 90%), and increased opening pressure (>180 mmH₂O in 90%). Additionally, CSF bacterial cultures are positive in >70% of patients, and Gram stain identifies organisms in >60% of cases.

Option B: The characteristic CSF abnormalities in fungal meningitis are a mononuclear or lymphocytic pleocytosis, an increased protein concentration, and a decreased glucose concentration.

Option C: The classic CSF abnormalities in tuberculous meningitis are elevated opening pressure, lymphocytic pleocytosis (10–500 cells/μL), elevated protein concentration in the range of 100–500 mg/dl, and decreased glucose concentration in the range of 20–40 mg/dL.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a rapidly progressing, edged-out ulcer on the lateral aspect of the nasal fold, below the eye. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Squamous Cell Carcinoma

The clinical description of a rapidly progressing, edged-out ulcer on a sun-exposed site like the lateral nasal fold is characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma(SCC).

SCC is a malignant tumour of keratinising cells of the epidermis or its appendages. It arises from the stratum basalis of the epidermis and is the second most common skin cancer. The primary risk factor and driving force for the development of this common cancer is UV exposure. Variants of SCC include, Bowen's disease and Erythroplasia of Queyrat.

It initially presents as smooth nodular, verrucous, papillomatous lesions. All these lesions later ulcerate and have a characteristic everted edge and are surrounded by inflamed, indurated skin. When a SCC appears in a scar it is known as a Marjolin’s ulcer.

Surgical excision is the treatment of choice SCC. It provides both histological confirmation and complete clearance. The excision margins depend on tumor size:

* lesions <2 cm require a 4-mm margin,

* while those >2 cm need a 1-cm margin.

Other options:

Option B: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is a slow-growing, locally invasive malignant tumor that originates from pluripotential epithelial cells of the basal epidermis and hair follicles, typically involving pilosebaceous skin.

Option C: Malignant Melanoma is a malignancy of melanocytes and may develop in the skin, mucous membranes, retina, or leptomeninges. There are four common macroscopic variants of malignant melanoma. It doesn’t present as an edged-out ulcer.

Option D: Keratoacanthoma presents with a reddish papule with a horny crust in the centre. It is a rapidly evolving tumour of the skin considered as a well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.
questions.learning: Squamous Cell Carcinoma — The clinical description of a rapidly progressing, edged-out ulcer on a sun-exposed site like the lateral nasal fold is characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma(SCC).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the line depicted in the image given below?
questions.explanation: The image shows a dark, vertical hyperpigmented line extending along the midline of the pregnant abdomen. This is the Linea Nigra, a common physiological skin change during pregnancy caused by increased melanocyte-stimulating hormone. It usually develops from the pre-existing, faint "linea alba" (Option C), which is the fibrous structure where the abdominal muscle aponeuroses meet. Striae gravidarum (Option A), or stretch marks, appear as reddish or purplish linear streaks, typically found on the lower abdomen, breasts, or thighs, rather than a single midline dark line. Chloasma (Option B), also known as the "mask of pregnancy," refers to blotchy, brownish hyperpigmentation specifically on the face. The Linea Nigra is completely benign and typically fades several months after delivery as hormone levels return to baseline. Identification of this classic sign is a routine part of the obstetric physical examination
questions.learning: The image shows a dark, vertical hyperpigmented line extending along the midline of the pregnant abdomen. This is the Linea Nigra, a common physiological skin change during pregnancy caused by increased melanocyte-stimulating hormone.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the statistical term for the value that occurs most frequently in a dataset?
questions.explanation: The mode is the measure of central tendency defined as the value that occurs with the highest frequency in a given data set. In a clinical setting, if "headache" is the most common symptom recorded among 100 patients, it represents the modal symptom. The median (Option A) is the middle value when the data is arranged in order. Standard deviation (Option C) is a measure of the dispersion or spread of data around the mean. The mean (Option D) is the arithmetic average of all values. The mode is particularly useful for categorical data or when identifying the "most typical" case in a distribution. Unlike the mean, the mode is not affected by extreme outliers, making it a robust measure for certain types of health statistics. Therefore, for the specific purpose of identifying the most frequent observation in patient records, the mode is the correct statistical term
questions.learning: The mode is the measure of central tendency defined as the value that occurs with the highest frequency in a given data set. In a clinical setting, if "headache" is the most common symptom recorded among 100 patients, it represents the modal symptom.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient presents with contralateral weakness of the arm and leg, along with ipsilateral facial weakness. The NCCT brain shows evidence of intracerebral hemorrhage. What is the most likely location of the bleed? NCCT-Non contrast CT
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pons

The clinical presentation of contralateral weakness of the arm and leg and ipsilateral facial weakness along with intracerebral hemorrhage in NCCT is a typical of a lesion in the pons.

Brainstem syndromes cause crossed hemiplegia with ipsilateral cranial nerve palsies and contralateral hemiplegia. Pontine syndromes occur due to the involvement of pontine branches of the basilar artery and anterior inferior cerebellar artery. They are

CNS lesion
Effects

Foville’s Syndrome/ Dorsal pontine syndrome

• Lateral gaze palsy
• Ipsilateral facial nerve palsy
• Contralateral hemiparesis

Millard–Gubler Syndrome/Ventral pontine syndrome

• Ipsilateral abducens nerve weakness
• Ipsilateral facial nerve palsy
• Contralateral hemiplegia

In Foville's syndrome, there is a dorsal pontine injury (lesion in the abducens nucleus) that causes lateral/ horizontal gaze palsy. In Millard-Gubler syndrome, there is a ventral pontine injury (lesion in the abducens fascicle) that causes lateral rectus weakness.

Locked-in syndrome occurs when a pontine stroke causes quadriplegia and paralysis of all voluntary muscles except vertical movements of the eyes and blinking. The vertical gaze nucleus, the rostral interstitial nucleus of medial longitudinal fasciculus, is located in the midbrain and is hence preserved.

Other options:

Option A: Basal ganglia → causes contralateral hemiplegia but does not cause ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy.
Option B: Midbrain → may cause oculomotor (III) palsy + contralateral weakness (Weber syndrome), but not isolated facial weakness.
Option C: Medulla → classically causes crossed findings (CN IX, X, XII) but not facial nerve involvement.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Universal health coverage (UHC) means that all people and communities receive the quality health services they need, without financial hardship. Which of the following are the challenges to implementing UHC?
options: Inequalities in the distribution, adequate support, and access to quality-assured products only in low-income settings
The purpose of UHC is to find a balance between countries' income, health provision, and financial burden
To provide healthcare to everyone regardless of the country's income
UHC only deals with the financial aspect of health and cannot cover health provisions for all
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. To provide healthcare to everyone regardless of the country's income

Providing healthcare to everyone, regardless of the country's income, is one of the challenges to implementing Universal Health Coverage. A challenge related to this is mobilising sufficient resources in low-income countries to provide equitable care.

UHC aims at ensuring that all people have access to quality health services without suffering financial hardship.

Components:

• Equity in access: Everyone receives the healthcare they need.
• Quality of services: Delivered in a manner that improves health outcomes.
• Financial protection: Avoiding financial hardship for those accessing services.

Challenges:

• Health inequities.
• Resource constraints in low- and middle-income countries.
• Balancing financial protection and service delivery.

Strategies to Achieve UHC:

• Strengthening health systems.
• Universal health insurance.
• Public-private partnerships.

Other options

Option A: Inequalities in the distribution, adequate support, and access to quality-assured products are a challenge, but they occur across income settings, not only in low-income ones.

Option B: The purpose of UHC to find a balance between countries’ income, health provision, and financial burden describes a goal of UHC and not a challenge.

Option D: UHC encompasses both financial protection and access to quality health services.
questions.learning: To provide healthcare to everyone regardless of the country's income Providing healthcare to everyone, regardless of the country's income, is one of the challenges to implementing Universal Health Coverage.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
The following are the disease frequencies in a population. Based on the number of cases which of the following is the correct match?

Disease 1: Number of cases last week 42 this week 43
Disease 2: Number of cases last week 2 and present week 42
Disease 3: Number of cases last week 6 and present week 1
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Endemic, epidemic, sporadic

Disease 1- the cases have been almost the same so it has to be endemic.
Disease 2- there is an alarming increase in the number of cases. It has to be an epidemic.
Disease 3- the number of cases has decreased without any explanation so it has to be sporadic.

Epidemic refers to the occurrence of a disease in excess of expected frequency.

A pandemic is an epidemic affecting a large population over a large geographical area crossing international boundaries.

An endemic disease is a regularly occurring disease in a population in expected frequency without any importation from outside.

Sporadic diseases present as scattered cases of infection without relation temporally/spatially.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with ulcerative colitis is experiencing three episodes of bleeding in stools per day but is otherwise stable. What is the appropriate treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 5-Aminosalicylic acid

Mild ulcerative colitis with limited bleeding and stable vitals is treated with 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) as first-line therapy. It acts locally to reduce mucosal inflammation and induces remission. Steroids and immunomodulators are reserved for moderate–severe or refractory disease. 5-ASA is standard initial treatment in mild UC. Mechanism of Action-

Inhibits:

• Cyclooxygenase (COX)
• ↓ Prostaglandins

Reduces local inflammation in colon

| Severity | Clinical features | Treatment

| -------- | ----------------- | ---------

| Mild–moderate | ≤4–6 stools/day, minimal systemic signs | 5-ASA ✔

| Moderate–severe | Frequent stools + systemic symptoms | Steroids

| Severe | Toxic megacolon risk | IV steroids / biologics
questions.learning: 5-Aminosalicylic acid Mild ulcerative colitis with limited bleeding and stable vitals is treated with 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) as first-line therapy.

Correct answer: B. Penile urethral stricture

The given image shows retrograde cystourethrogram with findings consistent with penile urethral stricture.

The male urethra can be visualized by retrograde urethrography (RGU) or voiding cystourethrogram (VCU), also known as micturating cystourethrogram (MCU).

In RGU, the urethra is visualized with the instillation of contrast into the anterior urethra (penile urethra and bulbar urethra). It is helpful for diagnosing anterior urethral abnormalities.

The following image shows an RGU with bulbar urethral stricture:

In VCU, after injecting contrast into the bladder using a Foleys catheter, the posterior urethra (membranous urethra and prostatic urethra) is visualized during micturition. It is helpful for diagnosing posterior urethral abnormalities and bladder abnormalities. It is the investigation of choice for vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) and posterior urethral valve.

questions.text: What is the name of the fracture depicted in the image, resulting from a fall from a significant height?
questions.explanation: The X-ray shows a pelvic fracture with widening of the pubic symphysis, giving the pelvis an appearance similar to an “open book.” This occurs due to anteroposterior compression forces, commonly seen in high-impact trauma such as falls from height or road traffic accidents. In an open book fracture, the pelvic ring is disrupted anteriorly, and the two halves of the pelvis are forced apart. This leads to: 1. 1. Widened pubic symphysis 2. 2. Possible sacroiliac joint disruption 3. 3. Risk of significant internal bleeding The mechanism described in the question (fall from significant height) supports a high-energy injury consistent with this fracture pattern. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Chauffeur fracture : Fracture of radial styloid (wrist), unrelated (C) Malgaigne fracture : Vertical shear injury with displacement, not symmetric opening (D) Bucket handle fracture : Seen in children, involves pelvic ring, different pattern

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A man is found dead in a swimming pool. On autopsy, both the lungs and stomach are filled with water, and there is mucoid froth around the nose and mouth. What is the most likely mode of death in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Wet drowning

Wet drowning is characterized by aspiration of water into the lungs and stomach, along with fine, persistent froth at the mouth and nostrils.

• Water enters airways → lungs fill with fluid → impaired gas exchange → hypoxia
• Swallowing of water → water present in stomach
• Froth formation:

• Due to mixing of air + water + mucus
• Appears as fine, white, persistent (mucoid) froth

Autopsy findings:

• Heavy, waterlogged lungs
• Frothy fluid in airways
• Water in stomach
• May have diatoms in organs (if antemortem drowning)

Why not other options:

• Dry drowning: No water in lungs (laryngospasm)
• Near drowning: Survival after drowning attempt
• Cardiac arrest: No typical drowning features

questions.text: The most common tumor of the lacrimal gland is?

questions.text: Which of the following is not correct regarding Behçet's disease?
options: Pathergy test is a criterion as per the ISG diagnostic criteria
Ulcers are common on the dorsum of the penis
Aphthous ulcers occur similar to Crohn’s disease

Correct answer: B. Ulcers are common on the dorsum of the penis

Behçet’s disease is like a restless storm that targets vessels of all sizes, leaving behind a trail of ulcers, eye inflammation, and systemic mischief.

• Strong association with HLA-B51
• Neutrophil hyperactivity → endothelial damage

| Oral | Recurrent aphthous ulcers (most common)

| Genital | Painful ulcers (scrotum in males)

| Eye | Bilateral uveitis, hypopyon

| Skin | Erythema nodosum, acneiform lesions

| Vessels | Thrombosis, aneurysms

| Test | Pathergy test positive

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old patient presents to the emergency department with acute shortness of breath. His heart rate is 120 beats per minute, and his BP is 80/60 mm Hg. An echocardiogram was done and reveals diastolic collapse of the right ventricle. X-ray was done and is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
options: Initiate diuretic therapy with blood pressure monitoring
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Perform pericardiocentesis

The key clue is: Right ventricular diastolic collapse on echocardiography

This is a classic sign of cardiac tamponade.

Other supporting clues:

| Finding | Significance

| ------- | ------------

| Hypotension | Reduced cardiac output

| Tachycardia | Compensatory response

| Acute dyspnea | Impaired cardiac filling

Diastolic collapse of the right ventricle on echocardiography with hypotension indicates acute cardiac tamponade.

Tamponade causes impaired ventricular filling, leading to obstructive shock.

Echocardiography

Most sensitive test.

Shows:

• Right atrial collapse
• Right ventricular diastolic collapse

Chest X-ray

Large effusion may show: Water-bottle-shaped heart.

The definitive and immediate treatment is pericardiocentesis to relieve pericardial pressure.

A) Diuretics

Would reduce preload, worsening hypotension.

B) Intra-aortic balloon pump

Used for cardiogenic shock, not tamponade.

D) Ventricular assist device

Used in severe heart failure, not acute tamponade.

Diuretics, IABP, or ventricular assist devices do not address the underlying obstruction.
