questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 29-year-old woman presents with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding after 6 weeks of amenorrhea. Transvaginal ultrasonography does not reveal an intrauterine gestational sac or any signs of ectopic pregnancy. Her serum β-hCG level is 1,200 IU/L, which is below the discriminatory zone. What should be the next step in management?
questions.explanation: In a hemodynamically stable patient with a pregnancy of unknown location, the immediate priority is to determine if the pregnancy is viable. The discriminatory zone for visualizing a gestational sac via transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) is typically IU/L. Since this patient’s level is 1,200 IU/L, the absence of an intrauterine sac is not diagnostic of an ectopic pregnancy. The next step is to repeat the serum β-hCG after 48 hours. A normal pregnancy should show a doubling of the level, whereas a plateauing or declining level suggests an ectopic pregnancy or early loss. Laparoscopy (Option A) and Dilatation and curettage (Option D) are invasive and reserved for higher β-hCG levels or clinical instability. Methotrexate (Option B) is only given after an ectopic pregnancy is confirmed. Therefore, expectant monitoring of the β-hCG trend is the appropriate standard of care
questions.learning: In a hemodynamically stable patient with a pregnancy of unknown location, the immediate priority is to determine if the pregnancy is viable. The discriminatory zone for visualizing a gestational sac via transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) is typically IU/L.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A female patient with a known case of thyroid malignancy was found to show high levels of serum calcitonin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Medullary thyroid carcinoma

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC). Histopathology shows the presence of amyloid deposits that are derived from the altered calcitonin molecules.

Medullary thyroid carcinoma is a tumor of parafollicular or C cells of the thyroid gland. They are derived from the neural crest cells of the ultimobranchial bodies.

Most of the MTCs occur sporadically. However, around a quarter of the cancers are associated with familial MTC, MEN2A, and MEN2B.

Patients with sporadic MTC present at an older age, whereas patients with familial MTC usually present at a younger age. Features of MTC include:

* Painful neck mass with cervical lymphadenopathy

* Dysphagia, dysphonia or dyspnea if locally invaded

* Diarrhoea due to increased intestinal motility by serotonin

* Cushingoid habitus due to ectopic ACTH production

* Metastasis is blood-borne

* Microscopically, they consist of sheets of neoplastic cells separated by collagen and amyloid stroma

It is diagnosed by careful family history, physical examination, raised calcitonin, CEA levels, and fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the mass.

Total thyroidectomy with central neck node dissection is the treatment of choice in MTC patients. External beam radiotherapy can be used in patients with unresectable tumors. Targeted therapy can be considered using vandetanib, sorafenib, sunitinib, and cabozantinib.

Prophylactic total thyroidectomy should be considered within 5years of age in MEN2A mutation and within 1year of age in MEN2B mutation.

Surgical management of MTC is as follows:

Extent of cancer
Surgery done

MTC without LN involvement

Total thyroidectomy + Central neck dissection (prophylactic)

MTC + level VI LN involved

Total thyroidectomy + Central neck dissection (therapeutic) + Modified radical neck dissection (prophylactic)

MTC + other LNs involved

Total thyroidectomy + Central neck dissection + Modified radical neck dissection (therapeutic)
questions.learning: Medullary thyroid carcinoma — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC). Histopathology shows the presence of amyloid deposits that are derived from the altered calcitonin molecules.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following can be prescribed in case of an open angle glaucoma with bronchial asthma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Latanoprost

Latanoprost can be given in a case of open-angle glaucoma with bronchial asthma.

Latanoprost is a PGF2α analog and it is not associated with systemic side effects like bronchospasm and hence can be given for asthmatic patients. Prostaglandin analogs are the first choice drugs for open-angle glaucoma.

Mechanism of action: It reduces intraocular pressure by altering the ciliary muscle tension and improving the outflow of the aqueous humor.

Advantages of latanoprost:

• Good efficacy
• Once-daily application
• Absence of systemic side effects

Disadvantage: High cost

Adverse effects:

• Blurring of vision
• Iris pigmentation
• Thickening and darkening of eyelashes
• Macular edema can occur especially in aphakic patients.

Other options:

Option A- Timolol is a non-selective beta-blocker used topically in glaucoma. It is associated with systemic effects by absorption through the nasolacrimal duct and can cause life-threatening bronchospasm in asthmatics and COPD patients. Hence they are not given in in this case.

Option B- Gemeprost is a PGE1 analog used for the termination of early pregnancy.

Option D- Mannitol infusion is given for acute congestive glaucoma and not for open-angle glaucoma. It causes decongestion of the eye by its osmotic action.
questions.learning: Latanoprost Latanoprost can be given in a case of open-angle glaucoma with bronchial asthma. Latanoprost is a PGF2α analog and it is not associated with systemic side effects like bronchospasm and hence can be given for asthmatic patients.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with a large breast lump measuring 9 × 10 cm. Histopathological examination reveals increased stromal cellularity with a characteristic leaf-like architecture. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a large, rapidly growing breast mass in a middle-aged woman is highly suspicious for a Phyllodes tumor. The definitive diagnostic clue provided is the histopathological finding of "increased stromal cellularity" and a "distinctive leaf-like structure" (cleft-like spaces lined by epithelium). The name "Phyllodes" is derived from the Greek word for "leaf-like." Giant fibroadenoma (Option B) can present similarly as a large mass but lacks the leaf-like stromal overgrowth and increased cellularity seen here. Inflammatory carcinoma (Option C) presents with skin changes like peau d'orange and redness rather than a discrete large lump. Ductal carcinoma (Option D) typically appears as a hard, irregular, fixed mass often with nipple changes or nodal involvement. Phyllodes tumors can be benign, borderline, or malignant and are treated with wide local excision with a 1 cm margin to prevent local recurrence

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old male met with an accident and came to the casualty with a contusion on the left precordium. His vitals are BP 120/80 mmHg, RR – 16/min. Normal heart sounds were heard, but decreased breath sounds on the left side, and the trachea deviated to the right. Which of the following is the first line of management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chest tube insertion

The given clinical scenario of trauma, decreased breath sounds, and tracheal deviation with stable vitals are suggestive of a simple pneumothorax. Management involves inserting a chest tube.

Traumatic pneumothorax can be:

• Simple pneumothorax - with hemodynamic stability
• Tension pneumothorax - without hemodynamic stability

Initial management of simple pneumothorax with open sucking wound involves prompt closing of the defect with a sterile occlusive plastic dressing (e.g., Opsite), taped on three sides to act as a flutter-type valve followed by chest tube insertion as soon as possible in a site remote from the injury site.

Other options:

Option A: Features of tension pneumothorax include hypotension, dyspnea, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation, absent or decreased breath sounds, hyper-resonant note on percussion and normal heart sounds. The first line of management is needle thoracocentesis in the 5th intercostal space in the midaxillary line.

Definitive management - insertion of an intercostal tube in the triangle of safety. If a sucking wound is present, then it is covered with gauze pieces and taped on 3 sides.

Option B and D: Pericardial tamponade resembles tension pneumothorax but there is no tracheal deviation, normal breath sounds, normal percussion note and muffled heart sounds. Initial management is by needle pericardiocentesis followed by definitive sternotomy or lateral thoracotomy.

REMEMBER RECENT UPDATE :(Acc to ATLS 10th edition ):

•

• In adults, the needle thoracotomy location changed to the 5th ICS mid-axillary line from the 2nd ICS midclavicular line.
• In the pediatric age group, the thoracotomy location remains at the 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line.
questions.learning: Chest tube insertion — The given clinical scenario of trauma, decreased breath sounds, and tracheal deviation with stable vitals are suggestive of a simple pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 19-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of arthralgia, urethral discharge, and gonococcal infections. Culture of the synovial fluid from the knee grows Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Which of the following investigations is most appropriate to evaluate for an underlying immunodeficiency in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Late complement deficiency (C5-C9)

Recurrent or disseminated Neisseria infections strongly suggest a defect in the membrane attack complex (C5–C9), which is essential for killing Neisseria due to their thin cell wall. Late complement deficiency classically presents with repeated gonococcal or meningococcal infections. Testing for C5–C9 levels or CH50 is therefore the most appropriate investigation.

| Defect / Deficiency | Organism Susceptibility | Mechanism

| ------------------- | ----------------------- | ---------

| C5–C9 (MAC)
(terminal) | Neisseria spp. (especially N. meningitidis) | Failure of complement-mediated lysis

| C3 deficiency | Pyogenic infections (Strep, Staph, H. influenzae) | Impaired opsonization

| C1, C2, C4 (early) deficiency | SLE-like disease | Immune complex deposition

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An 18-year-old male presents with eye pain, photophobia, and redness a few days after a minor injury while climbing a tree. Slit-lamp examination reveals distinct lesions surrounding a central focus of infection. Which diagnosis best explains these findings?
questions.explanation: The history of ocular trauma involving vegetative matter (climbing a tree) followed by a painful corneal infection is a classic clinical clue for fungal keratitis. The hallmark slit-lamp finding described—"distinct lesions surrounding a central infection site"—refers to satellite lesions. These are smaller infiltrates located away from the main primary ulcer, representing the outward spread of fungal hyphae through the corneal stroma. A reverse hypopyon (Option A) refers to emulsified silicone oil in the anterior chamber. A dendritic ulcer (Option B) is pathognomonic for Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) and has a branching tree-like pattern. A ring abscess (Option C) can occur in advanced Pseudomonas or Bacillus keratitis but is not the specific "surrounding lesion" pattern described here. Fungal ulcers are often dry in appearance with feathery margins. Therefore, satellite lesions are the definitive finding confirming a fungal etiology in this patient. Treatment involves topical antifungals like natamycin
questions.learning: The history of ocular trauma involving vegetative matter (climbing a tree) followed by a painful corneal infection is a classic clinical clue for fungal keratitis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 9-year-old boy presents with hematuria, hypertension, and facial puffiness over the past three days, along with a history of a throat infection two weeks earlier. Urine analysis shows albuminuria. Based on this clinical picture and recent infection, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This child presents with the classic nephritic triad: hematuria, hypertension, and facial puffiness, occurring two weeks after a throat infection. This latency period is characteristic of Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN), an immune-mediated complication of a pharyngeal or skin infection. The causative agent is Group A beta-hemolytic streptococci (GABHS), specifically nephritogenic strains. Group B streptococci (Option A) primarily cause neonatal sepsis. Staphylococcus aureus (Option B) is associated with acute endocarditis-related glomerulonephritis but lacks the classic post-throat infection latency. Staphylococcus epidermidis (Option D) is a common commensal often associated with prosthetic valve infections. PSGN results from the deposition of immune complexes in the glomerular basement membrane, leading to low C3 complement levels. Urinalysis characteristically shows RBC casts and "cola-colored" urine. Most children have a favorable prognosis with supportive care focusing on fluid management and blood pressure control. Antibiotics are used to clear the initial streptococcal infection if still present

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Sickness absenteeism of workers in the industry is used to evaluate__________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Health of the worker

Sickness absenteeism of workers in the industry is used to evaluate the health of the workers.

Sickness absenteeism refers to employees' self-reported absence from work due to health problems. The apparent cause for sickness absenteeism may or may not be due to actual sickness. These include

* Economic causes: reporting sick to avail a sick leave with pay

* Social causes: obligations such as weddings, and festivals

* Medical causes: due to occupational accidents

* Non-occupational causes: nutritional disorders, alcoholism and drug addiction.

Absenteeism is an index used in industries to assess the state of health of workers and their physical, mental and social well-being. Interventions to reduce sickness absenteeism should focus on areas, such as periodic medical checkups, monitoring work schedules, improving employees’ job satisfaction, and reducing workplace stress.
questions.learning: Health of the worker Sickness absenteeism of workers in the industry is used to evaluate the health of the workers. Sickness absenteeism refers to employees' self-reported absence from work due to health problems.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Identify the given condition and its treatment.
options: Staphylococcal scalded syndrome with Inj cephalexin
questions.explanation: The clinical image demonstrates widespread erythema and superficial desquamation, which is the hallmark of Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS). SSSS is caused by an exfoliative toxin produced by Staphylococcus aureus, which causes the top layer of the epidermis to detach, creating a "scalded" appearance. Treatment requires intravenous (IV) antistaphylococcal antibiotics to target the systemic bacterial cause, alongside supportive care similar to burn management. Epidermolysis bullosa (Option B) is a genetic disorder of skin fragility rather than an infection. Impetigo bullosa (Option C) is a localized form of staphylococcal infection presenting with large blisters but not widespread peeling. Erythema multiforme (Option D) is a hypersensitivity reaction characterized by "target lesions". Therefore, given the extensive peeling and pediatric presentation, SSSS treated with appropriate antibiotics is the correct diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical image demonstrates widespread erythema and superficial desquamation, which is the hallmark of Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: New Inability to recognize familiar faces is known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prosopagnosia

Prosopagnosia is the inability to recognize familiar faces

In humans, storage and recognition of faces is more strongly represented in the right inferior temporal lobe in right-handed individuals, though the left lobe is also active. Damage to this area can cause prosopagnosia, the inability to recognize faces.

Patients with this abnormality can recognize forms and reproduce them. They can recognize people by their voices, and many of them show autonomic responses when they see familiar as opposed to unfamiliar faces. However, they cannot identify the familiar faces they see. The left hemisphere is also involved, but the role of the right hemisphere is primary.

Other options:

Option A: Autotopagnosia -  inability to recognize or to orient any part of one's own body

Option C: Somatognosia - inability to identify any part of the body, either one’s own or another’s body

Option D: Tactile agnosia (aka stereognosia) -  inability to recognize objects by touch, in the presence of intact cutaneous and proprioceptive hand sensation; caused by a lesion in the contralateral parietal lobe

Pearl PF1351: CNS deficits and site of lesions

Term
Defnition
Site of lesion

Agnosia
Inability to accurately perceive objects through normally functioning sensory mechanisms
Posterior parietal cortex

Dyslexia

(word blindness)

Inability to interpret their meanings

(the person may be able to see words and even know that they are words but not be able to interpret their meanings)

Angular gyrus

Aphasia
inability to produce and/or understand language

All components of the language network are interconnected with each other and with

surrounding parts of the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes. Damage

to this network gives rise to language impairments resulting in aphasia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy is brought with a history of recurrent bacterial and fungal infections, mainly affecting the skin and respiratory system. He has experienced repeated episodes of abscess formation and lymphadenitis. An abnormal dihydrorhodamine (DHR) test is noted. Based on these findings, what is the most likely underlying condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical picture of recurrent infections by catalase-positive organisms (like Staphylococcus aureus or Aspergillus), multiple skin abscesses, and lymphadenitis in a young boy is highly suspicious for Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD). CGD is an immunodeficiency caused by defects in the NADPH oxidase complex, which prevents neutrophils from producing a "respiratory burst" (superoxide) to kill ingested pathogens. The Dihydrorhodamine (DHR) test is the modern gold standard for diagnosis; an abnormal pattern indicates that the cells cannot oxidize the DHR dye into a fluorescent form. Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID, Option B) presents earlier with failure to thrive and viral/protozoal infections. Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency (LAD, Option D) presents with delayed umbilical cord separation and "pus-less" infections, related to a defect in integrins or Sialyl Lewis X (Option C). CGD is usually X-linked. Prophylaxis with antibiotics and interferon-gamma can improve survival, while bone marrow transplant is curative
questions.learning: The clinical picture of recurrent infections by catalase-positive organisms (like Staphylococcus aureus or Aspergillus), multiple skin abscesses, and lymphadenitis in a young boy is highly suspicious for Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 45-year-old school teacher presents with hoarseness of voice and vocal fatigue. A flexible laryngoscopic examination is performed, and the image is shown below. Based on the laryngoscopic findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A 45-year-old teacher presenting with progressive hoarseness and voice fatigue suggests a chronic laryngeal condition. The key diagnostic clue comes from the laryngoscopic image, which shows irregular, white, thickened patches on the vocal cords. These findings are characteristic of keratosis of the larynx (laryngeal leukoplakia). Keratosis larynx is a precancerous condition caused by chronic irritation, such as prolonged voice use (common in teachers), smoking, or exposure to irritants. The lesions appear as white, hyperkeratotic plaques, which are typically irregular and patchy, unlike smooth or symmetrical lesions seen in other conditions. Why other options are incorrect: 1. Vocal nodules → Bilateral, symmetrical lesions at specific junctions 2. Reinke’s edema → Diffuse, bilateral swelling, often in smokers 3. Vocal polyp → Usually unilateral, smooth, and vascular
questions.learning: A 45-year-old teacher presenting with progressive hoarseness and voice fatigue suggests a chronic laryngeal condition. The key diagnostic clue comes from the laryngoscopic image, which shows irregular, white, thickened patches on the vocal cords.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 50-year-old man with a history of construction work presents with progressive shortness of breath and a chronic cough. High-resolution CT (HRCT) of the chest shows nodular opacities with a ground-glass appearance. Which condition is most likely associated with these radiological findings?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of a construction worker presenting with progressive dyspnea and cough suggests an occupational lung disease. On HRCT, the finding of multiple small, discrete nodular opacities—which may show a ground-glass appearance in early stages—is highly characteristic of Silicosis. These nodules typically predominate in the upper lobes and may eventually coalesce into large masses (Progressive Massive Fibrosis). Asbestosis (Option A) primarily involves the lower lobes and is characterized by pleural plaques and a pattern of interstitial fibrosis rather than discrete nodules. Anthracosis (Option C) refers to coal worker's pneumoconiosis, which has similar nodular patterns but a different occupational exposure. Bagassosis (Option D) is a hypersensitivity pneumonitis caused by moldy sugarcane dust and typically shows ill-defined centrilobular nodules rather than the distinct nodular fibrotic pattern of silicosis. Therefore, given the construction history and the HRCT nodularity, silicosis is the most likely diagnosis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are used to stop esophageal variceal bleed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A, B, C and D

All the given options can be used to stop esophageal variceal bleeding.

Image A shows the Sengstaken-Blakemore tube. It has 3 lumens - one aspiration port and 2 inflation balloons. They are:

• Gastric aspiration port
• Gastric balloon port
• Esophageal balloon port

The gastric balloon is inflated and tension is applied to the gastroesophageal junction. If this does not control the haemorrhage, the esophageal balloon is inflated as well, compressing the venous plexus between them. Only gastric contents can be aspirated.

Image B shows the Minnesota tube. It has 4 openings - 2 inflation tubes and 2 suction tubes i.e. both gastric and oesophageal aspiration ports are present, which allows the aspiration of both gastric and esophageal contents.

Images C and D both show an upper GI endoscope. They are used to identify the source of bleeding and once identified, sclerotherapy and endoscopic variceal banding are performed, which have been shown to control hemorrhage effectively.

Banding has a lower rate of complications. If bleeding does not stop by banding/sclerotherapy, balloon tamponade should be tried.

The protocol for the management of esophageal varices is given below.
questions.learning: A, B, C and D All the given options can be used to stop esophageal variceal bleeding. Image A shows the Sengstaken-Blakemore tube.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In a patient with lipoprotein lipase deficiency, which of the following is increased following a fatty meal?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chylomicron

After a fatty meal, chylomicrons are elevated in lipoprotein lipase deficiency.

Chylomicrons transport dietary lipids from the intestine to the peripheral tissues. They are synthesized in the intestine by assembling apo B-48 with lipids (mainly triacylglycerols). This is called a nascent chylomicron, which upon receiving apo C-II and apo E from HDL is remodelled into mature chylomicron.

Apo C-II activates lipoprotein lipase present on the endothelium. Lipoprotein lipase hydrolyzes the triacylglycerols into fatty acids and glycerol which are either used for storage or energy. Therefore, patients who are deficient in lipoprotein lipase or apo C-II (type I hyperlipoproteinemia) show increased levels of chylomicrons in the plasma after a fatty meal.
questions.learning: Chylomicron After a fatty meal, chylomicrons are elevated in lipoprotein lipase deficiency. Chylomicrons transport dietary lipids from the intestine to the peripheral tissues.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presents for evaluation of secondary amenorrhea. Menarche occurred at age 13, and her menstrual cycles were regular until she began combined oral contraceptive pills at age 20. She discontinued oral contraceptives 7 months ago in order to conceive but has not resumed spontaneous menses. She has no history of galactorrhea, visual disturbances, excessive exercise, or weight loss. BMI is 23 kg/m². Physical examination is unremarkable. Laboratory studies show normal TSH, prolactin, FSH, and LH levels. A urine pregnancy test is negative. She is prescribed oral medroxyprogesterone acetate for 10 days. Four days after completing the course, she experiences vaginal bleeding associated with mild cramping. Which of the following endometrial processes is most directly responsible for this patient’s bleeding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Apoptosis of endometrial cells

The progesterone withdrawal test is used to evaluate secondary amenorrhea.

Withdrawal bleeding after stopping medroxyprogesterone indicates:

• Adequate endogenous estrogen production
• An intact endometrium and outflow tract
• Chronic anovulation as the likely cause

Mechanism of withdrawal bleeding:

• Progesterone withdrawal causes breakdown of the functional layer of the endometrium
• This occurs through prostaglandin release, vasoconstriction of spiral arteries, and apoptosis of endometrial cells

Thus, endometrial shedding is primarily due to Apoptosis of endometrial cells

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the preferred treatment for a pediatric patient with symptomatic adenoid hypertrophy causing chronic nasal obstruction and sleep apnea?
questions.explanation: Adenoidectomy—the surgical removal of the adenoid tissue—is indicated for children who have significant lymphoid hypertrophy leading to complications like chronic nasal obstruction, persistent mouth breathing, or obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). If the child also has persistent otitis media with effusion (glue ear) causing hearing loss, an adenoidectomy with grommet (myringotomy tube) insertion (Option B) would be preferred; however, for isolated OSA and nasal symptoms, adenoidectomy alone is standard. Antibiotic therapy (Option C) might resolve an acute episode of adenoiditis but will not shrink chronically hypertrophied tissue. Watchful waiting (Option D) is generally inappropriate for a child already suffering from sleep apnea, which can lead to cognitive deficits, growth delay, and cardiovascular strain. Surgery is typically highly effective, leading to an immediate restoration of a normal nasal breathing pattern and significantly improved quality of sleep for the pediatric patient
questions.learning: Adenoidectomy—the surgical removal of the adenoid tissue—is indicated for children who have significant lymphoid hypertrophy leading to complications like chronic nasal obstruction, persistent mouth breathing, or obstructive sleep apnea (OSA).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the recommended treatment for Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome?
questions.explanation: Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (ZES) is caused by a gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma), which leads to massive gastric acid hypersecretion and severe peptic ulcer disease. The primary medical management objective is the profound suppression of acid production. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) like Omeprazole (Option B) are the first-line and most effective treatment for this purpose. PPIs irreversibly inhibit the H+/K+ ATPase pump, providing more potent and longer-lasting acid suppression than H2-receptor antagonists like Cimetidine (Option A). Misoprostol (Option C) is a prostaglandin analog used to prevent NSAID-induced ulcers but is insufficient for ZES hypersecretion. Aluminum hydroxide (Option D) is a simple antacid that only provides transient relief. While surgical resection of the gastrinoma is the definitive cure, high-dose PPI therapy is mandatory to manage symptoms and prevent life-threatening complications like perforation or bleeding. Therefore, Omeprazole is the gold standard for pharmacological management
questions.learning: Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (ZES) is caused by a gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma), which leads to massive gastric acid hypersecretion and severe peptic ulcer disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient in an ambulance is unresponsive and connected to monitoring equipment showing a specific cardiac rhythm. What is the immediate next step in management?
options: Put the patient in left lateral position
questions.explanation: The monitor displays Ventricular Fibrillation (VF), which is a disorganized, non-perfusing "arrest" rhythm. For an unresponsive patient in VF, the immediate and absolute life-saving actions are starting high-quality chest compressions (CPR) and providing defibrillation as soon as possible. Checking for a pulse (Option A) should take no more than 10 seconds, but in the presence of VF on the monitor, the priority is shock and compressions. Left lateral position (Option C) is for recovery, not cardiac arrest. Cardioversion (Option D) is synchronized to the QRS complex and is used for organized tachycardias; it cannot be used for VF because there are no complexes to synchronize to. Therefore, the rapid delivery of an unsynchronized shock (defibrillation) combined with mechanical support is the definitive standard of care. This protocol must be followed immediately to have any chance of restoring a viable cardiac rhythm

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: During a routine pediatric examination, a 4-year-old child is incidentally found to have a painless abdominal lump. Further assessment reveals a large, mobile mass confined to one side of the abdomen that does not cross the midline. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This question reinforces the core pediatric oncology pattern from Q.233. In a 4-year-old child, a large, painless, smooth abdominal mass that does not cross the midline is the classic clinical description of a Wilms tumor. Wilms tumor typically remains confined to the renal fossa of one side. In contrast, Neuroblastoma (Option A) often presents in younger children with a mass that is "knobby" and characteristically crosses the midline because it arises from the adrenal gland or sympathetic chain. Angiomyolipoma (Option B) is rare and often associated with tuberous sclerosis. Renal cell carcinoma (Option C) is extremely uncommon in this age group. Pediatricians must handle abdominal masses very gently during palpation to avoid the rare but possible risk of rupturing the tumor capsule, which could seed the peritoneum. Wilms tumor has a very good prognosis with modern multi-modal treatment consisting of nephrectomy and chemotherapy
questions.learning: This question reinforces the core pediatric oncology pattern from Q.233. In a 4-year-old child, a large, painless, smooth abdominal mass that does not cross the midline is the classic clinical description of a Wilms tumor.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In nasopharyngeal carcinoma, which of the following is a component of trotter's triad?
options: Conductive hearing loss, ipsilateral temporopa- rietal neuralgia, Palatal paralysis
Sensorineural hearing loss, contralateral tempo- roparietal neuralgia, palatal paralysis
Sensorineural hearing loss, ipsilateral temporo- parietal neuralgia, palatal paralysis
Conductive hearing loss, contralateral temporo- parietal neuralgia, palatal paralysis
questions.explanation: Conductive hearing loss, ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia, Palatal paralysis. Trotter's triad is a specific constellation of clinical findings indicating deep invasion of a nasopharyngeal carcinoma into the skull base. The three definitive components are: 1. Conductive hearing loss: Due to the tumor blocking the Eustachian tube, leading to middle ear effusion. 2. Ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia: Caused by the invasion of the maxillary nerve (CN V2). 3. Palatal paralysis : Resulting from the involvement of the levator veli palatini muscle or its nerve supply. Option A correctly lists these three features. All other options are incorrect as they mention sensorineural loss (Option B and C) or contralateral neuralgia (Option B and D). Trotter's triad is a classic board examination topic because it represents a late-stage, anatomical presentation of NPC. Therefore, because it describes the specific mechanical and neurological impacts of local tumor spread, Option A is the only accurate description of this clinical triad. .
questions.learning: Conductive hearing loss, ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia, Palatal paralysis. Trotter's triad is a specific constellation of clinical findings indicating deep invasion of a nasopharyngeal carcinoma into the skull base.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Ground-glass appearance on HRCT is seen in which of the following condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Silicosis

Silicosis on HRCT shows a ground-glass appearance.

Silicosis is due to the inhalation of crystalline silicon dioxide (silica) seen in individuals employed in sandblasting or rock mining. Macrophages phagocytose inhaled silica particles, thereby activating and releasing inflammatory mediators (IL-1, IL-8) that cause fibroblast recruitment.

Microscopy reveals coalescent nodules of whorled collagen fibers surrounded by a peripheral zone of silica-laden macrophages. HRCT shows a “crazy paving” pattern due to interlobular septal thickening on the background of ground-glass opacity.

Given below is a HRCT image of silicosis:

Option A: Asbestosis - X-ray shows peripheral reticular opacities predominantly in the lower zones. It predominantly affects the lower lobes of the lung, in contrast to other forms of pneumoconiosis, which affect the upper lobes.

Option C: Anthracosis/coal workers' pneumoconiosis is a pulmonary condition seen in coal miners. The inhaled carbon pigment is engulfed by alveolar or interstitial macrophages, which accumulate in the connective tissue. Initially, it causes simple coal workers pneumoconiosis with little or no pulmonary dysfunction. With continued exposure, lung tissue undergoes progressive massive fibrosis which is called complicated coal workers pneumoconiosis. The upper lobes of the lungs are commonly involved.

Simple coal workers' pneumoconiosis appears as small round nodular opacities with an occasional appearance of reticular or reticulonodular opacities. Compared to silicosis, the nodules in CWP tend to have less well-defined margins and a more granular appearance.

Option D: Cotton dust causes byssinosis and can induce occupational asthma. It is characterized clinically as occasional (early-stage) and then regular (late-stage) chest tightness toward the end of the first day of the workweek-Monday chest tightness.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: The maximum oxygen flow rate which can be kept with a conventional oxygen mask is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 10 L/min

The maximum oxygen flow rate which can be kept with a conventional oxygen mask is 10 L/min.

A conventional oxygen mask is a simple face mask that is used routinely in hospitals. It covers the nose and mouth of the patient. There are 2 exhalation ports through which the patient exhales carbon dioxide. This mask is held in place with elastic around the back of the head and a metal piece that fits over the nose. It provides 40% to 60% of O2 concentration and delivers O2 at the rate of 6 to 10 L/min.

Conventional oxygen therapy includes all the devices that are used in routine practices. It includes nasal prongs, low-flow nasal cannula, or masks. It is the main supportive treatment administered to patients after planned extubation.

Whereas if the question is asking about the maximum oxygen flow rate with conventional oxygen therapy, then it would include all the conventionally used devices. questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following lobes of the lung is affected when there is aspiration in supine position?
options: Upper part of right inferior lobe
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Upper part of right inferior lobe

The upper part of the right inferior lobe is prone to aspiration in the supine position. It is commonly seen in alcoholics.

The posterior segment of the right superior lobe and the superior segment of the inferior lobes are the most commonly involved lung sites when aspiration occurs in a recumbent patient.

The location of aspiration depends on the position of the patient since it is gravity-dependent. Aspiration while standing leads to infiltration of bilateral inferior lobes because of larger and more vertical corresponding bronchi, the middle lobes and the lingula.

Aspiration of contents into foreign substances into the bronchial tree, usually oral or gastric contents, produces aspiration pneumonia. Chemical (gastric acid) injury or bacterial infection complicates the condition.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following are unsaturated fatty acids? 1. Lauric acid 2. Linoleic acid 3. Oleic acid 4. Palmitic acid Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2 and 3

Unsaturated fatty acids are generally liquid at room temperature and are considered healthier because they help reduce LDL cholesterol and lower cardiovascular risk.

• 1. Lauric acid ✗

• A saturated fatty acid (12:0).
• Commonly found in coconut oil and palm kernel oil.

• 2. Linoleic acid ✓

• A polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA, 18:2).
• An essential fatty acid (Omega-6) that must be obtained from the diet.

• 3. Oleic acid ✓

• A monounsaturated fatty acid (MUFA, 18:1).
• Major fatty acid in olive oil and groundnut oil.

• 4. Palmitic acid ✗

• A saturated fatty acid (16:0).
• Commonly found in palm oil, butter, and animal fats.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 70-year-old male, with a history of smoking presents with progressive dyspnea and dry cough. Examination reveals clubbing and fine basal crackles. Spirometry shows low forced vital capacity (FVC) and low diffusion capacity (DLCO). CT Chest shows extensive bilateral reticular shadows and subpleural honeycombing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

The combination of elderly age, progressive exertional dyspnea, dry cough, clubbing, fine “Velcro” basal crackles, restrictive PFTs (↓FVC), ↓DLCO, and CT showing bilateral subpleural reticular opacities with honeycombing is classic for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis with a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern.

Why not the other options?

• B. Sarcoidosis: Typically shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, perilymphatic nodules, and upper/mid-zone predominance.
• C. COPD: Shows an obstructive pattern with ↓FEV₁/FVC; emphysema may show hyperinflation rather than restrictive physiology and classic basal honeycombing.
• D. Bronchiectasis: Characterized by permanent bronchial dilation, recurrent productive cough, and CT findings such as signet-ring sign, not subpleural honeycombing.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A resident doctor gets pricked with a needle while attending an HIV positive patient. The regimen to be given is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Zidovudine + Lamivudine + Indinavir

Amongst the given options, a three-drug combination of Zidovudine+Lamivudine+Indinavir is preferred.

Three drug combination is preferred as per the US Public health service guidelines, WHO guidelines, and MOHFW 2020 guidelines.

A PEP regimen for HIV should have Lamivudine + Tenofovir + Lopinavir/ritonavir to be taken for 4 weeks after exposure. It should ideally be started within 2 hours and definitely within 72 hours. Here as the Lopinavir/ritonavir is not part of the options, one can choose, the indinavir-based combination as the best of the available options.

Nevirapine is not preferred for use in PEP. Previous NACO 2018 guidelines mentioned the use of 2 drug combinations but it is no longer preferred.

Exposures that may warrant occupational PEP include:

• Parenteral or mucous membrane exposure (splashes to the eye, nose, or oral cavity)
• The following bodily fluids may pose a risk of HIV infection: blood, blood-stained saliva, breast-milk, genital secretions, and cerebrospinal, amniotic, rectal, peritoneal, synovial, pericardial, or pleural fluids.

Exposures that do not require PEP include:

• When the exposed individual is already HIV-positive
• When the source is established to be HIV-negative
• Exposure to bodily fluids that do not pose a significant risk: tears, non-blood-stained saliva, urine, and sweat.

To ensure no transmission has occurred, follow-up with HIV antibody testing should be done for at least 6 months post-exposure (e.g. at baseline, 6 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months).

Note: This is an AIIMS 2020 recall question. It may not reflect the latest guidelines. Kindly refer to the attached pearl for the same.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a risk factor for ectopic pregnancy? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Condom

Ectopic pregnancy occurs when implantation takes place outside the uterine cavity, most commonly in the fallopian tube.

Major risk factors include conditions that damage or impair tubal transport:

• Pelvic inflammatory disease
• Previous ectopic pregnancy
• Tubal surgery or tubal ligation
• Intrauterine device (if pregnancy occurs)
• Infertility treatment
• Smoking

Why the options differ:

• IUCDs reduce overall pregnancy risk, but if pregnancy occurs with an IUCD in place, the relative likelihood of ectopic pregnancy is increased
• Pregnancy after tubal ligation has a higher chance of being ectopic
• Oral contraceptive pills overall reduce pregnancy risk, but progesterone-only pills may slightly increase ectopic risk if contraceptive failure occurs
• Condoms protect against sexually transmitted infections and PID, thereby reducing the risk of ectopic pregnancy

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which type of mutation results in the reversal to wild type of phenotype when the mutant gene is suppressed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mutations in tRNA

Mutations in tRNA are known to suppress the mutant gene and cause reversal to wild phenotype. Such mutations are called suppressor mutations.

Suppressor mutations are secondary mutations that alter the phenotypes caused by an existing mutation. This is not to be confused with reversion mutations in which the original mutation has been lost. Instead, suppressor mutations return the phenotype caused by the original mutation to a more wild-type phenotype despite the presence of the original mutation. The suppressor mutation’s effect on the phenotype can vary from partial restoration to full restoration of the wild-type phenotype.

In prokaryotic and lower eukaryotic organisms, abnormally functioning tRNA molecules have been discovered that are themselves the results of mutations. Some of these abnormal tRNA molecules are capable of binding to and decoding altered codons, thereby suppressing the effects of mutations in the structural genes.

These suppressor tRNA molecules, usually formed as a result of alterations in their anticodon regions, are capable of suppressing certain missense mutations, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations. An example of suppressor mutation is illustrated below.

A primary mutation occurs changing the original codon sequence from UGG (Trp) to UAG (Stop). A secondary mutation occurs in the gene for a glutamine tRNA leading to the anticodon switch from a GUC to AUC. This mutant tRNA can recognize the UAG stop codon and insert glutamine in place of the stop, allowing translation to continue past the stop and suppressing the original mutation.

In the laboratory context, such suppressor tRNAs, coupled with mutated variants of aminoacyl- tRNA synthetases, can be utilized to incorporate unnatural amino acids into defined locations within altered genes that carry engineered nonsense mutations. The resulting labeled proteins can be used for in vivo and in vitro cross-linking and biophysical studies.
questions.learning: Mutations in tRNA Mutations in tRNA are known to suppress the mutant gene and cause reversal to wild phenotype. Such mutations are called suppressor mutations.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the earliest sign in Crohn's disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Aphthous ulcers

Aphthous ulcers, surrounded by a rim of erythematous mucosa, are the earliest lesions seen in a patient with Crohn's disease during endoscopy.

Crohn's colitis usually spares the rectum and is most severe in the ileocaecal region.

• In early Crohn's disease, small, punched-out aphthous ulcers are often seen (the result of submucosal lymphoid follicle expansion).
• In moderate disease, the aphthous ulcers coalesce into larger ulcers, which may take on the appearance of a star (stellate ulcers).
• As disease severity increases, submucosal edema and injury can result in cobblestoning of the mucosa (option A) and eventually the formation of serpiginous ulcers, which are typical findings in Crohn's disease.

Thorn-like extraluminal projections in barium studies are known as rose-thorn appearance, and are a typical sign of Crohn's disease. They represent deep penetrating linear ulcers or fissurings typically seen within stenosed terminal ileum with a thickened wall. (Options C and D)
questions.learning: Aphthous ulcers Aphthous ulcers, surrounded by a rim of erythematous mucosa, are the earliest lesions seen in a patient with Crohn's disease during endoscopy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following provides long-lasting results in a coronary artery bypass graft (CABG)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Internal mammary artery

The left internal mammary artery (LIMA) provides long-lasting results in a coronary artery bypass graft (CABG). The most important criterion in conduit selection is graft patency. The conduit with the highest patency rate is the left internal mammary artery or internal thoracic artery.

Left internal mammary artery > Radial artery > long saphenous vein represents the correct order of graft patency in a patient undergoing a CABG procedure.

Venous grafts:

* The long saphenous vein is the most common vein used as a conduit as it is straightforward to harvest, provides good length, and is easy to handle.

* The ten-year patency rate for long saphenous vein grafts is reported to be 50–60 percent.

Arterial grafts:

* The Left internal mammary artery (LIMA) or internal thoracic artery has become the conduit of choice for the left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery. The radial artery can be used as a second or alternative arterial bypass graft. Other arterial bypass grafts include the gastroepiploic artery and the inferior epigastric artery.

* Long patency rates of >98 percent have been reported.

Pearl PF1920: Indications for Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG)

Class I indications for CABG from the American College of Cardiology(ACC) and American Heart Association(AHA).

* Left main disease

* Three-vessel disease with or without proximal LAD disease

* Two vessel disease with proximal LAD disease

* Survivors of sudden cardiac death with presumed ischemia-mediated VT

Other indications for CABG include the following:

* Disabling angina

* Ongoing ischemia in the setting of a non–ST-segment elevation (MI) that is unresponsive to medical therapy

* Poor LV function but with viable, nonfunctioning myocardium above the anatomic defect that can be revascularized
questions.learning: Internal mammary artery — The left internal mammary artery (LIMA) provides long-lasting results in a coronary artery bypass graft (CABG). The most important criterion in conduit selection is graft patency.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The first primary tooth to erupt is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. lower central incisor

The lower (mandibular) central incisor is the first primary tooth to erupt at 5-7 months. However, the first secondary tooth to erupt is the first molar (maxillary or mandibular), at 6-7 years, followed by the lower central incisor.

* All primary teeth erupt by 1.5 – 2.5 years of age.

* All secondary teeth erupt by 17 -22 years of age.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements is not true regarding Marjolin's ulcer?
options: It is seen in sites of chronic wounds or scars.
It can progress to squamous cell carcinoma.
It is radioresistant due to avascularity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It rapidly progresses to malignancy

The incorrect statement regarding Marjolin's ulcer is that it rapidly progresses to malignancy.

Marjolin’s ulcer refers to a rare form of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma . It originates from areas of scarring or chronic wounds.

It progresses to full-fledged SCC gradually. The progression is gradual and slow. It has a long latency period of around 30 years. Since the ulcer occurs in scarred tissue without nerves and vessels, it is painless and radioresistant

Clinical signs of the tumour include:

* Ulceration

* Nodule formation

* An abrupt increase in size

* Everted or rolled wound margins

* Overgrowth of granulation tissue

* Tendency to bleed on manipulation

For the diagnosis, an edge-wedge biopsy can be done. MRI of the part and the regional node area is done to confirm the diagnosis. Treatment involves wide local excision, and in case of a large ulcer, amputation is required.

An image of Marjolin's ulcer is below:

Pearl PF0158: Marjolin’s Ulcer

* Low-grade cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma arising from

* Long-standing ulcer like venous ulcer

* Post-burn scar

* Chronic osteomyelitis

* Post-radiation ulcer.

* Slow progression to malignancy (SCC) since it is relatively avascular.

* Painless due to the absence of nerves in scar tissue.

* No secondary deposits since there are no lymphatics in scar tissue.

* Radioresistant due to avascularity.
questions.learning: It rapidly progresses to malignancy — The incorrect statement regarding Marjolin's ulcer is that it rapidly progresses to malignancy. Marjolin’s ulcer refers to a rare form of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma .

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A woman develops edema, visual disturbances, and signs of heart failure after consuming a particular food item. What is the most likely adulterant responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of edema, visual disturbances (specifically glaucoma), and heart failure is characteristic of Epidemic Dropsy. This condition is caused by the consumption of mustard oil adulterated with Argemone mexicana seeds, which contain the toxin Sanguinarine. Sanguinarine causes widespread capillary damage and permeability. BOAA (Option B) is the neurotoxin found in Lathyrus sativus (Khesari dal) that causes Neurolathyrism, a spastic paralysis of the legs. Pyrrolizidine alkaloids (Option C) cause Veno-Occlusive Disease (VOD) of the liver, leading to ascites. Aflatoxin (Option D) is a potent carcinogen produced by fungi on stored grains and is a major risk factor for liver cancer. Epidemic dropsy is a serious public health issue in areas where adulterated cooking oil is sold. Early diagnosis and supportive care are essential, as the cardiac failure can be rapidly fatal. Testing for the presence of Argemone oil is done using the simple Nitric Acid test or chromatography
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of edema, visual disturbances (specifically glaucoma), and heart failure is characteristic of Epidemic Dropsy. This condition is caused by the consumption of mustard oil adulterated with Argemone mexicana seeds, which contain the…

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman, recently married, was found dead at home. A suicide note was recovered, in which she mentioned that she was tortured for dowry by her in-laws. Under which section will the inquest be conducted? BNS - Bhartiya Nyaya Sanhita
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. BNSS section 196

The given clinical scenario of a female who died due to suicide because of dowry pressure by in-laws suggests a possibility of dowry death. A magistrate's inquest is done under BNSS Section 196 (Section 176 CrPC).

BNSS 196 (Section 176 CrPC) deals with magistrate's inquest in which the cause of death is not under natural circumstances. Magistrate inquest may be conducted by the District Magistrate, Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Tahsildar, or any other Executive Magistrate empowered by the State Government.

Indications for Magistrate Inquest:

* Dowry death

* Custodial rape

* Death in police custody or police interrogation

* Death in police firing

* Death in prison, reformatories, or Borstal school

* Death in a psychiatric hospital

* Cases of exhumation.

Other options:

Option A: Section 106 BNS (304A IPC) defines the punishment for causing the death of a person by any rash or negligent act, not amounting to culpable homicide, the punishment is imprisonment for up to 2 years and a fine.

Option B:  BNSS Section 194 (Section 174 CrPC) deals with the police inquest. It is done by suicide, homicide, killing by any animal or machinery or accident, and death under circumstances that raise suspicion of another person committing the offence.

Option C: BNS Sec 89 (IPC 313) deals with the causation of miscarriage of a woman with a child (and/or quick with child) without her consent. Only the person causing the abortion is liable to punishment.
questions.learning: BNSS section 196 — The given clinical scenario of a female who died due to suicide because of dowry pressure by in-laws suggests a possibility of dowry death.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The graph below shows the relationship between the log(dose) and the response of three drugs, A, B, and C. Which of these drugs has the highest potency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A

Drug A has the highest potency.

Potency:

• It is defined as the amount of drug needed to produce a given response. A highly potent drug evokes a given response at low concentrations and vice-versa.
• The more the curve is on the left in a dose-response curve (DRC), the greater is its potency.
• Thus, in the above image, the potency is Drug A >Drug B> Drug C.

Efficacy:

• It is defined as the maximum effect produced by the drug. It reflects the capacity of the drug to activate a receptor and produce the response.
• In the log dose-response curve, the perpendicular height represents the drug efficacy.
• Thus, in the above image, the efficacy is Drug A = Drug B > Drug C.
• Drugs having a similar pharmacological effect can have different efficacies e.g furosemide and metolazone are both diuretics but furosemide has greater efficacy than metolazone.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: What type of electrolyte imbalance is seen in refeeding syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypophosphatemia

Refeeding syndrome is a potentially life-threatening metabolic complication that occurs when nutrition, particularly carbohydrates, is rapidly reintroduced after prolonged starvation or severe malnutrition. The resulting insulin surge drives phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells, leading to profound hypophosphatemia, the hallmark electrolyte abnormality of refeeding syndrome.

• During starvation, total body phosphate stores become depleted.
• Refeeding with carbohydrates increases insulin secretion, which:

• Stimulates cellular uptake of glucose
• Drives phosphate into cells for ATP production

• This results in severe hypophosphatemia, which is the earliest and most characteristic laboratory finding.

Why not the other options?

• A. Hyperkalemia: Incorrect. Refeeding causes hypokalemia, as potassium shifts intracellularly under the influence of insulin.
• B. Hyponatremia: Incorrect. May occur due to fluid retention but is not the hallmark abnormality.
• C. Hypomagnesemia: Incorrect. Commonly occurs in refeeding syndrome but is less characteristic than hypophosphatemia.
questions.learning: Hypophosphatemia Refeeding syndrome is a potentially life-threatening metabolic complication that occurs when nutrition, particularly carbohydrates, is rapidly reintroduced after prolonged starvation or severe malnutrition.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Why do neoplastic cells utilize Warburg metabolism?
options: It decreases glucose utilisation by neoplastic cells
It forms metabolic intermediates which are needed for cell growth and multiplication
It provides more energy in the form of increased ATP production
It prevents apoptosis and makes the cancer cells immortal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It forms metabolic intermediates which are needed for cell growth and multiplication

Neoplastic cells utilize Warburg metabolism for the generation of metabolic intermediates, which are needed for cell growth and multiplication.

The Warburg Effect is a phenomenon in which there is an increase in the rate of glucose uptake and conversion into lactate(fermentation), even in the presence of oxygen. Cancer cells derive energy mainly from glycolysis.

Cancer cells utilize glycolysis (2 ATP) over mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (36 ATP) for glucose metabolism, even though the latter produces more ATP. It is because pure oxidative phosphorylation produces abundant ATP, but also burns glucose to CO2 and H2O, leaving no carbon moieties suitable for use as building blocks for lipids or proteins.

For this reason, rapidly growing cells, by undergoing glycolysis, produce carbon moieties that are needed for growth and cellular maintenance.

The image given below shows the comparison of glucose metabolism in normal cells versus cancer cells.

As a result of decreased ATP production, the main metabolic function of mitochondria in growing cells is not to generate ATP, but to carry
out reactions that generate cellular building blocks. For example, lipid biosynthesis.

Warburg effect is produced by growth factor receptors downstream signalling pathways. These include receptor tyrosine kinase/PI3K/AKT and MYC.

Clinically, cancer cells exhibiting the Warburg effect show a property of glucose hunger. This is used to visualize them via positron emission tomography (PET) scanning.
questions.learning: It forms metabolic intermediates which are needed for cell growth and multiplication Neoplastic cells utilize Warburg metabolism for the generation of metabolic intermediates, which are needed for cell growth and multiplication.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A partogram of a woman in labor is shown below. Oxytocin infusion has been administered. Mark the best management for the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cesarean section

Key Components of a Partogram

| Parameter | What it monitors

| --------- | ----------------

| Cervical dilation | Progress of labor

| Fetal descent | Head movement

| Uterine contractions | Strength and frequency

| Fetal heart rate | Fetal wellbeing

Two important reference lines are plotted:

| Line | Meaning

| ---- | -------

| Alert line | Expected progress of labor

| Action line | Indicates abnormal labor requiring intervention

Labor progress crosses alert line

↓

Close monitoring required

Labor progress crosses action line

↓

Immediate intervention

If labor crosses the action line despite oxytocin augmentation → Cesarean section.

Partogram shows full dilation, adequate contractions, 2+ moulding, fetal distress (decelerations, meconium) and head still 3/5 palpable per abdomen → cephalopelvic disproportion. Instrumental delivery is contraindicated when the head is not well engaged. Hence, emergency cesarean section is the correct management.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a postoperative patient who is hypotensive, which finding is considered a "sure sign" of abdominal wound dehiscence?
options: Widening of the abdominal scar with palpable edges
questions.explanation: In postoperative patients, the most definitive and “sure sign” of abdominal wound dehiscence is widening of the abdominal scar with palpable separation of wound edges. This finding indicates an actual failure of fascial closure, meaning the deeper layers of the abdominal wall have separated. It is a late and confirmatory sign, often preceding or associated with complications like burst abdomen or evisceration, and requires urgent surgical intervention. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Increased bowel sounds: This is a nonspecific finding and may occur during recovery from ileus or other benign conditions; it is not related to wound integrity. (B) Persistent abdominal pain: Pain is common postoperatively and may indicate various issues such as infection or inflammation, but it is not specific for dehiscence. (C) Serosanguinous drainage from the wound: Although it can be an early warning sign, it is not a definitive (“sure”) sign of dehiscence on its own
questions.learning: In postoperative patients, the most definitive and “sure sign” of abdominal wound dehiscence is widening of the abdominal scar with palpable separation of wound edges.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 52-year-old male has uncontrolled diabetes. Which one of the following tests will help in early detection of nephropathy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Urine albumin

Diabetic nephropathy is the leading cause of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and end-stage renal disease (ESRD). The earliest clinically detectable marker of diabetic nephropathy is moderately increased albuminuria (microalbuminuria), which reflects early glomerular damage before a decline in glomerular filtration rate (GFR).

Urine albumin estimation, preferably the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) in a spot urine sample, is the screening test of choice for early detection.

• Urine albumin (UACR) detects microalbuminuria (30–300 mg/day), the earliest manifestation of diabetic nephropathy. ⭐
• Early detection allows timely intervention with ACE inhibitors/ARBs, strict glycemic control, and blood pressure control to slow disease progression.

Why not the other options?

• A. Blood urea level: Rises only in advanced renal dysfunction and is not useful for early detection.
• B. Serum creatinine level: Often remains normal until approximately 50% of renal function is lost; therefore, it is an insensitive marker of early nephropathy.
• C. Ultrasonography: Useful for assessing kidney size and structural abnormalities but cannot detect early diabetic nephropathy.
questions.learning: Urine albumin Diabetic nephropathy is the leading cause of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and end-stage renal disease (ESRD). The earliest clinically detectable marker of diabetic nephropathy is moderately increased albuminuria (microalbuminuria), which…

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which physiological condition most strongly stimulates the release of vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone)?
questions.explanation: Vasopressin, also known as antidiuretic hormone (ADH), is secreted by the posterior pituitary in response to two main physiological stimuli: osmotic and hemodynamic. The most sensitive trigger is a rise in plasma osmolality (not hypotonicity or hypo-osmolality as in Options A and D). However, hypotension (Option C) or a decrease in effective circulating blood volume (hypovolemia) serves as a very potent trigger for its release. When blood pressure drops significantly, baroreceptors in the heart and large arteries signal the hypothalamus to release large amounts of vasopressin. Vasopressin then acts on the V1 receptors of vascular smooth muscle to cause vasoconstriction (increasing blood pressure) and on V2 receptors in the kidneys to increase water reabsorption. Hypertension (Option B) actually inhibits vasopressin secretion to help lower blood volume. Among the choices, hypotension is the only correct hemodynamic condition that stimulates secretion
questions.learning: Vasopressin, also known as antidiuretic hormone (ADH), is secreted by the posterior pituitary in response to two main physiological stimuli: osmotic and hemodynamic.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Opening of Bartholin’s duct is in the:
options: Vestibule outside the hymen at the junction of the anterior 2/3rd and posterior 1/3rd in the groove between the hymen and labium minus
Groove between labia majora and labia minora
Superficial perineal pouch at the junction of anterior 1/3rd and posterior 1/3rd
Periurethral region in anterior 1/3rd of labia minora
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vestibule outside the hymen at the junction of the anterior 2/3rd and posterior 1/3rd in the groove between the hymen and labium minus

The Bartholin’s glands (greater vestibular glands) are paired mucus-secreting glands located in the superficial perineal pouch, posterolateral to the vaginal opening. The Bartholin’s duct opens into the vestibule, outside the hymenal ring, at the junction of the anterior two-thirds and posterior one-third in the groove between the hymen and the labium minus. Clinically, this corresponds approximately to the 4 o’clock and 8 o’clock positions of the vaginal introitus.

Why not the other options?

• B. Groove between labia majora and labia minora: This is not the site of the duct opening.
• C. Superficial perineal pouch at the junction of anterior 1/3rd and posterior 1/3rd: The gland lies in the superficial perineal pouch, but the duct opens into the vestibule, not the pouch.
• D. Periurethral region in anterior 1/3rd of labia minora: This describes the location of the Skene’s (paraurethral) glands, not the Bartholin’s glands.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 20-year-old male patient presented with a headache and altered sensorium. MRI was performed, which revealed multiple ring-enhancing lesions. What will be the next step to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. MR spectroscopy

MR spectroscopy detects lipid-lactate peak, distinguishing tuberculomas from NCC. CBNAAT is for meningitis, biopsy is invasive, SWI detects bleeds. MR Spectroscopy

MRS analyzes metabolites inside the lesion, helping distinguish between different causes of ring lesions.

It is:

• Non-invasive
• Highly diagnostic
• Helps avoid biopsy in many cases

| Feature | Tuberculoma | Abscess | NCC | Metastasis

| ------- | ----------- | ------- | --- | ----------

| Number | Multiple | Single/multiple | Multiple | Multiple

| Enhancement | Ring | Ring | Ring | Ring

| MRS | Lipid peak | Amino acids | Variable | ↑ Choline

| Edema | Moderate | Marked | Mild | Variable

| Key clue | India, TB endemic | Infection signs | Scolex | Primary tumor

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The coding sequence present in the RNA molecule is CAAGGU. What will be the sequence in the template DNA strand from where it is transcribed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. ACCTTG

During transcription, the DNA sequence 5'ACCTTG3' serves as the template for synthesizing the RNA sequence 5'CAAGGU3'.

The template DNA strand is always complementary and antiparallel to the transcribed RNA strand. Given that the RNA sequence is:

5'- CAAGGU -3'

The complementary template DNA strand (which runs in the 3' → 5' direction) is:

3'- GTTCCA -5'

To match the 5' → 3' direction, we reverse it:

5'- ACCTTG -3'

Note: Unless otherwise specified, all sequences are written in the 5′ to 3′ direction.

According to Chargaff's rule in cellular DNA regardless of species:

* Adenine= Thymine, Guanine = Cytosine

* Sum of purine = Sum of pyrimidines i.e A+G=C+T.

When DNA is transcribed into RNA, the process involves complementary base pairing. Adenine (A) in DNA pairs with thymine (T), but in RNA, thymine is replaced by uracil (U). Similarly, cytosine (C) in DNA pairs with guanine (G) in both DNA and RNA. During transcription, RNA polymerase reads the DNA template and adds complementary RNA nucleotides accordingly.

Pearl PF0706: Differences between DNA & RNA Synthesis

RNA synthesis

DNA synthesis

Ribonucleotides are used

Deoxyribonucleotides are used

Uracil is the complementary base for Adenine

Thymine is the complementary base for Adenine

Primer is not involved as RNA polymerases have the ability to initiate synthesis de novo

Primer is necessary because DNA polymerases can only attach new DNA nucleotides to an existing strand of nucleotides

Only portions of the genome are vigorously transcribed or copied into RNA

The entire genome must be copied, once and only once during DNA replication

No highly active, efficient proofreading function

Highly active, efficient proofreading function is performed by DNA polymerase
questions.learning: ACCTTG During transcription, the DNA sequence 5'ACCTTG3' serves as the template for synthesizing the RNA sequence 5'CAAGGU3'. The template DNA strand is always complementary and antiparallel to the transcribed RNA strand.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Revised A 36-year-old man presented with complaints of bluish-black discolouration of sclera and pinna for last 6 months. Since childhood, his urine turns black on standing as shown in the image below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alkaptonuria

The clinical features along with the blackening of urine on standing are characteristic of alkaptonuria.

Alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive disorder of tyrosine metabolism, that develops due to the defect in homogentisate oxidase/ homogentisic acid 1, 2 - dioxygenase, which oxidizes homogentisate to maleylacetoacetate. The defect in this enzyme leads to the accumulation of homogentisate, which is then excreted in the urine.

Alkaptonuria is characterized by homogentisic aciduria, ochronosis, and arthropathy (joint pain).

Homogentisic aciduria is the black discoloration of urine on prolonged exposure to air caused due to oxidation of the excreted homogentisate.

Ochronosis, which is bluish-black pigmentation in connective tissue; generally occurs after the third decade of life and it occurs due to the accumulation of homogentisic acid and its oxidation products like benzoquinone acetic acid in connective tissue.

Arthritis generally begins in the third decade. Arthritis often begins in the spine and resembles ankylosing spondylitis in its large-joint distribution. Radiographs of the spine showing flattened and calcified intervertebral discs are pathognomonic. Other findings include degeneration of the intervertebral discs followed by disc calcification and eventually fusion of the vertebral bodies. Osteophyte formation and calcification of the intervertebral ligaments also occur.

Diagnosis: Blackish discoloration of urine on standing is diagnostic of alkaptonuria. The ferric chloride test will be positive.

The images below show pigmentation of the skin and an x-ray of the spine that shows calcification of intervertebral discs.
questions.learning: Alkaptonuria — The clinical features along with the blackening of urine on standing are characteristic of alkaptonuria. Alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive disorder of tyrosine metabolism, that develops due to the defect in homogentisate oxidase/…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is true about the Hayflick limit?
options: Human cells can divide a finite number of times only
Free radical oxidation level is unrestricted
RNA polymerase can function for. a finite number of times only
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Human cells can divide a finite number of times only

The Hayflick limit says that human cells can divide for a finite number of times.

The Hayflick limit is the number of divisions a cell population can go through in culture before division stops and enters a state known as senescence. With the exception of stem cells, all the other human cells have only a limited capacity for cell division. This biological clock is of great help in the study of the normal ageing process.

The number of cell divisions of the cultured cell is roughly related to:

• The age of the cell donors
• The longevity of the species

For example, fibroblasts from the human embryos, when sustained in tissue culture, divide about 50 times before they die. Those taken from person after birth divide only 20 to 30 times.
