questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A middle-aged female patient presented with slowly progressive motor weakness, nuchal rigidity, and difficulty in swallowing and carrying out day-to-day activities. A provisional diagnosis of multiple sclerosis is suspected. Which of the following cells are affected in multiple sclerosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Oligodendrocytes

Oligodendrocytes are affected in multiple sclerosis.

In multiple sclerosis, there is patchy destruction of myelin in the central nervous system and the axons are demyelinated. This causes loss of conduction or delayed conduction in the demyelinated axons. Oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells are involved in the formation of myelin. Hence, they are affected by multiple sclerosis.

Other options

Option A: Microglia are a part of the immune system. Microglia are scavenger cells that aid in the removal of cellular debris formed due to various diseases. They originate from macrophages outside of the nervous system and are unrelated to the neural cell types.

Option C: There are three types of macroglia - astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and Schwann cells. Astrocytes are found throughout the brain and they induce capillaries to form the blood-brain barrier. The astrocytes may be fibrous or protoplasmic.

Option D: Ependymal cells line the ventricular system. They are in contact with the cerebrospinal fluid and play a role in fluid homeostasis.
questions.learning: Oligodendrocytes Oligodendrocytes are affected in multiple sclerosis. In multiple sclerosis, there is patchy destruction of myelin in the central nervous system and the axons are demyelinated.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: KAT G mutation associated with:
questions.explanation: Resistance to Isoniazid (INH) in Mycobacterium tuberculosis is most commonly associated with a mutation in the katG gene. INH is a prodrug that must be activated by the catalase-peroxidase enzyme, which is encoded by katG. Mutations in this gene result in an ineffective enzyme that cannot activate the drug, leading to high-level resistance. Rifampicin resistance (Option B) is associated with mutations in the rpoB gene (RNA polymerase). Levofloxacin resistance (Option C) is linked to mutations in DNA gyrase genes (gyrA and gyrB). Ethambutol resistance (Option D) involves mutations in the embB gene, affecting cell wall synthesis. Other INH resistance mechanisms include mutations in the inhA promoter or the kasA gene. Understanding these genetic markers is essential for interpreting rapid molecular diagnostic tests like GeneXpert or Line Probe Assays for drug-resistant tuberculosis management
questions.learning: Resistance to Isoniazid (INH) in Mycobacterium tuberculosis is most commonly associated with a mutation in the katG gene. INH is a prodrug that must be activated by the catalase-peroxidase enzyme, which is encoded by katG.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which among the following is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Malignant melanoma

Malignant melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults

Intraocular tumours are tumors affecting the ocular tissue. They are often malignant. They are initially dormant but can cause secondary glaucoma based on the location. It can cause extraocular extension and finally metastasis if left untreated. Types of intraocular tumours:

* Malignant melanoma: Involves the choroid, ciliary body, or iris. Its start as lens-shaped masses and enlarges. Retinal melanoma can cause retinal detachment. Radiological investigations like CT, MRI, and radioactive tracers, fluorescein angiography are used for diagnosis. Treatment includes surgery, radiation therapy, and enucleation in severe cases

* Retinoblastoma: Is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in children. It presents as a yellow pupillary reflex and cataract. Diagnosis is via demonstration of calcifications in radiographs and CT. Treatment involves brachytherapy and surgery.

* Reticulum cell sarcoma: It is a primary neoplasm of histiocyte similar to a microglioma in the CNS

* Secondaries: These mostly arise from the breast and alimentary canal.
questions.learning: Malignant melanoma Malignant melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults Intraocular tumours are tumors affecting the ocular tissue.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with complaints of hearing loss. On examination, the Rinne test is positive in the left ear and negative in the right ear. Weber’s test shows lateralization to the left ear, and bone conduction is reduced in the right ear but normal in the left ear. How should these findings be interpreted?
options: Sensorineural hearing loss in left ear
Sensorineural hearing loss in right ear
Conductive hearing loss in left ear
Conductive hearing loss in right ear.
questions.explanation: Interpretation of tuning fork tests requires a combined analysis of all results. In this case, a negative Rinne in the right ear suggests either conductive loss or a "false negative" due to profound sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL). The bone conduction test is the deciding factor; because it is reduced in the right ear, it confirms sensorineural involvement. In SNHL, the Weber test lateralizes to the better-hearing ear. Since the sound lateralizes to the left, the left ear is the better ear, and the right ear is affected by SNHL. Options C and D (conductive loss) are ruled out because conductive loss would show lateralization to the poorer ear in the Weber test and normal bone conduction. Option A is incorrect as the left ear shows a positive Rinne and normal bone conduction, indicating it is likely the healthy ear. Thus, the clinical cluster confirms SNHL in the right ear
questions.learning: Interpretation of tuning fork tests requires a combined analysis of all results. In this case, a negative Rinne in the right ear suggests either conductive loss or a "false negative" due to profound sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A student develops urticaria after consuming seafood and seeks treatment. As she has an important examination approaching, she requires an antihistamine that will not cause sedation. Which drug would be the most appropriate choice in this situation?
questions.explanation: Fexofenadine is a second-generation H1 antihistamine that is highly selective for peripheral H1 receptors and has very poor penetration into the blood-brain barrier. Consequently, it is considered a truly non-sedating antihistamine, making it the ideal choice for a student who needs to remain alert for an exam. Pheniramine (Option A), Promethazine (Option B), and Hydroxyzine (Option C) are all first-generation antihistamines. These drugs are highly lipophilic and readily cross the blood-brain barrier, where they antagonize central H1 and muscarinic receptors, leading to significant sedation, drowsiness, and impaired cognitive function. In an emergency urticaria scenario, the rapid onset of a non-drowsy second-generation agent ensures clinical relief without compromising performance. Fexofenadine and others like Loratadine or Cetirizine are the preferred standard of care for daytime allergy management where psychomotor impairment must be avoided
questions.learning: Fexofenadine is a second-generation H1 antihistamine that is highly selective for peripheral H1 receptors and has very poor penetration into the blood-brain barrier.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which condition is typically characterized by lesions described as "dew drop on rose petal"?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chicken Pox

Varicella (Chickenpox) is an acute viral infection caused by the Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) and is characterized by a distinctive vesicular rash.

“Dew Drop on a Rose Petal” Appearance

• Refers to a clear vesicle (dew drop) on an erythematous base (rose petal).
• Considered the classic skin lesion of chickenpox.
• Lesions appear in successive crops, resulting in papules, vesicles, pustules, and crusts being present simultaneously.

Clinical Features of Chickenpox

• Fever and malaise
• Pruritic vesicular rash
• Centripetal distribution (trunk > extremities)
• Lesions at different stages of evolution

Why Other Options Are Incorrect

Molluscum Contagiosum: Umbilicated pearly papules caused by a poxvirus.

Measles: Maculopapular rash with Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa.

Pityriasis Rosea: Herald patch followed by a “Christmas tree” pattern rash and collarette scaling.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following helps to differentiate a fixed dilated pupil? A. Phenylephrine B. 1% Pilocarpine C. 0.1% Pilocarpine D. Cocaine 0.5% E. Epinephrine
options: A, B, C, D and E
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. B and C only

Among the given options, 1% pilocarpine and 0.1% pilocarpine can be used to differentiate fixed dilated pupil.

Fixed dilated pupil is seen in conditions such as third nerve palsy, Hutchinson's pupil (increased cranial pressure), Adie's pupil, and due to pharmacological mydriasis.

Pilocarpine acts as an agonist at cholinergic muscuranic receptors and ganglion stimulator to cause miosis of the pupil.

Normal strength pilocarpine (1-2%) constricts the dilated pupil of 3rd nerve palsy, whereas there will be no response if the dilation is due to pharmacological mydriasis (anticholinergic causes) such as accidental application of atropine.

0.1% pilocarpine is used to diagnose Adie's pupil. Adie's pupil constricts with weak concentrations of pilocarpine (0.1%), while the normal pupil does not. This is because the denervated sphincter of the iris is very sensitive to topical parasympathomimetics such as pilocarpine. 0.1% pilocarpine also helps differentiate Adie's pupil from Argyll Robertson pupil (ARP).

Note:

Cocaine test (2 to 4%) is done in Horner’s syndrome. In these patients, the small pupil fails to dilate on instillation of mydriatics such as Cocaine which is in contrast to the normal pupil which dilates on instilling cocaine. Alternatively, the small pupils of Horner's syndrome dilate with 1% apraclonidine.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is the term used to refer to the type of splint displayed in the image?
questions.explanation: The splint shown is best identified as a cock-up splint (wrist extension splint). The key feature is the firm forearm-based support holding the wrist in extension, which is the primary purpose of a cock-up splint. Although the image shows additional attachments (outriggers and elastic bands), the main structure and function center on maintaining wrist extension, which defines a cock-up splint. Cock-up splints are commonly used in: 1. 1. Radial nerve palsy (wrist drop) 2. 2. Post-injury or post-surgical immobilization 3. 3. Maintaining functional hand position Why other options are incorrect: (A) Wrist splint: Too general; cock-up is a specific type (C) Knuckle bender splint: Specifically flexes MCP joints, not seen here (D) Dynamic finger splint: While dynamic elements are present, the primary function here is wrist positioning

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Marsupialization is an ideal treatment of choice for condition X involving the female reproductive tract, the lesion responsible for condition X is located at?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bartholin gland

Marsupialization is an ideal treatment of choice for Bartholin cyst/abscess. The given clinical vignette is suggestive of leison of the Bartholin gland.

Bartholin glands:

Bartholin glands are the homologs of the male bulbourethral or Cowper glands. The ducts of these glands open in the groove between the hymen and the labia minora at approximately 5 and 7 o’clock positions. These glands are stimulated by sexual arousal. Bartholin glands are the homologs of the male bulbourethral or Cowper glands.

Clinical conditions :

* Bartholin cyst: Caused by obstruction of the Bartholin ducts by proteinaceous material or by inflammation from infection. Symptomatic or recurrent cysts may require marsupialization or gland excision.

* Bartholin abscess: An infected Bartholin cyst can lead to an abscess. It usually requires surgical drainage.

Pathology:

* These commonly involve the duct and are most commonly sexually transmitted. Infection is generally polymicrobial.

Clinical features:

* If the size is big, it might cause abdominal and vaginal discomfort with dyspareunia.

* A vulval cleft of 'S' shape is usually noted on inspection.

* It is fluctuant swelling and transillumination can be positive as the fluid collected is generally clear.

Treatment:

* Analgesics for pain

* Antibiotic for combating infections.

* Specific treatment include Marsupialization, Incision and drainage with word catheter placement and Bartholinectomy.

Notes:

In any woman above the age of forty with recurrent Bartholin cyst, a suspicion of Bartholin gland cancer should arise and the cyst wall should be sent for biopsy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A young female comes to the emergency department after consuming 100 tablets of aspirin. What should be the next step in management?
options: N-acetyl cysteine to replenish glutathione stores
Glucagon to control bradycardia and hypoglycemia
Give sodium bicarbonate to alkalize urine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Give sodium bicarbonate to alkalize urine

The next step in the management of this patient who consumed 100 tablets of aspirin is to give sodium bicarbonate to alkalize the urine.

Alkalinization of urine will be helpful in the removal of aspirin, which is a weakly acidic drug and is susceptible to ion trapping in the urine. It is done by administration of sodium bicarbonate in 1 L of 5% dextrose in water (D5W). It is infused intravenously at twice the maintenance fluid requirements.

Alkalinization of urine is contraindicated in renal failure or if fluid administration may worsen pulmonary edema or congestive heart failure.

Other options:

Option A: N-acetyl cysteine is used as an antidote for the treatment of paracetamol poisoning which replenishes glutathione stores in the liver.

Option B: Pralidoxime is also used in organophosphate poisoning. It regenerates active acetylcholinesterase and relieves skeletal muscle end-plate block. It is usually used as an adjuvant to atropine.

Option D: Glucagon is used in beta-blocker toxicity.
questions.learning: Give sodium bicarbonate to alkalize urine — The next step in the management of this patient who consumed 100 tablets of aspirin is to give sodium bicarbonate to alkalize the urine.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with a history of diabetes and hypertension underwent fundus fluorescent angiography (FFA) to evaluate his decreasing vision. The FFA yields an image as shown below, which is characteristic of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Macular ischemia

The fundus fluorescent angiography (FFA) image shows enlarged foveal avascular zone, seen as a hypofluorescent patch in the macula (white arrow), with surrounding capillary non perfused areas (blue arrow). Both of these are suggestive of macular ischemia.

The above mentioned findings when combined with the history of diabetes in this patient points towards the diagnosis of diabetic macular ischemia.

FFA images in a case of diabetic retinopathy are given below:

1. Non proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR)

• Punctate or pinpoint areas of hyperfluorescence - microaneurysms
• Abnormal branching of arteriovenous shunt - intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA)
• Patchy filling defects of ischemia due to capillary atrophy or non perfusion
• Increase in the size of hypoperfusion in foveal avascular zone in macular ischemia

2. Proliferative diabetic retinopathy(PDR)

• Fluorescein leakage - in retinal neovascularization.
• Leakage in the disc region suggests neovascularization of the disc (NVD) and leakage in other regions suggests neovascularization elsewhere (NVE).

The image below shows pinpoint areas of hyperfluorescence and areas of fluorescein leakage in the fundus.

Option B: Macular edema also known as cystoid macular edema (CME) is a collection of fluid between the outer plexiform layer and the inner nuclear layer of the retina following a break in the blood-retina barrier. On fundoscopy, a honeycomb appearance is seen, and on FFA, flower petal pattern can be seen. The below image shows the flower petal pattern on FFA as seen in CME.

Option C: Submacular hemorrhage also known as subretinal hemorrhage will obscure the choroidal dye visualization and appaers as ill defined areas of hypoperfusion in the corresponding area. The retinal vessels overlying the area would, however will be visualized. There are no assosciated features of pinpoint hyperfluorescence and vascular leakage that are usually seen with diabetic macular ischemia. The below given images show fluorescein angiography which reveal blocked fluorescence in the maculae of both eyes due to subretinal hemorrhages.

Option D: Premacular hemorrhage is a term used to define vitreous hemorrhage that occurs in the subhyaloid space. It is seen as a region of hypofluorescence with no overlying retinal vasculature visualization on FFA.
questions.learning: Macular ischemia — The fundus fluorescent angiography (FFA) image shows enlarged foveal avascular zone, seen as a hypofluorescent patch in the macula (white arrow), with surrounding capillary non perfused areas (blue arrow).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following components is absent in smooth muscle?
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle contraction differs significantly from skeletal and cardiac muscle. A major difference is that troponin is absent in smooth muscle. In striated muscles, troponin is the protein that binds calcium to initiate contraction. In smooth muscle, this role is taken over by a protein called calmodulin. Actin (Option A) and Myosin (Option B) are the primary contractile proteins present in all muscle types. Tropomyosin (Option C) is also present in smooth muscle, but its role is less clear than in striated muscle, where it blocks the myosin-binding sites on actin. Instead of the troponin-tropomyosin complex, smooth muscle relies on the phosphorylation of the myosin light chain by the enzyme Myosin Light Chain Kinase (MLCK). This unique biochemical pathway allows smooth muscle to maintain long-term contraction (tone) with very little energy expenditure, a feature essential for the function of blood vessels and the gastrointestinal tract
questions.learning: Smooth muscle contraction differs significantly from skeletal and cardiac muscle. A major difference is that troponin is absent in smooth muscle.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
A young athlete presented with chest pain and dyspnea. His brother passed away due to sudden cardiac death. He is diagnosed with HCM. A harsh systolic murmur is heard in the left sternal border. Which of the following will increase the murmur?

HCM - Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Valsalva

The clinical vignette of an athlete with chest pain and dyspnea whose family history is suggestive of sudden cardiac death due to HCM and a harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal border are all in favour of HCM murmur. It increases in intensity while performing the Valsalva manoeuvre.

The murmur of HCM is an ejection systolic murmur best heard at the lower left sternal border.

The intensity of the mid-systolic murmur is

Increased by -Valsalva strain phase, Standing posture, and exercise
Decreased by - Squatting, passive leg raising, and handgrip.

Valsalva manoeuvre involves the performance of forced expiration against a closed glottis.

HCM is the leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young adults. It is defined as left ventricular hypertrophy of >15mm on ECHO. The left ventricular myocardium is poorly compliant. This leads to abnormal diastolic filling and intermittent ventricular outflow obstruction, i.e.,  primarily diastolic dysfunction.

Gross features of HCM:

• Massive myocardial hypertrophy usually without ventricular dilation
• Asymmetric septal hypertrophy- disproportionate thickening of the ventricular septum relative to the left ventricle free wall
• Banana-shaped left ventricle- due to bulging of the ventricular septum into the lumen

The image given below shows changes in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy compared to a normal heart. HCM shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy and a thickened left ventricle wall.

Histologic features of the HCM:

Massive myocyte hypertrophy- with transverse myocyte diameters frequently greater than 40 μm, normal is approximately 15 μm.
Myofiber disarray- haphazard disarray of bundles of myocytes, individual myocytes, and contractile elements in sarcomeres within cells
Interstitial fibrosis and replacement fibrosis
The image given below is a histologic section of cardiac muscle showing myocyte disarray and extreme hypertrophy seen in an abnormal HCM septum.

Pathophysiology:

HCM is characterized by reduced stroke volume due to impaired diastolic filling. Approximately 25% of patients with HCM have dynamic obstruction to the left ventricular outflow as the anterior mitral leaflet moves toward the ventricular septum during systole. The compromised cardiac output in conjunction with a secondary increase in pulmonary venous pressure explains the exertional dyspnea seen in these patients.

Major clinical problems in HCM are atrial fibrillation, mural thrombus formation leading to embolization and stroke, cardiac failure, ventricular arrhythmias, and sudden death.

ECG - findings:

Prominent abnormal Q waves
P wave abnormalities
Left axis deviation
Deeply inverted T waves

Echocardiography:

LV wall thickness ≥15 mm
Systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve
LVOT obstruction
The management options in patients with HCM:

Beta-blockers
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
Disopyramide
Drugs to be avoided in patients with significant LVOT obstruction:

Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
Nitroglycerin
Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, ARBs
Diuretics
Preventive intra-cardiac defibrillator is indicated for patients with HCM and documented cardiac arrest or sustained ventricular tachycardia.

Note: Valsalva maneuver decreases the intensity of all murmurs except MVP (mitral valve prolapse) and HCM.
questions.learning: Valsalva — The clinical vignette of an athlete with chest pain and dyspnea whose family history is suggestive of sudden cardiac death due to HCM and a harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal border are all in favour of HCM murmur.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 51-year-old woman reports a palpable lump in her right breast discovered during a routine examination. The mass measures more than 5 cm, and ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes are palpable. If the lesion is confirmed to be malignant, what is the most likely stage of the disease?
questions.explanation: Breast cancer staging follows the TNM (Tumor, Node, Metastasis) system. In this clinical scenario, a tumor mass measuring over 5 cm is classified as T3. The presence of "palpable lymph nodes" in the "ipsilateral axilla" that are clinically suspicious signifies N1 status. The prefix "c" denotes "clinical" staging based on examination and imaging before surgery. Therefore, the likely clinical stage is cT3N1M0. Option C (cT4) is incorrect because T4 requires invasion into the chest wall or skin (e.g., ulceration, peau d'orange) regardless of size. Options B and D use the prefix "y," which denotes staging after neoadjuvant therapy (post-treatment staging), which has not occurred in this patient yet. Assuming no evidence of distant metastasis (M0), the findings of size >5cm and positive axillary nodes lead directly to the cT3N1M0 classification, placing the patient in Stage IIIA
questions.learning: Breast cancer staging follows the TNM (Tumor, Node, Metastasis) system. In this clinical scenario, a tumor mass measuring over 5 cm is classified as T3.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following agents is not commonly used in the management of bronchial asthma?
questions.explanation: Cholinergic drugs (parasympathomimetics) are not used in asthma because they stimulate muscarinic receptors, leading to bronchoconstriction and increased mucus secretion, which would severely worsen an asthma attack. Instead, anticholinergic drugs like Ipratropium are used to cause bronchodilation. Phosphodiesterase inhibitors (Option A), such as Theophylline, increase cAMP levels to relax bronchial smooth muscle. Steroids (Option B), such as Fluticasone or Prednisolone, are essential for reducing the underlying airway inflammation. Beta-agonists (Option C), like Salbutamol (SABA) or Salmeterol (LABA), are the mainstay for rapid relief and long-term control by stimulating beta-2 receptors to cause bronchodilation. Asthma management focuses on relaxing airway smooth muscle and suppressing immune-mediated inflammation. Because cholinergic stimulation is a primary physiological trigger for airway narrowing, these drugs are strictly avoided in asthmatic patients. Thus, Cholinergic drugs are the correct answer as they are contraindicated rather than utilized in asthma management
questions.learning: Cholinergic drugs (parasympathomimetics) are not used in asthma because they stimulate muscarinic receptors, leading to bronchoconstriction and increased mucus secretion, which would severely worsen an asthma attack.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
A child presented to the OPD with complaints of fatigue and muscle weakness while exercising. Laboratory investigations found that LCFA oxidation was affected. A muscle biopsy was done which revealed the presence of fat vacuoles. What is the probable diagnosis?

LCFA- Long-chain fatty acid

LPL- Lipoprotein lipase

LDL- Low-density lipoprotein
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Carnitine deficiency

The clinical scenario of a child with fatigue and muscle weakness on exercise with laboratory findings of LCFA oxidation deficiency and fat vacuoles on muscle biopsy suggests a diagnosis of carnitine deficiency.

Carnitine deficiency is a defect in fatty acid oxidation that leads to hypoketotic hypoglycemia and hyperammonemia. Carnitine transports activated LCFA (long chain fatty acyl CoA) from the cytoplasm to the mitochondria for beta-oxidation (as they cannot cross the mitochondrial membrane), carnitine deficiency impairs this transport causing accumulation of lipids (skeletal muscle weakness). This excess fatty acid inhibits the urea cycle causing hyperammonemia. Since beta-oxidation cannot occur, energy production is reduced, and there is hypoglycemia without a corresponding increase in ketone bodies (hypoketotic) during times of glucose depletion such as exercise.

The role of carnitine in the metabolism of fatty acids is demonstrated in the image below:

Clinical features of carnitine deficiency begin in childhood and include poor feeding, lethargy, liver dysfunction and hepatomegaly, hypotonia, and dilated cardiomyopathy. Treatment involves oral supplementation of carnitine.

Other options:

Option A: An increase in LDL can cause hyperlipoproteinemia, and reduced LDL can cause defective absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.

Option B: LPL is involved in hydrolysis of lipoproteins in the blood to free fatty acid and glycerol which are then taken up by the tissues. A defective LPL can cause type 1 familial chylomicronemia syndrome presenting as pancreatitis.

Option C: Fatty acid synthase is a multienzyme complex involved in fatty acid synthesis in the cytosol which when defective may impair energy production, essential fatty acids, and affect metabolic pathways. There is no accumulation of fat vacuoles since fatty acids are not synthesised.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Covaxin is a/an:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inactivated whole virus vaccine

Covaxin (BBV152) is an inactivated whole-virion SARS-CoV-2 vaccine developed by Bharat Biotech in collaboration with the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR). It contains chemically inactivated SARS-CoV-2 virus with an Algel-IMDG adjuvant to enhance the immune response.

Why not the other options?

• A. Live attenuated vaccine❌: Contains weakened live virus; Covaxin is not live.
• C. Protein subunit vaccine❌: Example: Novavax (Covovax).
• D. Viral vector vaccine❌: Example: Covishield (ChAdOx1 nCoV-19) and Sputnik V.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which element acts as the cofactor for the enzyme glutathione peroxidase?
questions.explanation: Glutathione peroxidase is a vital antioxidant enzyme that protects cells from oxidative damage by catalyzing the reduction of hydrogen peroxide and lipid hydroperoxides. Its structural and functional integrity depends on selenium, which is incorporated into the enzyme as the amino acid selenocysteine at the active site. Manganese (Option A) is a cofactor for mitochondrial superoxide dismutase (Mn-SOD). Copper (Option C) and Zinc are cofactors for the cytosolic version of superoxide dismutase (CuZn-SOD) and are also essential for cytochrome c oxidase. Magnesium (Option D) is a ubiquitous cofactor for almost all enzymes utilizing ATP, such as hexokinase. Selenium deficiency can lead to Keshan disease (a cardiomyopathy), primarily because of the resulting impairment in glutathione peroxidase activity and increased oxidative stress. This biochemical relationship highlights the importance of trace elements in the body's endogenous defense mechanisms against reactive oxygen species, a frequent theme in biochemistry and nutritional science examinations
questions.learning: Glutathione peroxidase is a vital antioxidant enzyme that protects cells from oxidative damage by catalyzing the reduction of hydrogen peroxide and lipid hydroperoxides.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with weakness of the lower half of the face on the right side, while forehead wrinkling is preserved. The lesion is most likely located in which of the following?
options: Upper motor neuron of the facial nerve
Lower motor neuron of the facial nerve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Upper motor neuron of the facial nerve

An upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion of the facial nerve causes contralateral weakness of the lower half of the face with preservation of forehead movements. This occurs because the upper facial muscles (forehead) receive bilateral corticobulbar innervation, whereas the lower facial muscles receive only contralateral corticobulbar innervation. Therefore, a unilateral UMN lesion affects only the contralateral lower face.

Why not the other options?

• B. Lower motor neuron of the facial nerve: Produces ipsilateral paralysis of the entire half of the face, including inability to wrinkle the forehead, close the eye, or smile (e.g., Bell’s palsy).
• C. Trigeminal nerve (CN V): Supplies the muscles of mastication and facial sensation; it does not cause facial expression weakness.
• D. Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII): Supplies the tongue muscles; injury causes tongue deviation toward the affected side, not facial weakness.
questions.learning: Upper motor neuron of the facial nerve — An upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion of the facial nerve causes contralateral weakness of the lower half of the face with preservation of forehead movements.

• Eonism refers to cross-dressing, typically for sexual arousal or identity expression, and falls under transvestic fetishism.
• Frotteurism involves rubbing against non-consenting individuals, commonly in crowded public spaces, and is one of the most frequent paraphilias in adolescent males.
• Necrophilia is sexual activity with corpses, often associated with severe psychopathology and legal consequences.
• Algolagnia is deriving sexual pleasure from pain, forming the basis of sadism/masochism spectra.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following models of disease causation is depicted in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sufficient component cause model

The model of disease causation depicted below is a sufficient component cause model.

It was developed by Rothman based on the idea that an outcome can only happen when a sufficient cause is present. A disease can have multiple sufficient causes. But, each sufficient cause can consist of a pie chart of component causes, a causal pie.  One component cause can be a part of more than one sufficient cause. A component cause can be considered necessary if it is a part of a disease's sufficient causes.

In the given model, each pie chart represents a sufficient cause made of component causes. Since B is present in all the charts, it can be considered a necessary cause. All the others are contributing causes.

Other options:

Option B: An epidemiological triad depicts the interrelationship between the causative agent, the host, and the environment. All of them contribute to disease development. The aim of an epidemiological triad is to identify how to break this relationship and prevent the outbreak of the disease.

Option C: PERT is used for network analysis. It is a type of quantitative management technique that helps in detailed planning and comprehensive supervision.

Option D: The web of causation considers all the predisposing factors and their complex interrelationship with each other. This model is ideally suited to study chronic disease. The web of causation does not imply that the disease is controlled only when all the multiple chains of causation are removed. Sometimes removal of one significant link is sufficient to control the disease.
questions.learning: Sufficient component cause model — The model of disease causation depicted below is a sufficient component cause model. It was developed by Rothman based on the idea that an outcome can only happen when a sufficient cause is present.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 20-year-old male patient presented with a history of lower backache and early morning stiffness for two years. He also gave a history of bilateral heel pain since 6 months. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ankylosing spondylitis

The given clinical scenario of a young male presenting with lower backache, heel pain, and early morning stiffness is suggestive of ankylosing spondylitis.

Ankylosing spondylitis is commonly seen in young males and has a strong association with HLAB27. The patient usually presents with complaints of recurring backache and early morning stiffness. Later the patient can develop other symptoms like generalized fatigue, pain, swelling of the joints, foot strain, tenderness at insertion of the achilles tendon, and intercostal pain.

Extra-articular manifestations include iritis, pericarditis, aortic incompetence, apical lobe fibrosis, generalized osteoporosis, and atlantoaxial joint subluxation.

On examination, there is a loss of normal lumbar lordosis, increased thoracic kyphosis, diminished spinal movements, and decreased chest expansion.

Other findings are:

• Positive Fleche's test - It is done to assess cervical spine involvement. Here the patient is asked to touch the wall with the back of the head without raising the chin.
• Positive tests for sacroiliac joint involvement such as the pump handle test, pelvic compression test, and Fabre’s test.

ASAS diagnostic criteria for ankylosing spondylitis:

Sacroiliitis on imaging plus ≥1 SpA feature:
or
HLA-B27 +ve plus ≥2 other SpA features

Sacroiliitis on imaging:

• Active (acute) inflammation on MRI highly suggestive of SpA-associated sacroiliitis

and/or

• Definite radiographic sacroiliitis according to modified New York criteria (grade >2 bilateral or grade 3 - 4 unilateral)

SpA features:

• Inflammatory back pain
• Arthritis
• Enthesitis (heel)
• Anterior uveitis
• Dactylitis
• Psoriasis
• Crohn’s disease or ulcerative
• colitis
• Good response to NSAIDs
• Family history of SpA
• HLA-B27
• Elevated CRP

X-ray findings in ankylosing spondylitis:

• Sacro-iliac joints:

• Cardinal sign/earliest sign– erosion and fuzziness of the sacroiliac joints
• Later- peri-articular sclerosis and bony ankylosis of the joint

• Vertebral changes:

• Earliest- flattening of the normal anterior concavity of the vertebral body (‘squaring’)
• Later- ossification of the ligaments around the intervertebral discs produces syndesmophytes (bridges) between adjacent vertebrae
• Bamboo spine appearance- due to bridging at several vertebral levels
• Long-standing cases are associated with osteoporosis. Wedging of the vertebral bodies produces hyperkyphosis of the spine.

• Progressive bony ankylosis or erosive arthritis may be seen in peripheral joints.

Bamboo-spine appearance is seen in the Xray of the lumbar spine below:

Other options:

Option B: TB spine (Pott's disease) is the commonest form of bone and joint tuberculosis. The clinical presentation can be variable with pain being the common symptom. The pain can be diffuse initially but later on, it gets localized to the affected segment. Stiffness is also seen as an early symptom. The patient can also present with swelling due to the formation of a cold abscess. Paraplegia and spinal deformities can occur at later stages.

Option C: Disc prolapse refers to protrusion or extrusion of the nucleus pulposus through a rent in the annulus fibrosis. The patient presents with low backache which can be acute or chronic. The patient can also present with pain radiating to the gluteal region, back of the thigh, and leg. This is referred to as sciatic pain. There can be paraesthesia in the dermatomes of the affected nerve roots.

Option D: Mechanical back pain is a broader term that includes all the causes that cause alternation in the spine mechanics. It includes conditions like osteoarthritis, lumbar spondylosis, osteoporosis, etc.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following viruses has the least teratogenic effect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Herpes simplex virus (HSV)-2

In the given list of viruses, herpes simplex virus (HSV)-2 has the least teratogenic effect.

HSV-2 presents as a genital tract infection transmitted via sexual contact. Premature labour or IUGR may occur if the primary infection is acquired during the last trimester. As the transplacental route of spread is uncommon, it is considered to have a less teratogenic effect on the baby.

Caesarean delivery is recommended in cases of active primary genital HSV infection because the virus shed from the cervix or lower genital tract during vaginal delivery is a major source of infection in the fetus.

Babies with neonatal herpes exhibit three categories of disease: (1) localized lesions of the skin, eye, and mouth, (2) encephalitis with or without skin involvement and (3) disseminated disease. It is treated with IV acyclovir.

Other options:

Option A: The varicella-zoster virus, which causes chickenpox, can pass through the placenta and result in congenital varicella syndrome (CVS). Hypoplasia of the limbs, psychomotor retardation, IUGR, chorioretinal scarring, cataracts and microcephaly are the characteristics of CVS. If maternal infection develops after 20 weeks, the risk of congenital malformation is almost absent. Varicella zoster immunoglobulin (VZIG) should also be given to newborns exposed within 5 days of delivery.

Option B: The transplacental spread of the rubella virus is known to cause congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) in the baby.  When this infection develops in the first, second or third months, there is a 60%, 25%, or 10% chance of significant abnormalities, respectively. Congenital rubella syndrome predominantly includes sensorineural deafness, patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), cataracts and retinopathy. The virus predominantly affects the fetus and is extremely teratogenic if contracted within the first trimester.

Option C: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) replicates in respiratory epithelial cells, salivary glands, and kidneys and persists in lymphocytes. The transplacental route primarily affects the foetus, resulting in microcephaly, intracranial calcification, hepatosplenomegaly, chorioretinitis, mental retardation, and sensorineural deafness. Unlike rubella, CMV may damage fetal organs throughout gestation.
questions.learning: Herpes simplex virus (HSV)-2 — In the given list of viruses, herpes simplex virus (HSV)-2 has the least teratogenic effect. HSV-2 presents as a genital tract infection transmitted via sexual contact.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In a diabetic patient presenting with a fungal infection involving the sinuses and periorbital region, along with significant visual impairment, which medication would be the most appropriate choice for treatment?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario—a diabetic patient with invasive fungal sinusitis and periorbital involvement (Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis)—is a surgical and medical emergency. Liposomal Amphotericin B is the gold-standard, first-line systemic antifungal agent for this condition. It provides broad-spectrum coverage against Mucorales and other aggressive molds while having a better safety profile regarding nephrotoxicity than conventional amphotericin. Itraconazole (Option A) and Ketoconazole (Option C) are oral azoles that lack the necessary potency for acute, invasive, life-threatening fungal infections of this nature. Broad-spectrum antibiotics (Option D) have no activity against fungi and would only be useful for secondary bacterial infections. The "notable visual impairment" suggests orbital invasion, which necessitates immediate intravenous therapy alongside aggressive surgical debridement of necrotic tissue. Therefore, intravenous Liposomal Amphotericin B is the definitive and life-saving pharmacological intervention for this patient

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following symptoms is least likely to be associated with a panic attack?
questions.explanation: A panic attack is a sudden episode of intense fear that triggers severe physical reactions when there is no real danger. Common physiological symptoms include "palpitations" (Option A), "chest discomfort" (Option C), sweating, and shortness of breath. Cognitive symptoms often include an intense "fear of losing control or dying" (Option B). While patients with chronic panic disorder may be at a higher risk for depression and suicidal ideation over time, a "suicide attempt" (Option D) is "least likely" to be a symptom of an acute panic attack itself. An attack is characteristically short-lived, usually peaking within 10 minutes, and the patient is typically paralyzed by the immediate somatic sensations of terror rather than engaging in deliberate self-harm during the event. Understanding these symptoms is vital because panic attacks often mimic medical emergencies, such as a myocardial infarction. Management includes reassurance, cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), and occasionally short-term benzodiazepines or long-term SSRIs to reduce the frequency of attacks

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which artery is used for arteriovenous shunting with the great saphenous vein for hemodialysis, and is located behind the medial malleolus and 2.5 cm in front of the tendocalcaneus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior tibial artery

The posterior tibial artery, located behind the medial malleolus and 2.5 cm in front of the tendocalcaneus, that is used for arteriovenous (AV) shunting with the great saphenous vein for hemodialysis.

The posterior tibial artery is situated behind the medial malleolus and approximately 2.5 cm in front of the tendocalcaneus, making it a suitable site for creating an AV fistula with the great saphenous vein. This location allows for optimal access and ensures that the shunt can handle the necessary blood flow for effective dialysis with the great saphenous vein. However, they are not commonly used for AV shunting in common practices.

Arteries used for AV shunting include the radial artery and the brachial artery in the upper arm, which are frequently employed for hemodialysis access. In the lower leg, the anterior tibial artery and the peroneal (fibular) artery are less commonly used for this procedure.

Other options:

Option A: In comparison, the anterior tibial artery is located on the anterior aspect of the leg and runs down the front of the tibia, not behind the medial malleolus.

Option C: The peroneal (fibular) artery is situated on the lateral side of the leg, travelling alongside the fibula, and is also not located behind the medial malleolus.

Option D: The fibular circumflex artery is a small artery and is not commonly used for hemodialysis access. It is not a standard choice and does not fit the anatomical location described, as it is a branch of the anterior tibial artery.
questions.learning: Posterior tibial artery — The posterior tibial artery, located behind the medial malleolus and 2.5 cm in front of the tendocalcaneus, that is used for arteriovenous (AV) shunting with the great saphenous vein for hemodialysis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a patient with Meckel’s diverticulum, what is the most likely underlying cause of right lower abdominal pain accompanied by rebound tenderness?
questions.explanation: In clinical practice, lower right abdominal pain accompanied by rebound tenderness (McBurney’s point tenderness) is most commonly caused by acute appendicitis, even in patients known to have a Meckel's diverticulum. While Meckel's diverticulum can become inflamed (Meckel's diverticulitis) and mimic the symptoms of appendicitis, standard appendicitis remains a far more prevalent cause of localized peritoneal irritation in the right lower quadrant. Regarding the distractors, perforation (Option A) typically presents with more diffuse, generalized peritonitis rather than localized pain. Intestinal obstruction (Option B) usually presents with colicky pain, distension, and vomiting rather than localized rebound tenderness. Cholecystitis (Option D) presents with right upper quadrant pain and a positive Murphy’s sign. Therefore, given the classic clinical location and findings, appendicitis is the most probable diagnosis
questions.learning: In clinical practice, lower right abdominal pain accompanied by rebound tenderness (McBurney’s point tenderness) is most commonly caused by acute appendicitis, even in patients known to have a Meckel's diverticulum.

| Type II (Compression Achalasia) | Intermittent periods of pan-esophageal pressurization (> 20% of swallows) due to some preserved but uncoordinated esophageal body peristalsis and failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax. | Good response to therapy.

| Type III (Spastic Achalasia) | Spastic contractions in the distal esophagus and failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax. | Least common type. Often harder to treat and may require more aggressive therapy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following tests would a surgeon advise first in a patient with a large thyroid swelling?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thyroid function tests

Assessing the biochemical function of the thyroid i.e. thyroid function test (TFT) is the first investigation done in any thyroid condition.

Evaluation of any thyroid disease should begin with the assessment of TSH, T3, and T4. TSH is the only test necessary in most patients with thyroid nodules that clinically appear to be euthyroid.

If a discrete swelling is associated with hyperthyroidism, it indicates a toxic adenoma. This is followed by an ultrasound of the neck or radioiodine uptake. Findings in thyroid swelling associated with thyroid neoplasia include microcalcification and increased vascularity. FNAC should be used under ultrasound guidance, on all nodules that fall outside a fully benign category.

Modalities for evaluation of thyroid swelling include:

* Laboratory evaluation

* TSH

* T3

* T4

* Thyroid imaging

* Ultrasound

* Radioisotope scanning

* CT/MRI

* Biopsy techniques

* Fine needle aspiration biopsy (FNA)

* Tru-cut/core-needle biopsy

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Identify the diagnosis.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Syndactyly

The image shows the middle two toes being fused together which is a condition called 'Syndactyly'.

Syndactyly is the fusion of digits that can involve either the fingers or toes. It is a congenital malformation and can be of various degrees based on the extent of fusion of the tissues involved:

* Simple-only soft tissue

* Complex- skin and bone fused

* Incomplete- only part of the web

* Complete- entire web is affected

Pathophysiology: due to lack of apoptosis during development of the digits.

Treatment: Mild or incomplete syndactyly of central digits need no treatment.

If it disrupts the function of the handthen surgical separation of the conjoined structures and reconstruction is needed.

Note:

Syndactyly of border digits can cause progressive deformity with growth and thus this needs early surgical correction.

Care is taken not to injure the digital arteries when multiple digits are involved by separating only one side of a digit at a time.

Other options:

Symphalangism: congenital stiffness of the proximal interphalangeal joints of the fingers.

Polydactyly: extra digits are present in fingers or toes.

Brachydactyly: undergrowth of a digit seen in syndromes like Turner's syndrome.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the option with the least risk of TOLAC (trial of labor after cesarean)?
questions.explanation: For a woman planning a Trial of Labor After Cesarean (TOLAC), the type of previous uterine scar is the most important factor in determining the risk of uterine rupture. A Low-segment transverse incision (Option C) is associated with the least risk of rupture (approximately 0.5–1%). A previous Classical C-section (Option A), involving a vertical incision in the active upper segment of the uterus, carries the highest risk (up to 12%) and is a contraindication for TOLAC. Pre-eclampsia (Option B) and Breech presentation (Option D) are clinical factors that may influence the success of labor or necessitate a repeat C-section for other reasons, but they do not define the structural "risk" of the scar itself. Candidates for TOLAC must have a documented low-transverse scar, a pelvis clinically adequate for the fetal size, and immediate access to emergency surgery and neonatal resuscitation. This evidence-based selection is critical for providing women with the option of a safe vaginal birth after a previous cesarean

questions.text: A male had a vasectomy 1 month ago and the couple asks the doctor if they have to take any precautions while having sex. What advice should be given?
options: Oral contraceptive pills for 1 month for the woman
Hormonal treatment given for 2 more months for the man
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Use condoms for 3 months

The best advice is to use condoms for 3 months as the sperms are stored in the reproductive tract for upto 3 months.

Vasectomy

* Vasectomy consists of dividing the vas deferens and disrupting the passage of sperms.

* It is done through a small incision in the scrotum, under local anaesthesia. The sterility is not immediate. The sperms are stored in the reproductive tract for up to 3 months. The couple must therefore abstain from intercourse during this period or use other methods of contraception.

* Approximately, 20 ejaculates clear the semen of all sperms. Two semen analysis reports must confirm the absence of sperms before the man can be declared sterile.

* No- scalpel technique has been now adopted. One single incision is made with a special forceps and skin stitch is not required. Clips and plugs can be applied over the vas instead of cutting. Vasectomy is cheaper than tubectomy

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A woman was attacked by a rabid dog. The dog develops symptoms and passes away within a week. Which method is most effective for diagnosing rabies antemortem?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. DFAT - Direct fluorescent antibody test

The most effective method for diagnosing rabies antemortem is DFAT (direct fluorescent antibody test).

Direct immunofluorescence test (direct-IF), also called a direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) test, can be performed to detect rabies nucleoprotein antigens in specimens by using specific monoclonal antibodies tagged with fluorescent dye. Because of its high sensitivity and specificity, the DFA test is considered the “gold standard” method for rabies diagnosis. The best specimen is the hair follicle of the nape of the neck of the dog (most sensitive). Corneal impression smear can also be used. It is usually positive in the late stage with a sensitivity of 30%.

Negri bodies are pathognomonic of rabies virus infection. These are spherical-shaped cytoplasmic inclusion bodies. They contain an eosinophilic matrix, basophilic granules, and viral antigens. Negri body detection in histopathological staining of brain biopsies (hippocampus)—for postmortem diagnosis of rabies.

Rabies is a fatal infection of the central nervous system transmitted by the bite of a rabid animal. It is caused by rhabdoviruses. These viruses are enveloped, rod- or bullet-shaped, and contain single-stranded RNA.

Clinical features of rabies can be categorised into three phases: prodromal, encephalitic phase, and coma. The prodromal phase is characterised by malaise, anorexia, headache, and irritability. This is followed by the encephalitic stage, characterised by abnormal behaviour and seizures. They develop hydrophobia. Attempts to drink liquids cause painful spasms of the pharynx and larynx, producing a choking sensation. Therefore, the patients develop a phobia of even the sight or sound of water. Finally, seizures, coma, and death occur.

Laboratory diagnosis can be done on a postmortem or antemortem basis. Postmortem diagnosis is done by the demonstration of Negri bodies. These bodies are common in the pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus and Purkinje cells of the cerebellum. Antemortem diagnosis is done from corneal scrapings, saliva, or skin biopsy. Demonstration of the virus is done using direct immunofluorescence.

Other methods used in the diagnosis are intracerebral inoculation in the mice, tissue culture, ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay), and PCR (polymerase chain reaction). Seller's technique (basic fuchsin and methylene blue in methanol) is used to stain brain impression smears, which has the advantage of allowing for simultaneous fixation and staining.

Reducing the stray dog population and vaccinating all dogs is the most cost-effective and logical way to reduce the incidence of rabies. The Animal Birth Control initiative by the Government of India is aimed at achieving this goal.

Rabies is a highly fatal viral disease caused by the Lyssavirus type 1, which affects the central nervous system. Dogs are considered the major source of rabies infection. Thus, immunization of dogs at the age of 3-4 months and booster doses at regular intervals are recommended to control rabies.

The spread of rabies can be:

* Centripetal:

* The virus enters the peripheral neurons, and it moves via retrograde fast axonal transport towards the spinal cord or brainstem at a speed of up to 250 mm/day

* Once within the CNS, it spreads quickly to other regions in the CNS through fast axonal transport. It infects neurons primarily but may rarely infect astrocytes.

* Centrifugal:

* After CNS infection is established, it spreads along the sensory and autonomic nerves to the salivary glands, adrenal glands, and skin.

* The rabies virus replicates in acinar cells of the salivary glands and is secreted in the saliva of rabid animals that serve as vectors.

External examination of the brain shows intense edema and vascular congestion. Neuronal dysfunction associated with an inflammatory reaction is seen, which is most severe in the brainstem involving the basal ganglia, spinal cord, and dorsal root ganglia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the probable diagnosis made from the MRI image given below?
questions.explanation: The MRI image reveals destruction of adjacent vertebral bodies and the intervening disc space, accompanied by a large prevertebral and paravertebral fluid collection. This is the hallmark of Pott’s spine (Spinal Tuberculosis). The fluid collection is known as a "cold abscess" because it lacks the intense acute inflammation of a pyogenic infection. Multiple myeloma (Option A) causes multiple "punched-out" lytic lesions but usually spares the disc space. Ankylosing spondylitis (Option B) shows fusion and syndesmophytes without abscess formation. Pyogenic spondylitis (Option C) presents with more acute, rapid bone destruction and systemic toxicity compared to the subacute nature of TB. Because Pott’s spine characteristically involves two adjacent vertebrae, destroys the disc, and forms large paravertebral abscesses, it is the definitive diagnosis

The risk factors of ovarian carcinoma are:

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Resistant hypertension is defined as?
options: BP >160/90 mmHg with three or more anti-hypertensives
BP >140/90 mmHg with three or more anti-hypertensives
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. BP >140/90 mmHg with three or more anti-hypertensives

Resistant hypertension is defined as blood pressure being persistently >140/90 mmHg despite taking three or more antihypertensive agents, including a diuretic.

Resistant hypertension is more common in patients aged >60 years than in younger patients.

Resistant hypertension may be related to pseudohypertension (high office blood pressure and lower home blood pressure measurements), nonadherence to therapy, and secondary causes of hypertension including obesity, excessive alcohol intake, and primary aldosteronism.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Who is responsible for handling the investigation in the case of a custodial death?
questions.explanation: Under the laws of India (specifically Section 176 of the CrPC), an inquest in the case of a custodial death—any death that occurs while a person is in police or judicial custody—must be conducted by a Judicial Magistrate. This mandatory legal requirement is designed to ensure an impartial, independent investigation into the cause and circumstances of the death, serving as a safeguard against potential human rights abuses or cover-ups. A Police inspector (Option A), Jail superintendent (Option B), or Superintendent of Police (Option C) are not legally authorized to lead this specific type of death inquiry, as they are part of the very system where the custody occurred. The Judicial Magistrate has the power to examine witnesses, record statements, and order a post-mortem examination by a medical board if necessary. This transparent process is a fundamental principle of justice and the rule of law, ensuring that the state is held accountable for the safety and lives of all individuals under its detention
questions.learning: Under the laws of India (specifically Section 176 of the CrPC), an inquest in the case of a custodial death—any death that occurs while a person is in police or judicial custody—must be conducted by a Judicial Magistrate.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In the 18th century, the British East India Company smuggled which of the following drugs to China?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Opium

The British East India Company smuggled opium into China in exchange for tea, silk and porcelain pots.

Opium derived from the immature seedpods of the opium poppy (Papaver somniferum), was originally indigenous to the present-day territory of Turkey. The introduction of opium to China occurred during the late 6th or early 7th century CE, facilitated by Turkish and Arab traders.

During this time, tobacco smoking moved from North America to China, resulting in widespread opium smoking. Opium addiction and imports increased in the first century of the Qing era (1644–1911/12). To address the issue, the Yongzheng emperor (1722–35) banned opium trafficking and consumption in 1729. Despite hurdles, the trade continued, and in 1796, the Jiaqing emperor banned opium imports and cultivation. Opium sales survived despite these laws.

In the early 18th century, the Portuguese made a lot of money importing opium from India and selling it in China. British traders became China's main suppliers in 1773. The British East India Company monopolized Bengali opium farming. The company developed an inexpensive and productive opium poppies cultivation method in this location. The US and other Western nations traded Turkish and Indian opium.

The opium trade was pursued by Britain and other European nations as a means to address their persistent trade deficit with China. In Europe, there existed a substantial and notable demand for Chinese commodities such as tea, silks, and porcelain pots. Conversely, in China, there was a very limited market for Europe's manufactured goods and other trade items. As a result, Europeans were required to utilize gold or silver as payment for Chinese goods. The opium trade, which resulted in a consistent demand for opium among Chinese individuals addicted to the substance, effectively addressed the persistent trade imbalance by facilitating the importation of opium from Western countries.

Opium was not carried by the East India Company. Due to the Chinese restriction, the corporation outsourced it to “country traders”—private traders entitled to transport commodities from India to China. Smugglers on the Chinese shore bought opium from country traders. The traders gave the East India Company their sales of gold and silver. The corporation spent its gold and silver in China on profitable things to sell in England.

Opium imports into China rose from 200 chests in 1729 to 1,000 in 1767 and 10,000 between 1820 and 1830. Although chest weight varied by origin, it averaged 140 pounds (63.5 kg). By 1838, China imported 40,000 chests annually. China lost the balance of payments to Britain for the first time. Opium distribution networks had evolved across China, frequently with corrupt officials' help. High opium addiction levels affected imperial troops and officials.
questions.learning: Opium — The British East India Company smuggled opium into China in exchange for tea, silk and porcelain pots. Opium derived from the immature seedpods of the opium poppy (Papaver somniferum), was originally indigenous to the present-day territory of Turkey.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Chronic malnutrition is best measured by?
questions.explanation: Height-for-age is the most reliable indicator for measuring chronic malnutrition, as it reflects long-term nutritional deficiencies that lead to stunting. Stunting, defined as a height-for-age Z-score below -2 standard deviations, indicates that a child has failed to reach their linear growth potential due to ongoing poor health or nutrition. Weight-for-age (Option B) is used to identify children who are underweight, but it does not distinguish between acute and chronic malnutrition. Weight-for-height (Option C) and Body Mass Index (Option D) are primary measures for acute malnutrition or wasting, reflecting recent or rapid weight loss rather than long-term growth trends. Wasting indicates a high risk of mortality and requires immediate intervention, whereas low height-for-age indicates a permanent loss of growth that occurred over an extended period. Therefore, for assessing the long-term nutritional status of a population or individual, height-for-age is the gold standard
questions.learning: Height-for-age is the most reliable indicator for measuring chronic malnutrition, as it reflects long-term nutritional deficiencies that lead to stunting.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
Which of the following are the true statements about amyloidosis?

1. It is an extracellular protein.
2. It is called amyloid because of starch deposition.
3. Beta-pleated sheets are seen on X-ray crystallography
4. AL is a secondary type of amyloidosis.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1,2,3

The true statements about amyloidosis are:

• It is an extracellular protein.
• It is called amyloid because of starch deposition.
• Beta-pleated sheets are seen on X-ray crystallography.

Amyloidosis refers to extracellular deposits of fibrillar proteins.

Abnormal fibrils are produced by the aggregation of misfolded proteins. The fibrillar deposits bind a wide variety of proteoglycans and glycosaminoglycans, including heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate, and plasma proteins, notably the serum amyloid P component (SAP). Amyloid appears as an amorphous, eosinophilic, hyaline, extracellular substance.

The adsorbed proteins contain abundant charged sugar groups that give the deposits staining characteristics that resemble starch. Hence, these deposits were called amyloid.

It could be classified as systemic, localized, or hereditary amyloidosis. Microscopically, all types of amyloid deposits are made up of continuous, nonbranching fibrils. A characteristic cross-β-pleated sheet conformation is visualized on X-ray crystallography and infrared spectroscopy.

The stain used for amyloid deposits is congo red staining, which imparts pink to red color to the amyloid under ordinary light and apple-green birefringence under polarised microscopy.

AL type(Immunoglobulin light chain amyloidosis) of protein belongs to primary amyloidosis. It is seen in multiple myeloma and other monoclonal plasma cell proliferation.

The image shows a congo-red stained biopsy specimen with the following:

(A) Focal positive staining (orange-red) of amorphous extracellular material

(B) Apple-green birefringence under polarized light.

The next best step is to determine the type of precursor protein by immunohistochemistry, immunoelectron microscopy, or extraction and biochemical analysis using mass spectrometry.
questions.learning: 1,2,3 The true statements about amyloidosis are: • It is an extracellular protein. • It is called amyloid because of starch deposition. • Beta-pleated sheets are seen on X-ray crystallography.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding sutures in surgery? I. Barbed sutures have the advantage of eliminating the need for knots. II. Vertical mattress sutures help in eversion of wound edges. III. Aberdeen knot is used for continuous suturing. IV. Silk is preferred for subcuticular suturing. Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

An ideal surgical suture should provide adequate tensile strength, cause minimal tissue reaction, be easy to handle, and maintain wound approximation until healing occurs. Different suturing techniques and suture materials are selected according to the tissue involved and the desired wound healing characteristics. The following statements are true:

• I. Barbed sutures have the advantage of eliminating the need for knots: Barbed sutures contain unidirectional or bidirectional barbs that anchor the tissue, eliminating the need for knot tying, reducing operative time and distributing tension evenly.
• II. Vertical mattress sutures help in eversion of wound edges: The vertical mattress suture provides excellent wound edge eversion and distributes tension, making it useful for wounds under tension.
• III. Aberdeen knot is used for continuous suturing: The Aberdeen knot is a secure knot used to terminate continuous sutures, commonly in abdominal wall and skin closure.

Why is IV incorrect?

• IV. Silk is preferred for subcuticular suturing: Subcuticular suturing is usually performed with absorbable monofilament sutures such as Monocryl (poliglecaprone), Vicryl Rapide, or PDS for better cosmetic results. Silk, a braided non-absorbable suture, causes greater tissue reaction and is not preferred.
questions.learning: I, II and III — An ideal surgical suture should provide adequate tensile strength, cause minimal tissue reaction, be easy to handle, and maintain wound approximation until healing occurs.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What does the given pedigree chart indicate?
questions.explanation: The pedigree shows a pattern where an affected mother transmits the condition to all her children, regardless of sex. In the first generation, the affected female has multiple children, and all of them are affected. This is a hallmark feature of mitochondrial inheritance, as mitochondria are inherited exclusively from the mother. In the next generation, an affected male does not transmit the disease to any of his children, which further confirms mitochondrial inheritance, since fathers do not pass mitochondrial DNA to offspring. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Autosomal Dominant (AD): Would show transmission from both males and females equally, including father-to-child transmission. (B) Autosomal Recessive (AR): Typically skips generations and affects both sexes equally without strict maternal inheritance. (D) X-linked Recessive (XLR): More common in males and shows no male-to-male transmission, but does not show transmission to all children of affected females. The strict maternal transmission pattern confirms a mitochondrial disorder
questions.learning: The pedigree shows a pattern where an affected mother transmits the condition to all her children, regardless of sex. In the first generation, the affected female has multiple children, and all of them are affected.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of facilitated diffusion across a cell membrane?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glucose transport via GLUT4

Facilitated diffusion is a type of passive transport in which molecules move down their concentration gradient across the cell membrane with the help of specific carrier or channel proteins, without the use of ATP.

Glucose transport via GLUT4 is a classic example of facilitated diffusion. GLUT4 is an insulin-regulated glucose transporter found mainly in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue. After insulin stimulation, GLUT4 transporters move to the cell membrane and allow glucose to enter the cell along its concentration gradient without energy expenditure.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Sodium–potassium pump: This is primary active transport that uses ATP to move Na⁺ out and K⁺ into the cell against their gradients.
• Endocytosis: A vesicular transport mechanism that requires energy and is not diffusion.
• Water movement through aquaporins: This is osmosis through channel proteins, not carrier-mediated facilitated diffusion.
questions.learning: Glucose transport via GLUT4 Facilitated diffusion is a type of passive transport in which molecules move down their concentration gradient across the cell membrane with the help of specific carrier or channel proteins, without the use of ATP.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient undergoes split-thickness skin grafting for a burn injury of the arm. On the sixth postoperative day, he develops stiffness of the arm during physiotherapy. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Passive extension of the joint under direct visualization of the graft
Remove the graft and regraft the area
questions.explanation: By post-operative day 6, a split-thickness skin graft is in the early phase of fibrovascular ingrowth. If the patient develops stiffness during movement, the most appropriate management is passive extension under direct visualization. This allows the therapist to gently increase the range of motion while ensuring that the graft is not experiencing shearing forces that could cause displacement or partial loss. Surgical excision of contractures (Option A) is only performed on mature, months-old scars, not on a fresh graft. Continuing physiotherapy blindly (Option C) risks damaging the fragile graft if the stiffness is due to improper adhesion. Removing the graft (Option D) is unnecessary unless there is clear evidence of total graft failure, such as infection or necrosis. Thus, cautious supervised movement is the preferred rehabilitation strategy
questions.learning: By post-operative day 6, a split-thickness skin graft is in the early phase of fibrovascular ingrowth. If the patient develops stiffness during movement, the most appropriate management is passive extension under direct visualization.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In an experimental study, norepinephrine was administered to guinea pigs, leading to an increase in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure along with a reduction in heart rate. Which physiological mechanism best explains this response?
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine (NE) is a potent -adrenergic agonist that causes widespread vasoconstriction, leading to a significant increase in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure. Although NE also stimulates -receptors in the heart (which would normally increase heart rate), the rapid rise in systemic blood pressure stretches the baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch. This baroreceptor stimulation triggers a reflex vagal (parasympathetic) response from the medulla, which overrides the direct cardiac effect and causes a compensatory decrease in heart rate (reflex bradycardia). Option A and B are incorrect because NE is an agonist, not a blocker. Baroreceptor inhibition (Option D) would result in a faster heart rate due to a loss of parasympathetic tone. Thus, the paradox of increased blood pressure coupled with a decreased heart rate is entirely explained by the baroreceptor reflex
questions.learning: Norepinephrine (NE) is a potent -adrenergic agonist that causes widespread vasoconstriction, leading to a significant increase in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure.

questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following channels is not typically present on the luminal membrane of principal cells of the glomerular/renal collecting system?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Na-K +ATPase

In principal cells of the collecting duct:

• Luminal (apical) membrane: ENaC (Na⁺ reabsorption), ROMK (K⁺ secretion), Aquaporin-2 (ADH-regulated water reabsorption)

The Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase is located on the basolateral surface, where it maintains the sodium gradient driving luminal sodium reabsorption; therefore, it is not present on the luminal membrane.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following antibodies is the most reliable marker for diagnosing an acute infection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. IgM

IgM is the first antibody produced during the initial immune response to an antigen.

Its early appearance in serum makes it the most reliable marker of acute or recent infection.

IgM levels rise rapidly and decline as class switching to IgG occurs.

IgG indicates past exposure or immunity, while IgA and IgE have specialized roles.

↓

↓

Class switching (with T-cell help)

↓

| -------- | ------------ | --------- | -----------

| IgM | Early | Acute infection | First responder

| IgG | Late | Past infection | Memory
