questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with complaints of fatigue and is found to have a hemoglobin level of less than 9 g/dL. Peripheral blood smear examination reveals sickle-shaped red blood cells. What is the most appropriate management strategy for this patient?
questions.explanation: The presence of "sickle-shaped" red blood cells confirms the diagnosis of Sickle Cell Anemia. A hemoglobin level below 9 g/dL combined with clinical symptoms like fatigue indicates a severe anemic state. The most appropriate immediate management for symptomatic, severe anemia in this context is a blood transfusion (Option B). This quickly elevates the oxygen-carrying capacity and dilutes the concentration of sickled cells. IV antibiotics (Option A) would only be indicated if there were signs of concurrent infection. Deferoxamine (Option C) is an iron chelator used for chronic iron overload, not for acute anemia. "Wait and watch" (Option D) is dangerous when a patient is symptomatic with significantly low hemoglobin. For sickle cell patients, simple or exchange transfusions are critical interventions to prevent or treat complications such as acute chest syndrome or stroke during anemic crises
questions.learning: The presence of "sickle-shaped" red blood cells confirms the diagnosis of Sickle Cell Anemia. A hemoglobin level below 9 g/dL combined with clinical symptoms like fatigue indicates a severe anemic state.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A wildlife photographer presents with a blackish lesion at the site of a mite bite from a few days back. He also gives a history of fever and rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Scrub typhus

In the above clinical scenario, a history of mite bite followed by the development of a characteristic eschar at the bite site along with fever and rash suggests a diagnosis of scrub typhus.

Scrub typhus, also known as chigger-borne typhus, is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi. The vector is trombiculid mite. Humans are infected when they are bitten by the mite larvae known as chiggers. The incubation period is 1-3 weeks. Patients develop a characteristic eschar at the site of the mite bite, along with regional lymphadenopathy and maculopapular rash. It can be associated with fever, headache, and conjunctival injection. Meningoencephalitis, myocarditis, and pneumonia can be seen in severe cases.

Serologic assays are used for diagnosis. Weil-Felix reaction is a heterophile agglutination reaction used for diagnosis, wherein the sera are tested for agglutinins to the O antigens of certain Proteus strains OX19, OX2, and OXK. OXK is agglutinated only in scrub typhus. Doxycycline is the treatment of choice for both adults and children.

In Scrub typhus both the adult and nymphal stages of mites are free living in nature, hence they do not feed on vertebral hosts. The larval stage(chigger) feeds on the vertebrate host and pick up the rickettsiae. Rodents are the mammalian reservoir for scrub typhus. Eschar can be seen in the image below:

Other options:

Option A: Anthrax- Cutaneous anthrax (Hide Porter’s disease) present as a black eschar at the site of entry. At the site of entry of organism or spores, a papule develops in about 1–7 days. This develops into a vesicle that later breaks down into an ulcer with a black, central, necrotic eschar surrounded by edematous skin. The disease used to be common in dock workers, carrying loads of hides and skins on their bare backs. Renal involvement is unlikely to be seen in this condition.

The image below shows its characteristic rash:

Option C : Rocky Mountain spotted fever is a rickettsial infection transmitted by ticks (Dermacentor andersoni). It is the most serious type of fever. Symptoms include fever, headache, Rash, muscle pain and lack of appetite. Early treatment with doxycycline is recommended to prevent death and severe illness.

The rash is shown in the image below:

Option D : Epidemic typhus: Epidemic typhus is caused by Rickettsia prowazekii and the vector is louse. Its incubation period is 10 to 14 days. The disease starts with fever and chills. A characteristic rash appears on the fourth or fifth day, starting on the trunk and spreading over the limbs but sparing the face, palms, and soles.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with recurrent sinusitis and repeated lung infection. Genetic testing shows a mutation in CFTR gene. Which test is considered gold standard to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sweat Chloride Test

A child with recurrent sinopulmonary infections and a CFTR gene mutation is suspected to have cystic fibrosis. The gold standard test for confirming the diagnosis is the sweat chloride test, which demonstrates elevated chloride levels due to defective chloride transport.

• Cystic fibrosis is caused by mutation in the CFTR gene leading to thick, viscous secretions
• Common features include recurrent sinusitis, chronic lung infections, malabsorption, and failure to thrive
•

Sweat chloride test:

•

≥60 mmol/L is diagnostic

• 30–59 mmol/L is intermediate
• Newborn screening and genetic testing support diagnosis but confirmation is by sweat test

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 55-year-old male undergoing chemotherapy presents with progressive shortness of breath, dry cough, and fatigue over the past 2 weeks. He is afebrile and denies chest pain or sputum production. On examination, fine basal crepitations are heard. Chest X-ray reveals bilateral reticulonodular infiltrates. High-resolution CT (HRCT) of the chest confirms interstitial lung disease. Pulmonary function tests show a restrictive pattern with FEV1 = 61% of predicted and normal FEV1/FVC ratio. Notably, there is no evidence of bone marrow suppression. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bleomycin

Bleomycin causes dose-dependent pulmonary fibrosis presenting with dry cough, dyspnea, and restrictive lung disease. HRCT showing interstitial infiltrates with preserved marrow function is characteristic.

Bleomycin

↓

Free radical formation

↓

Lung tissue damage

↓

Interstitial inflammation

↓

Fibrosis → restrictive lung disease

Unlike many chemotherapeutics, bleomycin has minimal bone marrow suppression. Pulmonary toxicity is its hallmark adverse effect.

| Drug | Toxicity

| ---- | --------

| Bleomycin | Pulmonary fibrosis

| Cisplatin | Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity

| Cyclophosphamide | Hemorrhagic cystitis

| Vincristine | Peripheral neuropathy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A middle-aged woman presented with dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and infertility. On examination, you note fixed, tender, retroverted uterus and tender nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endometriosis

This patient presents with symptoms of dyspareunia and dysmenorrhea with a fixed retroverted uterus and tenderness in the pouch of Douglas most likely suffering from endometriosis.

For minimal disease, medical management with NSAIDs and oral contraceptive pills are given if associated menstrual complaints are present. OCPs inhibit gonadotropin release and decrease the menstrual flow. For moderate to severe diseases, oral progestogens, GnRH agonists or danazol that antagonize estrogenic effects on the endometrium causing endometrial atrophy are used.

Surgery is preferred in infertile women because hormonal treatment would delay pregnancy. Endometrial deposits are destroyed by electrocautery/laser and resection of endometrioma can be done. Laparoscopic uterosacral nerve ablation (LUNA) to control pain .Total hysterectomy with bilateral oophorectomy is a definitive and most effective therapy for women with endometriosis who do not wish to retain fertility.

Pearl PF1294: Endometriosis

Sites of Endometriosis:

* Pelvic endometriosis: Pelvic peritoneum, the pouch of Douglas, uterosacral ligament.

* Rectovaginal endometriosis.

* Ovarian endometriosis.

* Chocolate cyst of the ovary.

* Other sites—appendix, pelvic lymph nodes.

* Metastatic— lungs, umbilicus, scar endometriosis.

One pathology review revealed that endometriosis has been identified on all organs except the spleen.

Examination findings in endometriosis:

* Abdomen: Cystic swelling, fixed and tender.

* Pelvis: Cystic tender mass.

* Vaginal examination: Fixed, tender, retroverted uterus. Tenderness in the lateral fornices (indicative of endometriosis even if no mass).

* Speculum inspection of the Posterior fornix: Bluish/blackish puckered spots on speculum, tender to touch. The presence of puckered spots is pathognomonic of endometriosis.

* Posterior Fornix Palpation: Uterosacral ligaments & pouch of Douglas feel thickened and shotty with multiple small palpable nodules. This is called the cobblestone feel of uterosacral ligaments.
questions.learning: Endometriosis — This patient presents with symptoms of dyspareunia and dysmenorrhea with a fixed retroverted uterus and tenderness in the pouch of Douglas most likely suffering from endometriosis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the part of the cochlear implant marked?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Grounding electrode

In a cochlear implant, the grounding electrode is an extracochlear electrode placed outside the cochlea (often in temporalis muscle or subperiosteal region) to complete the electrical circuit.

• Electrode array: Inserted into cochlea → stimulates auditory nerve
• Receiver-stimulator: Implanted under the skin → receives signals from external device
• Grounding electrode: Provides reference/return path for electrical current

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug is preferred for management of diabetes in a patient with cardiac and renal failure?
questions.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors (such as empagliflozin and dapagliflozin) are the preferred drugs for managing diabetes in patients with both cardiac and renal failure because of their strong cardioprotective and renoprotective benefits, independent of glucose control. These drugs act on the proximal renal tubules to inhibit sodium–glucose cotransport, leading to glycosuria and natriuresis. This results in osmotic diuresis, reduced preload and afterload, improvement in heart failure outcomes, and slowing of chronic kidney disease progression. Pioglitazone (Option B) is contraindicated in heart failure due to fluid retention and weight gain, which can worsen cardiac function. Metformin (Option C), although first-line for type 2 diabetes, is contraindicated in advanced renal failure because of the risk of lactic acidosis. Sulfonylureas (Option D) increase the risk of prolonged hypoglycemia, especially in renal impairment due to reduced drug clearance. Thus, SGLT2 inhibitors provide the greatest overall benefit with the lowest risk in diabetic patients with concomitant heart failure and chronic kidney disease, making them the drug of choice in this scenario
questions.learning: SGLT2 inhibitors (such as empagliflozin and dapagliflozin) are the preferred drugs for managing diabetes in patients with both cardiac and renal failure because of their strong cardioprotective and renoprotective benefits, independent of glucose control.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following contrast agents is safe to use in renal failure patients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ultrasound contrast agent

Ultrasound contrast agents are gas-filled microbubbles that are administered intravenously to the systemic circulation. Hence, considered as low risk in patients with renal impairment.

Ultrasound contrast agents are used to enhance the visibility of blood vessels, organs, and tissues during ultrasound imaging. These agents typically consist of tiny gas-filled microbubbles encapsulated within a shell. When injected intravenously, they flow through the bloodstream and resonate in response to ultrasound waves, producing strong echoes that enhance the ultrasound image.

Perflutren/Optison is an ultrasound contrast agent. Levovist (consisting of galactose microparticles, air bubbles, and palmitic acid) is another example of an ultrasound contrast agent. Sulfur hexafluoride with a phospholipid shell is also used as an ultrasound contrast agent.

Other options:

Option A: Gadolinium contrast used in MRI is predominantly excreted through the kidney. In renal failure, it gets accumulated in the body and releases gadolinium ions. Since the ion is toxic, the body tries to contain it by fibrosis resulting in multisystem painful fibrosis called nephrogenic systemic fibrosis.

Option B: Iodinated ionic contrast agents increase the risk of Contrast-induced nephropathy(CIN). Hence alternative imaging methods, without iodinated contrast media, should be chosen in patients with considerably impaired renal function (CKD 4 or 5).

Option C: Non-ionic contrast agents have a lower risk of causing adverse reactions compared to ionic contrast agents. They are generally better tolerated by patients, with fewer incidences of allergic reactions and nephrotoxicity. However, USG contrast agents are among the safest in renal failure patients.
questions.learning: Ultrasound contrast agent Ultrasound contrast agents are gas-filled microbubbles that are administered intravenously to the systemic circulation. Hence, considered as low risk in patients with renal impairment.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In a suspected murder case, the court summoned a doctor to provide his opinion and testify as a witness. This form of evidence is commonly referred to as ____?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Expert witness

The doctor in this scenario is referred to as an expert witness.

As per Section 39 (1) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) (earlier Section 45 of the Indian Evidence Act), an expert witness is a person who is skilled in technical or scientific matters and capable of drawing opinions and conclusions from the facts observed by him or by others.  Examples: Doctor, firearm expert, fingerprinting expert, handwriting expert.

Witness: A witness is a person who gives evidence regarding facts. Sections 124 to 139 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) (earlier Sections 118 to 134 of the Indian Evidence Act) deal with various aspects of witnesses.

Other types of witnesses:

* A common witness is a person who gives evidence about the facts observed by them. The first-hand knowledge rule refers to the concept that the witness must show that he was capable of perceiving the fact by one of his own senses and that he actually observed this fact. It applies to all common witnesses who give evidence about the facts observed or perceived by him/her.

A doctor can be both a common and an expert witness.

Common witness - When he describes the wounds on the body.

Expert witness - When he says that the wounds were antemortem or post-mortem, or they were suicidal, homicidal, or accidental, or gives an opinion regarding the cause of death.

* A hostile witness is one who has some interest or motive for concealing part of the truth or for giving completely false evidence (Sec 227 of BNS/Sec 191 IPC). There must be some evidence to prove that the witness has retracted from his earlier statement or is not desirous of disclosing the truth, or has exhibited an element of hostility. If a witness is declared as hostile, he can be cross-examined by the same side's lawyer.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Microfilariae with sheathed tail and two nuclei at the tail tip is suggestive of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Brugia malayi

The most likely organism based on the description of the microfilariae is Brugia malayi.

The microfilariae of B. malayi are sheathed and have kinks and secondary curves. The tail tip has two nuclei - a terminal and a subterminal one. It has nocturnal periodicity.

The female filarial worms, which belong to the phylum Nematoda, give birth to larvae known as microfilariae. Some of the microfilariae retain their egg membranes and are known as sheathed microfilariae. They can be further differentiated on the basis of the arrangement of nuclei in the tail.

Classical filariasis is due to obstruction of lymphatics by the adult worms resulting in lymph stasis. This leads to leakage of lymph into the tissues causing hard pitting (brawny) edema. It can present as acute adenolymphangitis, hydrocele, or elephantiasis which is shown below.

Occult filariasis (Meyers-Kouwenaar syndrome) results from a hypersensitivity reaction to the microfilarial antigens. Here, the microfilariae are not found in the blood. Symptoms include hepatosplenomegaly, nocturnal cough, or arthritis. Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia is a manifestation of occult filariasis which presents as low-grade fever, weight loss, and dry nocturnal cough. There is marked eosinophilia and raised serum IgE levels. It is managed with diethylcarbamazine.

Other options:

Option A - Microfilariae of Wuchereria bancrofti are sheathed and the tail tip lacks nuclei. It has nocturnal periodicity.

Option C - Loa loa causes subcutaneous filariasis which presents as swellings on the extremities (Calabar/fugitive swellings). It can also cause conjunctival granulomas and proptosis. The nuclei are arranged in a row up to the tail tip of the sheathed microfilariae. It exhibits diurnal periodicity.

Option D - Onchocerca volvulus (blinding filaria) causes onchocerciasis. The microfilariae are unsheathed and the nuclei do not extend to the tail tip. Patients present with subcutaneous nodules (onchocercoma), dermatitis, photophobia, or even blindness. It is non-periodic.
questions.learning: Brugia malayi — The most likely organism based on the description of the microfilariae is Brugia malayi. The microfilariae of B. malayi are sheathed and have kinks and secondary curves.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is the most common site for an extragonadal germ cell tumor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mediastinum

Extragonadal germ cell tumor is most commonly seen in mediastinum.

Extragonadal germinal cell tumors (EGGCTs) are rare tumors that predominantly affect young males. Seminomas account for 30-40% of these tumors, and nonseminomatous germ cell tumors (NS-GCTs) account for 60-70%.

Common sites:

• Mediastinum (50-70%)
• Retroperitoneum (30-40%)
• Pineal gland (5%)
• Sacrococcygeal area (less than 5%)
questions.learning: Mediastinum Extragonadal germ cell tumor is most commonly seen in mediastinum. Extragonadal germinal cell tumors (EGGCTs) are rare tumors that predominantly affect young males.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old chronic smoker came to the medicine outpatient department with complaints of upper chest discomfort and drooping of an eyelid. He also complained of pain radiating to the upper arm and a tingling sensation in the 4th and 5th digits of his left hand. The chest X-ray is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pancoast tumor

Upper chest pain with ipsilateral ptosis (Horner syndrome) and ulnar nerve involvement (C8–T1: 4th–5th digit paresthesia) is classic for a Pancoast tumor.

It arises from the lung apex, invading the brachial plexus and sympathetic chain.

Apical lung tumor (Pancoast)

↓

Invades brachial plexus (C8–T1)

↓

Arm pain + paresthesia (4th & 5th digits)

↓

Invades sympathetic chain

↓

Horner’s syndrome:

- Ptosis

- Miosis

- Anhidrosis

| Option | Condition | Key Feature | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | --------- | ----------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A. Pancoast tumor ✅ | Apical lung cancer | Horner’s + arm pain | ✔ Classic presentation | ✔ Correct | C8–T1 involvement

| B. Upper lobe pneumonia | Infection | Fever, consolidation | Acute illness | ❌ No neuro symptoms | Air bronchogram present

| C. SVC obstruction | Venous blockage | Facial swelling, dilated veins | Mediastinal tumor | ❌ No Horner’s or arm pain | “Full face + neck veins”

| D. Aspergilloma | Fungal ball | Cavity with fungus ball | Hemoptysis | ❌ No neuro signs | Moves with position

Upper lobe pneumonia and aspergilloma do not cause neurogenic symptoms, and SVC obstruction presents with facial swelling.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with a sudden onset of breathlessness. Based on the radiological image provided, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The radiological image displays the characteristic "Steeple Sign," which represents subglottic narrowing of the airway. This finding is pathognomonic for Laryngotracheobronchitis, commonly known as Croup. Croup typically presents in children with sudden shortness of breath, a barking cough, and inspiratory stridor. Epiglottitis (Option A) would show a "thumbprint sign" on a lateral X-ray due to supraglottic swelling and is a more severe, life-threatening emergency. Bronchitis (Option C) involves inflammation of the lower bronchi and does not cause subglottic narrowing. Laryngomalacia (Option D) is a congenital condition causing chronic stridor due to a floppy epiglottis, typically diagnosed clinically rather than by an acute "steeple sign". Thus, the visual narrowing of the upper trachea confirms croup as the diagnosis
questions.learning: The radiological image displays the characteristic "Steeple Sign," which represents subglottic narrowing of the airway. This finding is pathognomonic for Laryngotracheobronchitis, commonly known as Croup.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A female patient presented with acne that is not resolving on oral isotretinoin and antibiotics therapy. Which of the following is the next best investigation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Evaluate for hyperandrogenism

The next best step for a female patient with acne that is resistant to oral isotretinoin is to check for hyperandrogenism.

Hyperandrogenism usually manifests as hirsutism, acne, and/or androgenic alopecia. Acne that is persistent, moderate to severe, or late-onset raises concern for PCOS or other causes of hyperandrogenism.

The pathogenesis of acne vulgaris involves

• Blockage of the follicular opening by hyperkeratosis
• Sebum overproduction
• The proliferation of commensal Propionibacterium acnes
• Inflammation

Management is directed at minimizing inflammation, decreasing keratin production, antibiotics, and antiandrogens to diminish sebum production.

Other options:

Option A: Looking for dietary triggers could be considered, but there is limited evidence to support a direct relationship between specific food items and acne.

Option C: Since the patient has not shown improvement even with antibiotic therapy, it is reasonable to consider checking for antibiotic resistance. However, evaluating for hyperandrogenism should be prioritized due to its potential role in the patient's condition.

Option D: Looking for drug triggers may be relevant in some cases, but it is less likely to be the primary cause of acne that is not responding to isotretinoin and antibiotics. Drug-induced acne typically resolves once the offending drug is discontinued.
questions.learning: Evaluate for hyperandrogenism — The next best step for a female patient with acne that is resistant to oral isotretinoin is to check for hyperandrogenism.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 6-week-old boy was brought by his parents with complaints of noisy breathing, present since a few days after birth. Inspiratory stridor is heard. It subsides with prone positioning and increases with crying. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Laryngomalacia

The above clinical scenario of a 6-week-old child with inspiratory stridor which is relieved in the prone position is suggestive of laryngomalacia.

Laryngomalacia is the most common congenital abnormality of the larynx and the most common cause of stridor in children. It is characterized by excessive flaccidity of the supraglottic larynx which is sucked in during inspiration producing stridor and sometimes cyanosis. The presentation is just after birth and subsides by 2 years. Stridor improves(decreases) in the prone position, and worsens during feeding. The cry is normal. Laryngomalacia leads to the collapse of supraglottic structures during inspiration which results in airway obstruction.

The given image shows omega-shaped glottis on direct laryngoscopy.

Treatment of Laryngomalacia:
Mostly, it self-corrects by 2 years of age.
A tracheostomy may be required for some cases of severe respiratory obstruction.
Supraglottoplasty is required in cases of severe laryngomalacia.

Stridor is noisy respiration produced by turbulent airflow through narrowed air passages. Stridor may be heard during inspiration, expiration or both.

Inspiratory stridor is seen in supraglottic lesions. It is often produced in obstructive lesions of the supraglottis or pharynx, e.g. laryngomalacia or retropharyngeal abscess.
Expiratory stridor is produced in lesions of the thoracic trachea, primary and secondary bronchi, e.g. bronchial foreign body, and tracheal stenosis. (option B)
Biphasic stridor is seen in lesions of the glottis, subglottis, and cervical trachea, e.g. laryngeal papillomas, vocal cord paralysis, and subglottic stenosis. (options C & D)
questions.learning: Laryngomalacia — The above clinical scenario of a 6-week-old child with inspiratory stridor which is relieved in the prone position is suggestive of laryngomalacia.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following options correctly describes the enzyme used in this test (RT-PCR)?
questions.explanation: The Reverse Transcriptase Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) is the gold standard for detecting RNA viruses, such as Poliovirus, which causes acute flaccid paralysis. The critical first step of this test involves the enzyme Reverse Transcriptase, which is an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (Option B). This enzyme transcribes the viral RNA template into a complementary DNA (cDNA) strand. Only after this conversion can the cDNA be amplified by a standard DNA-dependent DNA polymerase (Option C). DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (Option A) is used in natural transcription to create RNA from DNA. RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (Option D) is an enzyme used by certain RNA viruses to replicate their genome but is not the tool used for RT-PCR assays. Understanding this enzymatic pathway is essential for interpreting molecular diagnostics. Thus, the specific capability to synthesize DNA from an RNA template defines the "Reverse Transcriptase" used in RT-PCR
questions.learning: The Reverse Transcriptase Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) is the gold standard for detecting RNA viruses, such as Poliovirus, which causes acute flaccid paralysis.

• AF is a supraventricular tachycardia from ectopic foci/reentry circuits within atria; atrial rate 400–600/min, ventricular rate 100–160/min.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes is responsible for the immortality of the cancer cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Telomerase

Telomerase is the enzyme that prevents the shortening of telomeres.

With every cell division, there is some shortening of telomeres at the ends of chromosomes. Once the telomeres are shortened beyond a certain point, it may cause cell-cycle arrest or apoptosis. This is called replicative senescence.

Telomerase is present in some cells, like the germ cells, and absent in most somatic cells.

Reactivation of telomerase is a critical step in the development of about 85% of human cancers, which enables the cells to divide several times than normal.
questions.learning: Telomerase Telomerase is the enzyme that prevents the shortening of telomeres. With every cell division, there is some shortening of telomeres at the ends of chromosomes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a history of recurrent vomiting undergoes arterial blood gas analysis, which shows a pH of 7.5, PaCO₂ of 48 mm Hg, and HCO₃⁻ of 30 mm Hg. Based on these findings, what is the most likely acid–base disorder?
questions.explanation: The blood gas findings show an elevated pH (7.5), confirming alkalosis. The primary cause is an elevated bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) of 30 mEq/L, which results from the loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl) during vomiting. The body responds through respiratory compensation—hypoventilation to retain —which explains the elevated of 48 mm Hg. Metabolic acidosis (Option B) would feature a low pH and low . Respiratory acidosis (Option C) is characterized by a low pH and high . Respiratory alkalosis (Option D) involves a high pH with a low due to hyperventilation. Thus, the clinical context of vomiting combined with the metabolic laboratory values clearly points to metabolic alkalosis with partial respiratory compensation as the most likely acid-base disturbance in this patient
questions.learning: The blood gas findings show an elevated pH (7.5), confirming alkalosis. The primary cause is an elevated bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) of 30 mEq/L, which results from the loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl) during vomiting.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Identify the graph below:
questions.explanation: The given graph shows multiple successive peaks of cases over time rather than a single sharp peak. This pattern is characteristic of a propagated epidemic, where the disease spreads from person to person. Each peak represents a new generation of cases occurring after an incubation period. The gradual rise and fall, along with repeated peaks, indicate ongoing transmission rather than a one-time exposure. Why other options are wrong: (A) Point source epidemic: This shows a single, sharp peak with cases occurring within one incubation period due to a common exposure (e.g., food poisoning). The graph here has multiple peaks, so it is not point source. (B) Common source continuous exposure: In this pattern, cases rise gradually and remain elevated over a prolonged period without distinct peaks. The graph instead shows fluctuating peaks, not a plateau. (C) Intermittent exposure: This shows irregular peaks separated by gaps, corresponding to repeated exposures. However, in this graph, peaks are more regular and progressively increase, suggesting person-to-person spread. Thus, the pattern best fits a propagated epidemic
questions.learning: The given graph shows multiple successive peaks of cases over time rather than a single sharp peak. This pattern is characteristic of a propagated epidemic, where the disease spreads from person to person.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-year-old child presents with profuse diarrhea and vomiting, along with deeply sunken eyes and complete absence of urine output. On examination, the child is severely dehydrated, lethargic, tachypneic, and hypotensive with a blood pressure of 80/60 mmHg. In this clinical scenario of severe dehydration with shock, which intravenous fluid should be administered for management?
questions.explanation: The child presents with severe dehydration and hypovolemic shock, indicated by lethargy, hypotension (80/60 mmHg), tachypnea, sunken eyes, and anuria. This is a life-threatening condition requiring immediate intravenous fluid resuscitation. In pediatric diarrheal dehydration, Ringer lactate (RL) is the preferred fluid because it is a balanced crystalloid solution containing electrolytes such as sodium, potassium, calcium, and chloride. Importantly, the lactate component is metabolized to bicarbonate, helping to correct metabolic acidosis, which commonly occurs due to severe diarrhea. The addition of 5% dextrose is beneficial in children to prevent hypoglycemia and provide energy, especially when oral intake is compromised. Why other options are wrong: (A) ORS → Not suitable in shock or severe dehydration (C) Normal saline → Effective but may cause hyperchloremic acidosis; less physiological than RL (D) Dextrose → Does not restore intravascular volume
questions.learning: The child presents with severe dehydration and hypovolemic shock, indicated by lethargy, hypotension (80/60 mmHg), tachypnea, sunken eyes, and anuria.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: During a pediatric consultation, a 14-year-old presents with delayed growth, absent pubertal development, and a history of frequent fractures from minimal trauma. On examination, additional features are noted (as described). These findings are most likely associated with which condition?
questions.explanation: The combination of clinical and physical features documented points toward Trisomy 21, also known as Down syndrome. The provided images show "blue sclera" (sometimes seen in connective tissue variants associated with syndromes) and a pathognomonic "Simian crease" or single transverse palmar crease. Down syndrome patients frequently exhibit delayed growth, intellectual disability, and an increased risk of osteopenia, leading to frequent fractures. While blue sclera is most classically associated with Osteogenesis Imperfecta, the palmar finding is a major physical marker for Trisomy 21. Trisomy 13 (Option A) and Trisomy 18 (Option D) typically involve more severe midline defects and have very low survival rates into the teens. Klinefelter syndrome (Option B) typically presents with tall stature and gynecomastia after puberty rather than short stature and frequent childhood fractures. Therefore, given the specific constellation of delayed development and distinct dermatoglyphic markers, Trisomy 21 is the most likely diagnosis

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 23-year-old woman accompanied by her mother-in-law comes to the infertility clinic. She has been having regular intercourse for 6 months but is not able to conceive. What is the next best step?
options: Reassure and review the couple after 6 months
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Reassure and review the couple after 6 months

The next best step would be to reassure and review the couple after 6 months.

The inability to conceive after 1 year of unprotected intercourse of reasonable frequency is described as infertility.

Infertility evaluation is offered to any couple that has failed to conceive after 1 year of regular unprotected intercourse. There is a decline in the conception rate and a rise in poor pregnancy outcomes in older women hence, the majority of experts concur that in women older than 35, evaluation may be considered after 6 months. Since the woman is 23 years old and has tried conceiving for only 6 months, it is advisable to review them in another 6 months if they fail to conceive.

Infertility workup includes the following if required:

(1) Ovulation and evaluation for the diminished ovarian reserve-

(2) Evaluation of Female reproductive tract abnormality-

• Hysterosalpingography
• Sonography
• Laparoscopy
• Hysteroscopy- The preferred way to diagnose intrauterine anomalies is an endoscopic assessment of the uterine cavity. Both an operating room and a doctor's office can be used for hysteroscopy. It has the ability to concurrently diagnose and treat the abnormalities.

(3) Semen analysis
questions.learning: Reassure and review the couple after 6 months — The next best step would be to reassure and review the couple after 6 months. The inability to conceive after 1 year of unprotected intercourse of reasonable frequency is described as infertility.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What plasma protein is found in the highest concentration?
questions.explanation: Human plasma contains a variety of proteins that serve essential physiological functions. Among these, albumin is the most abundant, typically accounting for approximately 55% to 60% of the total plasma protein content. It is synthesized in the liver and is vital for maintaining oncotic pressure and transporting various molecules like hormones and fatty acids. Globulins (Option B) are the second most prevalent group, including alpha, beta, and gamma globulins (antibodies), and generally comprise about 35% of plasma proteins. Fibrinogen (Option C) is a large protein involved in blood clotting and is present in much lower concentrations, making up roughly 4%. Bence Jones proteins (Option A) are abnormal light-chain proteins found in the urine and blood of patients with multiple myeloma and are not a standard component of healthy plasma. Therefore, albumin is the correct choice as the highest concentration plasma protein
questions.learning: Human plasma contains a variety of proteins that serve essential physiological functions. Among these, albumin is the most abundant, typically accounting for approximately 55% to 60% of the total plasma protein content.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with a history of a thorn prick injury sustained one week earlier. Subsequently, he developed a chain of ulcers distributed along the course of the lymphatic vessels. Which organism is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: The history of a thorn prick followed by ulcerative lesions along the lymphatic drainage is characteristic of sporotrichosis. This subcutaneous infection is caused by the dimorphic fungus Sporothrix schenckii, which is commonly found on thorns and rose bushes. It typically affects gardeners and laborers, spreading through the lymphatic channels to create nodules that ulcerate. Coccidioides immitis (Option A) primarily causes a respiratory illness known as valley fever and is not associated with this specific lymphatic pattern. Aspergillus flavus (Option B) is associated with invasive aspergillosis and aflatoxin production, not trauma-induced lymphatic ulcers. Trichophyton rubrum (Option D) is a dermatophyte causing superficial skin infections like athlete’s foot rather than deep lymphatic spread. Diagnosis is often confirmed via microscopy showing characteristic "cigar-shaped" yeast cells
questions.learning: The history of a thorn prick followed by ulcerative lesions along the lymphatic drainage is characteristic of sporotrichosis. This subcutaneous infection is caused by the dimorphic fungus Sporothrix schenckii, which is commonly found on thorns and rose bushes.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient presented with headache, vomiting, and fever. Meningitis was suspected. While performing a lumbar puncture, which is the last structure you will pierce just before entering the lumbar cistern?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Arachnoid membrane

The arachnoid membrane is the last structure you will pierce while performing a lumbar puncture, just before entering the lumbar cistern.

Lumbar puncture is a diagnostic procedure done to obtain a sample of cerebrospinal fluid from the subarachnoid space. During the procedure, the following structures are pierced to reach the subarachnoid space, in the given order:

• Skin
• Subcutaneous tissue
• Supraspinous ligament
• Interspinous ligament
• Ligamentum flavum
• Dura mater
• Arachnoid membrane

Indications:

• Diagnosis of suspected meningitis and subarachnoid hemorrhage
• Spinal anesthesia and intrathecal administration of antibiotics/chemotherapy
• Therapeutic relief of pseudotumor cerebri, less frequently

Contraindications for lumbar puncture include:

• Thrombocytopenia or other bleeding diatheses (including anticoagulant therapy)
• Raised intracranial pressure
• Spinal epidural abscess
• Infection over the site

Site of the procedure:

In adults, the spinal cord ends at the level of the lower border of the L1 vertebra. Lumbar puncture is usually performed at L3-L4 space (below L1 vertebra) to avoid potential needle trauma to the spinal cord.

Technique:

The patient is usually placed in the lateral recumbent position. An alternative position is the sitting position, useful in obese patients to determine the midline. L3-L4 space is located by palpating the right and left posterior superior iliac crests and moving the fingers medially toward the spine at the same level.

A local anesthetic like 1% lidocaine is administered. A 22-gauge needle is advanced through the skin. In the lateral recumbent position, the bevel should face up, and in the sitting position, it should face to one side or the other, to avoid injury to the dural fibers. There is a loss of resistance as the needle enters the epidural space. Dura and then arachnoid are next pierced, to release CSF.
Complications following lumbar puncture:

Post-dural puncture headache (PDPH) is a common post-procedure symptom. It occurs due to loss of CSF through the dura which causes traction on the pain-sensitive intracranial structures. The headache in PDPH is typically frontal or occipital. The smaller the needle used, the lesser the risk of PDPH.

Other complications include infections, bleeding, cerebral herniation, and radicular pain.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following sodium transporters are present maximally in the early part of the PCT?

1. Na-K-ATPase
2. Na-glucose cotransporter
3. Na-H antiporter
4. Na-HCO3 symporter
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 3

The sodium transporters present in the early part of PCT are Na-K-ATPase, Na+-glucose cotransporter (SGLT) and Na+-H+ antiporter.

Reabsorption of sodium in different parts of the nephron are:

• Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT):

• Nearly 60% of the filtered sodium is reabsorbed in the PCT. Solutes mainly absorbed in the proximal tubule are sodium, chloride, bicarbonate, phosphate, lactate, glucose, amino acids etc.
• Na+ is actively pumped from these cells into the interstitial space by Na-K ATPase in the basolateral membrane after travelling by cotransport or exchange via the tubular lumen into the tubular epithelial cells along its concentration and electrical gradients. It extrudes three Na+ in exchange for two K+ that are pumped into the cell.
• In early PCT, the main sodium channels used for reabsorption are Na+-glucose cotransporter (SGLT), Na+-H+ antiporter, Na+-amino acid cotransporter, Na+-phosphate cotransporter, etc.
• In distal PCT, due to high chloride concentration in the lumen, it favours NaCl reabsorption, driven by Cl− gradient.
• The total solute and water reabsorption are proportional to each other. Thus, the entire proximal tubule also reabsorbs nearly 60% of the filtered water (isosmotic reabsorption).

• Loop of Henle:

• The thin descending limb has no active transport of Na+ outside the lumen but the loop is permeable to water, making the tubular fluid hypertonic.
• A thick ascending limb reabsorbs nearly 30% of the Na+ by Na–2Cl–K cotransporter, an example of secondary active transport. This loop is impermeable to water. Since some of the solutes are reabsorbed and water is not reabsorbed, it dilutes the tubular fluid.

• Distal convoluted tubule: Approximately 7% of the filtered load of sodium chloride is reabsorbed in the early distal tubule. This occurs due to the presence of sodium chloride co-transporter. Even this segment dilutes the tubular fluid as it is impermeable to water.
• Cortical collecting tubule: The remaining 3% of the filtered Na+ is absorbed via ENaCs (epithelial sodium channels) in this duct.  This portion is regulated by aldosterone to maintain homeostasis in Na+ balance.

questions.text: Increase in which of the following hormone is responsible for Hyperpigmentation in Addison's disease?

Correct answer: A. ACTH

In Addison disease, low cortisol removes negative feedback on the pituitary, causing marked elevation of ACTH. ACTH is derived from POMC, which also produces MSH, stimulating melanocytes and causing diffuse hyperpigmentation.

| MSH | POMC | Stimulates melanocytes

| Cortisol | Adrenal cortex | Negative feedback

| | |

Aldosterone and ADH do not affect skin pigmentation. Cortisol is decreased, not increased, in primary adrenal insufficiency.

400-700 ml of ORS to be given in the first four hours.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the tendon marked in the image.
questions.explanation: The tendon marked in the image is the Flexor carpi radialis (FCR). This tendon runs along the anterior aspect of the forearm and becomes prominent near the wrist, passing laterally (towards the thumb side) before inserting at the base of the second and third metacarpals. Its position and direction in the image match this typical anatomical course. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Flexor carpi ulnaris: This tendon lies on the medial (ulnar) side of the forearm, closer to the little finger. In the image, the marked tendon is positioned laterally, so it cannot be FCU. (C) Palmaris longus: This is a thin, superficial tendon that runs centrally over the wrist and inserts into the palmar aponeurosis. It is usually more slender and lies between FCR and FCU, unlike the thicker, laterally placed tendon shown. (D) Median nerve: This is not a tendon but a nerve. It runs deep in the forearm and passes through the carpal tunnel, so it does not appear as a superficial tendon. Thus, the correct answer is (A) Flexor carpi radialis

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old male with known history of asthma developed sudden onset breathlessness, and wheezing . He was rushed to the emergency, where the preliminary assessment was done. The pulse is 140/min, respiratory rate 28/min, and the FEV1 is 40% of the predicted value. Which of the following is the best next step in treatment in this case?
options: A high concentration of oxygen should be given by a face mask + Salbutamol nebulisation
High doses of SABA to be given by a nebulizer only
Sedatives should be added to alleviate anxiety
Nebulized anticholinergics to be added immediately as the mainstay of treatment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A high concentration of oxygen should be given by a face mask + Salbutamol nebulisation

The clinical scenario given above is suggestive of severe, acute attack of asthma. The best next step in the treatment would be to give a high concentration of oxygen should be given by a face mask + Salbutamol nebulisation .

Management of acute attack of asthma:

* A high concentration of oxygen should be given by face mask and oxygen saturation should be maintained at >90%.

* The mainstay of treatment are high doses of SABA given either by nebulizer or via a metered-dose inhaler (MDI) with a spacer.

* In severely ill patients with impending respiratory failure, IV β2-agonists may be given.

* A nebulized anticholinergic may be added if there is not a good response to β2-agonists alone.

* In patients who are refractory to inhaled therapies, a slow infusion of aminophylline can also be given.

Features of Acute severe attack of asthma include:

* Inability to speak a complete sentence in one breath

* Pulse >120/min

* Respiratory rate >25/min

* FEV1 between 33 to 50% of predicted

* Pulsus paradoxus of >10 mmHg

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Hemoglobin with iron in ferric form is _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Methemoglobin

Hemoglobin with iron in ferric form is methemoglobin.

Hemoglobin structure:

* Each consists of a tetramer of globin polypeptide chains: a pair of α-like chains and a pair of β-like chains.

* HbA (α2β2): Major adult hemoglobin

* HbF (α2γ2): Fetal Hemoglobin

* HbA2 (α2δ2): Minor adult hemoglobin

* Each globin chain enfolds a single heme moiety, consisting of a protoporphyrin IX ring complexed with a single iron atom in the ferrous state (Fe2+).

* Each heme moiety can bind a single oxygen molecule.

* The hemoglobin tetramer is highly soluble, but individual globin chains are insoluble.

* Unpaired globin precipitates, forming inclusions that damage the cell and can trigger apoptosis.

Methemoglobin is formed when hemoglobin is oxidized to contain iron in the ferric [Fe3+] rather than the normal ferrous [Fe2+] state. The presence of iron in the ferric state results shift of the oxygen-dissociation curve to the left. This shift leads to increased affinity of the ferrous iron for oxygen and thus impaired oxygen release to the tissue.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: How is a broken vaccine vial disposed, according to biomedical waste management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Puncture proof blue bin

A broken vaccine vial is disposed of in a puncture-proof blue bin, according to biomedical waste management (BMW).

According to BMW, broken or discarded contaminated glass materials such as vials, ampules, etc are disposed of in boxes marked with blue color. It is then disinfected either by washing with detergent, autoclaving, or microwaving and sent for recycling.

The methods used for treatment and disposal of healthcare waste are:

• Incineration: This is a dry oxidation process done using high temperatures.
• Chemical disinfection: Chemicals are added to waste to kill or inactivate the microorganisms.
• Wet and dry thermal treatment: Shredded infectious waste is exposed to high temperature, high-pressure steam and it resembles an autoclave sterilization process.
• Microwave irradiation: Microorganisms are killed using high-frequency microwave.
• Land disposal.
• Inertization: Waste is mixed with cement and other substances before disposal to reduce toxicity.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a community, there are usually 40-50 reported cases of dengue every week. This week, there were 48 reported cases. This would classify as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endemic

The given scenario is an example of an endemic disease.

Endemic diseases are those that have a constant presence and /or usual prevalence of a disease or infectious agent in a population within a geographic area.

Epidemic refers to an increase, often sudden, in the number of cases of a disease above what is normally expected in that population in that area.

Outbreak carries the same definition of an epidemic, but is often used for a more limited geographic area.

Sporadic diseases occur in a haphazard and irregular manner from time to time.
questions.learning: Endemic — The given scenario is an example of an endemic disease. Endemic diseases are those that have a constant presence and /or usual prevalence of a disease or infectious agent in a population within a geographic area.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In familial adenomatous polyposis, which of the following all are true? 1. Presence of >100 colorectal polyps 2. Positive family history 3. Autosomal recessive inheritance 4. Genetic mutation on chromosome 5 Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Why is B correct?

• 1. Presence of >100 colorectal polyps: Correct. Classical FAP is defined by the presence of more than 100 adenomatous colorectal polyps.
• 2. Positive family history: Correct. Since FAP is autosomal dominant, most patients have a positive family history (although \~20–30% arise from new mutations).
• 4. Genetic mutation on chromosome 5: Correct. Mutation occurs in the APC gene on chromosome 5q21.

Incorrect statement:

• 3. Autosomal recessive inheritance: Incorrect. FAP is autosomal dominant.

• (Autosomal recessive polyposis is MUTYH-associated polyposis)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 34-year-old male presented with a painless mass in the right inguinal region. On examination, there is a cough impulse on the index finger and the swelling reaches down to the scrotum and is reduced completely by pressing it through the deep inguinal ring with a gurgling sound. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Indirect inguinal hernia

A swelling that reduces when pressing through the deep inguinal ring suggests a case of indirect inguinal hernia.

Indirect inguinal hernias are by far the most common type of hernia. A femoral hernia passes through the femoral triangle whereas an umbilical hernia protrudes through the umbilicus.

A direct inguinal hernia emerges through Hesselbach's triangle. The boundaries of Hesselbach’s triangle are:

* Lateral - inferior epigastric artery

* Medial - lateral border of rectus abdominis

* Inferior - inguinal ligament

The test being performed in the above image is 3 finger test or Zieman’s test which is used to differentiate groin hernias.

After reducing the hernia, The examiner places his index finger on the deep inguinal ring, middle finger on the superficial inguinal ring, and ring finger over the saphenous opening. Now the patient is asked to cough or to hold the nose and blow.

Interpretation: When the impulse is felt on the,

* Index finger: The given case is one of the indirect herniae.

* Middle finger: The given case is one of the direct herniae.

* Ring finger: The given case is one of the femoral herniae.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding the fluid management of pediatric inpatients with burn injuries? 1. The Parkland formula estimates the amount of fluid to be replaced over 24 hours. 2. Volume of fluid (mL) = 4 mL × Weight (kg) × Total body surface area burn (%). 3. Additional maintenance fluid therapy is also to be given to the child. 4. Half of the resuscitation volume should be given over 6 hours and the remaining half over the next 18 hours. Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 3

Fluid resuscitation is the cornerstone of management in major pediatric burn injuries. The Parkland formula is used to estimate the initial 24-hour fluid requirement, but unlike adults, children also require additional maintenance fluids because of their higher metabolic rate and limited glycogen stores.

Why is B correct?

• 1. The Parkland formula estimates the amount of fluid to be replaced over 24 hours. ✅

• It calculates the initial fluid requirement for the first 24 hours after a burn.

• 2. Volume of fluid (mL) = 4 mL × Weight (kg) × Total body surface area burn (%). ✅

• This is the Parkland formula using Ringer’s lactate.

• 3. Additional maintenance fluid therapy is also to be given to the child. ✅

• Children require maintenance fluids in addition to Parkland resuscitation to meet their physiological needs and prevent hypoglycemia.

• 4. Half of the resuscitation volume should be given over 6 hours and the remaining half over the next 18 hours. ❌

• The correct regimen is:

• First half over the first 8 hours from the time of burn
• Remaining half over the next 16 hours
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 Fluid resuscitation is the cornerstone of management in major pediatric burn injuries. The Parkland formula is used to estimate the initial 24-hour fluid requirement, but unlike adults, children also require additional maintenance fluids because…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is seen in physiological jaundice?
options: Increased indirect bilirubin, increased urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine
Increased indirect bilirubin, absent urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine
Increased direct bilirubin, increased urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine
Increased direct bilirubin, absent urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increased indirect bilirubin, increased urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine

In physiological jaundice, there is increased indirect bilirubin, increased urobilinogen, and absent bilirubin in urine.

Physiological jaundice (icterus neonatorum) is due to increased bilirubin production from the breakdown of fetal red blood cells combined with transient limitation in the conjugation of bilirubin by the immature neonatal liver. It first appears on the 2nd or 3rd days usually peaks on the 4th day at 5-6 mg/dL and decreases to <2 mg/dL between the 5th and 7th days after birth.

Physiological jaundice would lead to an increase in indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin. Increased levels of unconjugated bilirubin in the blood lead to increased production of urobilinogen which would be present in the urine. Urine bilirubin is not usually found in this condition.

Risk factors for physiological jaundice include maternal age, maternal diabetes, prematurity, drugs (vitamin K3, novobiocin), polycythemia, male sex, trisomy 21, cutaneous bruising, blood extravasation as in cephalhematoma, breastfeeding, weight loss, and a family history of physiological jaundice.

On the other hand, in pathological jaundice, the appearance of jaundice is within the first 24 hours after birth and may be present at or beyond the age of 2 weeks in term babies and 3 weeks in preterms babies. Other signs of pathological jaundice include an increase in serum bilirubin exceeding 5mg/dL within a 24-hour period, a serum bilirubin level greater than 12mg/dL in a full-term infant or between 10-14mg/dL in a preterm infant, and a direct bilirubin level more than 2mg/dL at any given time. Jaundice visible on the palms and soles, unresponsiveness to phototherapy, and a rapid rise in bilirubin levels during phototherapy indicate pathological jaundice.

When the concentration of unconjugated bilirubin exceeds 20-25mg/dL, bilirubin would penetrate the blood-brain barrier and lead to kernicterus.

Phototherapy is initiated in babies with pathological jaundice when the bilirubin levels exceed the 95th percentile on the total serum bilirubin (TSB) normogram. Babies are kept at a distance of 30-45 cm from the UV lamp (460-490 nm) with eyes and gonads covered. It is avoided in babies with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia due to the risk of bronze-baby syndrome. Dehydration and hypocalcemia are potential complications and breastfeeding is encouraged.

Exchange transfusion (ET) is done in cases of bilirubin encephalopathy, Rh incompatibility with significant hemolysis, and bilirubin values exceeding TSB cutoffs for ET.
questions.learning: Increased indirect bilirubin, increased urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine In physiological jaundice, there is increased indirect bilirubin, increased urobilinogen, and absent bilirubin in urine.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the diluting segment of the kidney?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ascending thick loop of Henle

The ascending thick limb of the loop of Henle is called the diluting segment.

In the ascending limb, there is the movement of Na+ and Cl– out of the tubular lumen, and the tubular fluid becomes more dilute.

When the fluid reaches the top of the ascending limb, it becomes hypotonic to plasma.
questions.learning: Ascending thick loop of Henle — The ascending thick limb of the loop of Henle is called the diluting segment. In the ascending limb, there is the movement of Na+ and Cl– out of the tubular lumen, and the tubular fluid becomes more dilute.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which organism is most commonly responsible for gas gangrene?
questions.explanation: Clostridium perfringens (particularly type A strains) is the classic and most common causative organism for gas gangrene, also known as clostridial myonecrosis. The organism produces an alpha-toxin (lecithinase) that damages cell membranes and increases capillary permeability, leading to tissue necrosis and the production of gas bubbles (crepitus). Clostridium difficile (Option A) causes pseudomembranous colitis following antibiotic use. Clostridium tetani (Option B) is responsible for tetanus, which presents with spastic paralysis. Clostridium botulinum (Option D) produces a neurotoxin that causes flaccid paralysis. Diagnosis of gas gangrene is clinical, characterized by rapid onset of pain, blackish skin discoloration, and crepitus within the wound
questions.learning: Clostridium perfringens (particularly type — A strains) is the classic and most common causative organism for gas gangrene, also known as clostridial myonecrosis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Aldosterone secretion is maximally stimulated by______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hyperkalemia

Hyperkalemia and activation of renin-angiotensin system are the most potent stimulators of aldosterone secretion.
questions.learning: Hyperkalemia Hyperkalemia and activation of renin-angiotensin system are the most potent stimulators of aldosterone secretion.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with complete inability to move the eyes in any direction, indicating paralysis of all extraocular muscles. Where is the lesion most likely located to cause this global ophthalmoplegia?
questions.explanation: Extraocular muscle movements are controlled by three cranial nerves: the oculomotor (CN III), trochlear (CN IV), and abducens (CN VI). The nuclei for these nerves are located within the brainstem. Specifically, the CN III and CN IV nuclei are in the midbrain, while the CN VI nucleus is in the pons. A significant lesion involving both the midbrain and the pons would disrupt the origins of all these motor nerves, resulting in total ophthalmoplegia (the inability to move the eyes in any direction). The frontal eye field (Option A) is responsible for initiating voluntary conjugate horizontal gaze; a lesion there causes gaze deviation, not total paralysis. The cerebral surface (Option B) handles higher visual processing, and the spinal cord (Option D) has no role in eye movement. Therefore, because the entire lower motor neuron control system for the eyes resides in the brainstem, a midbrain-pons lesion is the definitive anatomical site
questions.learning: Extraocular muscle movements are controlled by three cranial nerves: the oculomotor (CN III), trochlear (CN IV), and abducens (CN VI). The nuclei for these nerves are located within the brainstem.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A handwashing awareness session was conducted in a community. The correct sequence of events here is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Awareness > interest > evaluation > adoption

The correct sequence of events in this health awareness session is: awareness > interest > evaluation > adoption.

1. Awareness Stage: The individual becomes aware of the innovation. He is exposed to innovation but has only limited information about it. At this stage, he doesn’t give much attention to the new product.

2. Interest and Information Stage: The individual becomes interested in innovation and tries to collect more information. He tries to know about qualities, features, functions, risk, producers, brand, colour, shape, price, incentives, availability, services, and other relevant aspects.

3. Evaluation Stage: The consumer considers accumulated information and use it to evaluate the innovation and judge the worth of innovation. He compares different aspects of innovation like qualities, features, performance, price, after-sales services, etc., with the existing products to arrive at the decision whether the innovation should be tried out.

4. Adoption Stage: If trial produces satisfactory results, finally the consumer decides to adopt/buy the innovation. He purchases the product.

The four approaches to health education:

* Regulatory approach

* Service approach

* Health education approach

* Primary health care approach

Regulatory approach

Health Education approach
Primary health care approach

Government intervention to alter human behaviour laws
Facilities are provided by the government for use
Awareness-> interest->Evaluation
The health of the people, for the people, by the people where principles of community participation and intersectoral coordination are stressed

Ex: Child marriage Act, No smoking in public places; Helmet law
Ex: The government provided latrines free of cost yet people did not use them because its need was not felt
Ex: Adoption of ORS for diarrhoea
questions.learning: Awareness > interest > evaluation > adoption — The correct sequence of events in this health awareness session is: awareness > interest > evaluation > adoption.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 6-year-old child is brought for complaints of short stature. His height is comparable with his parent's height and his bone age corresponds to his chronological age. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Familial short stature

A child with short stature with his height comparable to his parent's height and bone age that equals chronological age, the likely diagnosis is familial short stature.

This child's height is normal according to his genetic potential determined by the parent's height. The body proportion is appropriate and bone age equals the chronological age with normal growth velocity. They achieve puberty at an appropriate age and their final height is within their target range.

The relationship between bone age and chronological age is summarised below

* Bone age = chronological age in familial short stature

* Bone age > chronological age in precocious puberty

* Bone age < chronological age in other causes like constitutional delay, undernutrition, genetic diseases, and endocrine causes.

Other options:

Option B: Children with constitutional delay are normal during the first year and fall behind till 3 years, after which the velocity becomes normal. Bone age is lower than chronological age(corresponds to the height age). The onset of puberty is also delayed and they achieve a normal final height. History of delayed puberty and delayed height spurt is usually present in one or both parents.

Option C: Children with undernutrition show other features of malnutrition such as low mid-upper arm circumference and low weight, with a bone age lower than chronological age.

Option D: Children with growth hormone deficiency have bone age lower than chronological age and other signs like crowding of mid-facial structures, and depressed nasal bridge.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presented with paradoxical respiration. Which of the following nerves is most likely to be affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. D

Paradoxical respiration occurs due to the damage of the phrenic nerve, which is marked as D, in the given image.

The structures marked in the image are:

A. Right vagus nerve

B. Left vagus nerve

C. Recurrent laryngeal nerve

D. Right phrenic nerve

Paradoxical movements in the chest are as follows:

• Paradoxical respiration - the abnormal movement of the chest wall or abdominal wall, where they move in during inspiration instead of moving out. It is seen in flail chest.
• Paradoxical movement of the diaphragm - normally, the diaphragm moves down during inspiration. However, in cases of phrenic nerve palsy, the affected side of the diaphragm moves upward (paradoxical respiration) due to diaphragmatic paralysis. The gold standard investigation to detect this is the electrical or magnetic stimulation of the phrenic nerve with a recording of the compound muscle action potential and/or the transdiaphragmatic pressure. This can be observed on ultrasound or fluoroscopy.
questions.learning: D Paradoxical respiration occurs due to the damage of the phrenic nerve, which is marked as D, in the given image. The structures marked in the image are: A.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The image given below is from a chronic smoker's oral examination. Identify the lesion given.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Leukoplakia

The given image with a white lesion of the tongue in a smoker is suggestive of oral leukoplakia

Leukoplakia is a premalignant condition of the oral cavity. It is seen anywhere in the upper aerodigestive tract. It may represent squamous hyperplasia, dysplasia, and/or carcinoma with an associated risk of malignant transformation

It is defined as a clinical white patch that cannot be characterized clinically or pathologically as any other disease. Risk factors include tobacco (including cigars, cigarettes, beedi, and pipes), alcohol consumption and chronic irritation.

A biopsy should be done to establish a diagnosis and an appropriate work-up is done if carcinoma is identified. Cessation of smoking, elimination of the areca nut/pan habit, and reduction in alcohol consumption should be encouraged. For lesions with moderate to severe dysplasia, surgical excision or laser surgery should be the treatment of choice.

Oral hairy leukoplakia is a different entity caused by the Epstein-Barr virus(EBV). It is due to the reactivation of EBV occurring in association with immunodeficiency commonly from HIV infection. It presents as white corrugated plaque over the lateral border of the tongue, which cannot be rubbed off.

Other white lesions of oral mucosa:

* Lichen planus

* Discoid lupus erythematosus

* White spongy nevus

* Candidiasis
questions.learning: Leukoplakia — The given image with a white lesion of the tongue in a smoker is suggestive of oral leukoplakia Leukoplakia is a premalignant condition of the oral cavity.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Given below is the image of a 33-hour chick embryo. Which of the following is derived from the marked structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ribs

The structure marked in the given image is the para-axial mesoderm. The ribs are derived from the para-axial mesoderm.

During the third week of embryological development, the process of gastrulation occurs, which refers to the formation of the three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. This is followed by the formation of the notochord, which is the axial structure, which induces the formation of the neural tube above it. During the formation of the neural tube, some cells at the lateral border dissociate and form the neural crest cells, which is sometimes referred to as the fourth germ layer.

After the formation of the notochord, which is the axial structure, the mesoderm on either side can be seen to be organized into three layers as follows:

1. Para-axial mesoderm - Thickened plate of the mesoderm close to the midline, on either side of the notochord. This forms the somitomeres and somites, which have the following derivatives:

• Dermatome: Forms the segmental dermis of the skin
• Myotome: Forms the skeletal muscle
• Sclerotome: Forms the vertebral column and ribs

2. Intermediate mesoderm - Longitudinal strip of mesoderm that connects the para-axial with the lateral plate mesoderm. The urinary (Option A) and genital systems are derived from the intermediate mesoderm.

3. Lateral plate mesoderm - A thinner layer of mesoderm that lies laterally. This layer develops a large cavity called the intraembryonic coelom that gives rise to pericardial, pleural (Option C), and peritoneal cavities.

The neural crest cells also contribute to the formation of structures as follows:

In the trunk region, they form melanocytes, sensory ganglia (Option B), sympathetic and enteric neurons, Schwann cells, and adrenal medulla cells.
In the cranial region, they contribute to the craniofacial skeleton, neurons for cranial ganglia, satellite glial cells, and melanocytes.
questions.learning: Ribs — The structure marked in the given image is the para-axial mesoderm. The ribs are derived from the para-axial mesoderm.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A male patient presents with hematuria and recurrent urinary tract infections. On contrast- enhanced CT (CECT), the abnormality indicated by the arrows is seen in the image below. What is the condition identified by these findings?
questions.explanation: The coronal CECT image displays a classic congenital anomaly where the lower poles of both kidneys are fused across the midline. This "isthmus" of renal tissue or fibrous band typically crosses anterior to the aorta and is trapped beneath the inferior mesenteric artery, which defines a Horseshoe Kidney. This condition predisposes patients to stasis, leading to recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs) and hematuria due to stone formation. Polycystic kidney disease (Option A) would show multiple, large, fluid-filled cysts bilaterally. Hydronephrosis (Option C) refers to the dilation of the renal pelvis, which may occur as a secondary complication of horseshoe kidney but is not the primary anatomical diagnosis pictured. A pancake kidney (Option D) involves the fusion of both kidneys into a single, lobulated pelvic mass, unlike the distinct "horseshoe" shape seen here. Thus, the characteristic fusion across the midline identifies it as a horseshoe kidney

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false regarding deep vein thrombosis (DVT)?
options: Most common clinical presentation is pain and tenderness in calf
Some cases may directly present as pulmonary thromboembolism
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mostly bilateral

Most cases of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) are unilateral. It is bilateral in only 30% of the individuals.

DVT refers to thrombosis of the deep venous system.

Caused by:

• Postoperative thrombosis (most common cause)
• Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs)
• After childbirth
• Immobility

Sites:

• Pelvic veins—common
• Leg veins—common in femoral and popliteal veins (common on the left side).

Fever is the earliest symptom, which is also most commonly accompanied by pain and tenderness in the calf and thigh (option C).

The following signs could be elicited:

• Positive Homan's sign: Resistance of calf muscles on passive foreceful dorsiflexion of the foot.

• Mose's sign: Gentle squeezing of the lower part of the calf from side to side is painful.
• Neuhof's sign: Thickening and deep tenderness seen on deep palpation of the calf muscles.

Sometimes, the thrombus may get dislodged and present as pulmonary thromboembolism (option D) with features of dyspnoea, tachypnoea, and chest pain.

Clinical features are unreliable for making a definitive diagnosis (option A), and a venous Doppler is the best modality for confirming DVT. It reveals a non-compressible dilated vein. The likelihood of pulmonary embolism can be predicted using modified Wells criteria.

Patients with DVT should be immediately started with subcutaneous low molecular weight heparin (LMWH). If contraindicated due to renal insufficiency or thrombocytopenia-related conditions, they should be started on fondaparinux (indirect factor Xa inhibitor) or bivalirudin (direct thrombin inhibitor). Anticoagulants should be administered for a minimum period of 3 months. Vena cava filters are used in patients with bleeding risks (like hemophilia).
questions.learning: Mostly bilateral Most cases of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) are unilateral. It is bilateral in only 30% of the individuals.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What type of cataract is typically seen on slit- lamp examination in a patient with a history of long-term corticosteroid use?
questions.explanation: Prolonged use of corticosteroids, whether topical, systemic, or inhaled, is a well-known cause of "Posterior Subcapsular Cataract" (PSC). On slit lamp examination, these appear as a granular, "bread-crumb" like opacity located in the central posterior cortex of the lens. PSCs are particularly disabling because they are located near the nodal point of the eye, causing significant glare and vision loss in bright light. Option A (Morgagnian) is a stage of age-related cataract where the cortex liquefies. Option C (Sunflower cataract) is characteristic of Wilson's disease (copper deposition). Option D (Snowflake cataract) is classic for uncontrolled diabetes mellitus. PSCs can also be seen in patients with chronic intraocular inflammation (uveitis) or high myopia. Because steroid-induced cataracts can occur rapidly, any patient on long-term steroid therapy must undergo regular ophthalmic examinations to monitor for both cataract formation and secondary ocular hypertension (glaucoma)
