questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a hernia medial to the inferior epigastric artery. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate management for the same?
options: Direct hernia and Lichtenstein mesh repair
Indirect hernia and Lichtenstein mesh repair
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Direct hernia and Lichtenstein mesh repair

The given clinical scenario of a hernia medial to the inferior epigastric artery is suggestive of a direct hernia, for which Lichtenstein mesh repair is the appropriate surgical method for its management.

The contents of a direct hernia protrude outward, forward, and medial to the inferior epigastric artery and the deep inguinal ring. Whereas, the contents of an indirect hernia protrude lateral to the inferior epigastric artery. The sac of an indirect inguinal hernia passes from the deep inguinal ring obliquely towards the superficial inguinal ring and then to the scrotum.

A direct hernia protrudes through the Hesselbach triangle, which is a zone of weakness for direct hernias.

A Lichtenstein mesh repair is currently one of the most frequently used methods for treating an inguinal hernia. It is done for the reconstruction of the inguinal floor in adults. It is an anterior tension-free mesh repair that reduces the chances of recurrence of a hernia. A piece of prosthetic nonabsorbable mesh is used to bridge the defect in this repair.

Other surgical methods used for the repair of an inguinal hernia are:

• Bassini repair - It is done for the reconstruction of the inguinal floor in adults. In this method, a mesh is not used. It is associated with a high recurrence and is not used frequently now. It is used only in cases of hernial strangulation and peritonitis where the use of a mesh is not preferred. It is performed by suturing the transversus abdominis and internal oblique musculoaponeurotic arches/conjoined tendon to the inguinal ligament.
• Shouldice repair - It is a multilayered repair, where the posterior wall of the inguinal canal is strengthened by continuous sutures. It involves double-breasting of the transversalis fascia. It is associated with a very low recurrence rate.
• Gilbert repair (plug and patch repair) - It is an extension of Lichtenstein’s original mesh repair and has now become the most commonly performed primary anterior inguinal hernia repair. In this technique, a cone-shaped plug of polypropylene mesh is used. It is deployed like an upside-down umbrella when inserted into the internal inguinal ring to occlude the hernia
• McVay repair (Cooper's ligament repair) is used for the correction of direct inguinal hernia, large indirect hernia, recurrent hernia, femoral hernias (particularly suited for strangulated femoral hernias). In this method, the transversus abdominis aponeurosis is approximated to Cooper's ligament.
• Stoppa-Rives repair - It is used for the repair of large, recurrent, or bilateral hernias. In this method, a sub-umbilical midline incision is given to place a large mesh into the preperitoneal space.
• Herniotomy - It is used to treat inguinal hernia in a child which occurs due to the presence of a patent processus vaginalis. Therefore in herniotomy, the repair of the inguinal ring is not done.
questions.learning: Direct hernia and Lichtenstein mesh repair — The given clinical scenario of a hernia medial to the inferior epigastric artery is suggestive of a direct hernia, for which Lichtenstein mesh repair is the appropriate surgical method for its management.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which specific cells are responsible for producing and secreting renin?
questions.explanation: Renin is a proteolytic enzyme that plays a fundamental role in the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS), which regulates blood pressure and fluid balance. It is synthesized and secreted by the juxtaglomerular (JG) cells (Option C). These specialized smooth muscle cells are located primarily in the walls of the afferent arterioles as they enter the glomerulus. JG cells function as baroreceptors that release renin in response to decreased blood pressure or sympathetic stimulation. The macula densa (Option B) consists of specialized tubular cells that sense sodium chloride levels in the distal tubule and signal the JG cells to release renin, but they do not secrete it themselves. Standard tubular cells (Option A) are involved in reabsorption and secretion but not renin production. Therefore, the JG cells are the definitive source of renin, which eventually leads to the formation of Angiotensin II and systemic vasoconstriction
questions.learning: Renin is a proteolytic enzyme that plays a fundamental role in the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS), which regulates blood pressure and fluid balance.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which Leopold's maneuver is done to assess the lie of the fetus?
questions.explanation: Leopold’s maneuvers are a systematic method of abdominal palpation used in obstetrics to assess the fetal lie, presentation, position, and engagement. Among these, Leopold’s first maneuver (fundal grip) is specifically used to determine the fetal lie. In this maneuver, the examiner palpates the uterine fundus using both hands to identify which fetal pole occupies the upper part of the uterus. If the head is felt in the fundus, the fetus is in a breech presentation, while if the breech is felt, it suggests a cephalic presentation, both indicating a longitudinal lie. If neither pole is clearly identified, it may indicate a transverse or oblique lie. Leopold’s second maneuver assesses fetal position by locating the back and limbs. Leopold’s third maneuver identifies the presenting part above the pelvic inlet, and Leopold’s fourth maneuver evaluates engagement of the presenting part. Therefore, the first maneuver is most important for determining the fetal lie
questions.learning: Leopold’s maneuvers are a systematic method of abdominal palpation used in obstetrics to assess the fetal lie, presentation, position, and engagement.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the epithelial lining of the trachea?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium

The trachea is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium.

The trachea is a tube-like structure that allows air to pass between the larynx and the bronchi.

The trachealis muscle is a smooth muscle located at the posterior wall of the trachea. It connects the ends of the C-shaped tracheal cartilage rings and completes the posterior part of the tracheal wall.

The histological image below is that of the trachea as identified by the presence of pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium lining, the serous and mucous glands, and hyaline cartilage.

The histological section of the trachea shows the following structures:

* Respiratory epithelium

* Basement membrane

* Submucosal glands (both serous and mucous parts)

* Perichondrium

* Tracheal cartilage

* Trachealis muscle (smooth muscle).
questions.learning: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium — The trachea is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium. The trachea is a tube-like structure that allows air to pass between the larynx and the bronchi.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A male patient who is HIV-positive, presents with persistent headaches, confusion, and fever. Further cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed a positive India ink stain. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cryptococcus

The image clinical scenario indicates meningitis caused by the fungus cryptococcus.

Cryptococcus neoformans is an opportunistic fungus that is found worldwide as a saprophyte in soil enriched with pigeon droppings. It may cause infection in immune-competent people, resulting in a flu-like illness with complete recovery.

Infection in immunocompromised people like AIDS patients or patients with hematological malignancies results in meningoencephalitis.

The image below shows India ink preparation which is employed to detect the presence of capsulated yeast, cryptococcus neoformans. It induces negative staining by creating a black, semi-opaque background that makes the capsule of the yeast clearly visible. Cryptococcus has a polysaccharide capsule which is demonstrated as clear halos against a black background.

Mucicarmine stain can also be used in the identification of cryptococcus. The image given below shows mucicarmine stained specimen of lung tissue containing cryptococci.

Culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) at 37'C appears as smooth, mucoid, and creamy white. The cryptococcal antigen(in serum and CSF) is sensitive and specific and can be demonstrated by the latex agglutination test.

Treatment of cryptococcal meningitis involves a combination therapy of amphotericin B with flucytosine. Fluconazole can be added with these drugs in AIDS patients to prevent relapse.
questions.learning: Cryptococcus — The image clinical scenario indicates meningitis caused by the fungus cryptococcus. Cryptococcus neoformans is an opportunistic fungus that is found worldwide as a saprophyte in soil enriched with pigeon droppings.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which amino acid serves as the principal buffer in blood because of its ability to both accept and donate protons at physiological pH?
questions.explanation: Histidine is the only amino acid that functions effectively as a buffer at physiological pH (7.4). This is because its imidazole side chain has a pKa of approximately 6.0, which is close enough to the blood's pH to allow it to both accept and donate protons. Arginine (Option B) has a pKa of 12.5, which is far too high to act as a buffer in the body. Tryptophan (Option C) and Tyrosine (Option D) have minimal buffering capacity because their side chains are either non-ionizable or have pKa values (10.1 for tyrosine) that are not relevant at physiological pH. Histidine residues are particularly abundant in hemoglobin, where they play a vital role in the Bohr effect, helping to maintain blood pH while regulating oxygen delivery to tissues
questions.learning: Histidine is the only amino acid that functions effectively as a buffer at physiological pH (7.4). This is because its imidazole side chain has a pKa of approximately 6.0, which is close enough to the blood's pH to allow it to both accept and donate protons.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An AIDS-positive patient came with a history of fever, vomiting, and meningismus. Which of the following tests help in the rapid diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Blood assay for cryptococcal antigen

Blood assay for cryptococcal antigen help in the rapid diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis.

Latex agglutination tests are mainly used for the detection of carbohydrate antigens of encapsulated microorganisms. In latex agglutination tests, an antigen-specific antibody (either polyclonal or monoclonal) is fixed to latex beads. When the clinical specimen from the patient is added to a suspension of the latex beads, the antibodies bind to the antigens on the microorganism forming a lattice structure, and agglutination of the beads occurs.

Cryptococcal meningitis is the most common cause of meningitis in an immunocompromised HIV patient. It generally occurs in untreated patients, with CD4+ T cell counts <100/μL.

It presents with subacute meningoencephalitis with fever, nausea, vomiting, altered mental status, headache, and meningeal signs. The CSF profile shows elevations in WBC with lymphocyte predominance, elevated protein levels, and reduced to normal levels of glucose. The CSF opening pressure is usually elevated

Diagnosis is made by demonstration of yeast cells or cryptococcal antigen in CSF. India ink stain is used to demonstrate capsulated budding yeast cells in CSF as they have a distinctive appearance because their capsules exclude ink particles. But its very much subjective and hence is less preferred over other methods for rapid diagnosis. Rapid detection of cryptococcal antigen in CSF and blood can also be done. Colonies develop within a few days on most media at room temperature or 37°C.

Treatment

*  Induction – IV or Liposomal Amphotericin B with Flucytosine for at least 2 weeks, continuing with Amphotericin alone ideally until the CSF culture turns negative.

*  Maintenance -  Oral Fluconazole until the CD4+ T cell count has increased to >200 cells/μL for 6 months in response to cART.

*  Primary Prophylaxis - Oral Fluconazole when CD4+ T cell count is <100/μL.
questions.learning: Blood assay for cryptococcal antigen Blood assay for cryptococcal antigen help in the rapid diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis. Latex agglutination tests are mainly used for the detection of carbohydrate antigens of encapsulated microorganisms.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida with polyhydramnios develops profuse postpartum bleeding after an intern prematurely attempts placental removal during a normal delivery. Examination reveals an intact placenta with a portion of the uterus protruding outside the vaginal introitus. The patient is in hemorrhagic shock, and initial resuscitative measures have been started. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acute uterine inversion is a rare but life-threatening complication where the uterine fundus collapses into the endometrial cavity and turns "inside out," often protruding through the cervix. The primary risk factors in this case are "polyhydramnios" (causing a distended, thin-walled uterus) and "premature traction on the umbilical cord" (forced removal of the placenta before it has separated). The hallmark finding is a mass (the uterus) protruding from the introitus and the absence of the fundus upon abdominal palpation. Amniotic fluid embolism (Option A) causes sudden collapse without an anatomical uterine mass. Postpartum hemorrhage (Option B) is a general term for bleeding; uterine inversion is a specific cause of severe PH. Uterine rupture (Option D) usually happens before delivery and presents with different clinical signs. Management involves aggressive fluid resuscitation and immediate manual replacement of the uterus (Johnson's maneuver) under anesthesia. If the placenta is still attached, it should not be removed until the uterus is repositioned to prevent further hemorrhage
questions.learning: Acute uterine inversion is a rare but life-threatening complication where the uterine fundus collapses into the endometrial cavity and turns "inside out," often protruding through the cervix.

questions.text: Thalidomide should not be used in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HIV-assosiated peripheral neuropathy

Thalidomide is an immunomodulatory drug used for several inflammatory and dermatologic conditions but is contraindicated in peripheral neuropathy because it can cause or worsen neuropathy.

Uses of thalidomide:

• Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) – drug of choice
• Behçet syndrome (oral/genital ulcers)
• HIV-associated aphthous ulcers
• Multiple myeloma

Major adverse effects:

• Peripheral neuropathy (dose-related, often irreversible)
• Severe teratogenicity (phocomelia)
• Sedation, constipation, thrombosis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In the diagram showing the development of ovarian follicles, which structure is indicated at this stage of follicular progression?
questions.explanation: The diagram illustrates the sequential development of follicles within the ovary. The structure indicated by the arrow—characterized by a large, fluid-filled cavity—is an antral follicle (also known as a secondary or Graafian follicle) . This cavity, the antrum, is filled with follicular fluid containing high concentrations of hormones. Primordial follicles (Option C) are the quiescent microscopic clusters seen at the beginning of the cycle. Primary follicles (Option A) are slightly larger but lack an antrum. The corpus luteum (Option D) is the solid glandular structure that forms after ovulation occurs, visible in the "Luteal phase" section of the diagram. Because the visual shows a mature follicle containing an obvious central fluid space just prior to the ovulation marker, it is definitively the antral stage. Recognizing these stages is fundamental for understanding the hormonal regulation of the menstrual cycle

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 80 year old male presented with diminution of vision since 2 years. The right eye was red and painful. On examination, the IOP was 50 mmHg in left eye and 16 mmHg in right eye. The right eye had deep anterior chamber with some cells and flare. What could be the possibility?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phacolytic glaucoma

Phacolytic glaucoma is a lens-induced secondary open-angle glaucoma seen in elderly patients with long-standing hypermature cataract.

• Elderly patient with gradual visual loss (cataract history)
• Painful red eye
• Very high IOP (e.g., \~50 mmHg)
• Deep anterior chamber (open angle)
• Cells and flare in anterior chamber due to inflammatory response

Pathophysiology:

• Leakage of lens proteins from hypermature cataract
• Macrophages ingest proteins → block trabecular meshwork
• Leads to acute rise in IOP

Why not others:

• Phacomorphic glaucoma:

• Due to intumescent lens → shallow anterior chamber (angle closure)

• Malignant glaucoma:

• Shallow/flat anterior chamber, usually post-surgery

• Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis:

• Chronic, mild uveitis with low-grade inflammation, not markedly raised IOP

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in an immuno compromised patient from a low socioeconomic background who presents with low-grade evening fever, weight loss, and a soft, non- tender cervical swelling that shows a positive fluctuation test?
questions.explanation: The clinical picture describes a "cold abscess," which is a hallmark of Tubercular Lymphadenitis (Option B). The patient's immunocompromised status and lower-income background are significant risk factors for tuberculosis. "Mild nightly fever" and weight loss are classic constitutional symptoms of TB. A soft, non-tender, fluctuating mass in the neck without signs of acute inflammation (redness or heat) is the definition of a cold abscess, usually resulting from the liquefaction of caseous lymph nodes. A branchial cyst (Option A) is a congenital swelling located at the upper third of the sternocleidomastoid but lacks systemic symptoms. A thyroglossal cyst (Option C) is a midline mass that moves with tongue protrusion. A lipoma (Option D) is a painless, slow-growing fatty mass that is slip-sign positive but does not fluctuate. Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) or biopsy is required to confirm the presence of acid-fast bacilli or granulomatous inflammation
questions.learning: The clinical picture describes a "cold abscess," which is a hallmark of Tubercular Lymphadenitis (Option B). The patient's immunocompromised status and lower-income background are significant risk factors for tuberculosis.

questions.text: Which of the following combinations is not seen in the case of twin pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Dichorionic monoamniotic (DCMA)

Dichorionic monoamniotic (DCMA) combination is not seen in twin pregnancies.

The table below describes the types of amnion and chorion seen in different types of twins, depending on the time of division.

Time of division after fertilization
Type of twin

0 - 4 days (morula)
Dichorionic diamniotic (DCDA)

4 - 8 days (blastocyst)
Monochorionic diamniotic (MCDA)

8 - 12 days (implanted blastocyst)
Monochorionic monoamniotic (MCMA)

>13 days (formed embryonic disc)
Conjoined twins

In monochorionic diamniotic gestation, the twins are separated only by the two amniotic membranes, with no intervening chorion. So, a thin 'T sign' is formed at the point at which the amnions meet the placenta. It is best seen in the latter part of the first trimester or at the beginning of the second trimester. In monochorionic monoamniotic gestation, there is an absence of a dividing membrane.

In dichorionic gestation, the twins are separated by amniotic membranes and an intervening chorion. So, a thicker twin peak sign or lambda (λ) sign is formed at the point at which the amnions meet the placenta. It is best seen in the first trimester.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect about baroreceptors?
options: Located in the thick muscle layer
Afferent fibers pass via the glossopharyngeal nerve branch
Sensitive to changes in arterial pressure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Located in the thick muscle layer

Arterial baroreceptors are stretch receptors sensitive to changes in arterial pressure.

They are located in the adventitia of the carotid sinus and aortic arch, not in the thick muscle layer, thick muscle layer = tunica media, baroreceptors are located in the adventitia and elastic wall regions

Baroreceptors are mechanoreceptors that detect stretch in arterial walls.

| Location | Nerve Supply

| -------- | ------------

| Carotid sinus | Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)

| Aortic arch | Vagus nerve (CN X)

Pathway:

1️⃣ Increased BP stretches arterial wall

2️⃣ Baroreceptors increase firing

3️⃣ Signals sent to medulla (nucleus tractus solitarius)

4️⃣ Sympathetic activity decreases

5️⃣ Parasympathetic activity increases

Result: Decreased heart rate and blood pressure

Afferent impulses from the carotid sinus travel via the glossopharyngeal nerve (Hering’s nerve).

Thus, location in the thick muscle layer is incorrect.

| Reflex | Receptor Location | Stimulus | Afferent Nerve | Response

| ------ | ----------------- | -------- | -------------- | --------

| Baroreceptor reflex | Carotid sinus, Aortic arch | ↑ Blood pressure | CN IX (carotid), CN X (aortic) | ↓ HR, ↓ BP

| Bainbridge reflex | Right atrium | ↑ Venous return / atrial stretch | Vagus | ↑ Heart rate

| Bezold–Jarisch reflex | LV wall receptors | Ventricular stretch/ischemia | Vagal C fibers | Bradycardia, hypotension

| Cushing reflex | Brainstem | ↑ Intracranial pressure | CNS | Hypertension + bradycardia

| Chemoreceptor reflex | Carotid bodies | Hypoxia, hypercapnia | CN IX, X | ↑ respiration, ↑ BP

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: An 18-year-old girl with primary amenorrhea presents to the OPD. She has Tanner stage IV secondary sexual characters. Her karyotype is 46XX. FSH is 5 and LH is 13. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mullerian agenesis

Clinical clues

• 18-year-old girl
• Primary amenorrhea
• Tanner stage IV secondary sexual characters
• Karyotype: 46XX
• FSH = 5, LH = 13 (near normal)

These findings indicate normal ovarian function but absence of uterus, which is typical of Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser Syndrome.

MRKH syndrome occurs due to failure of Müllerian duct development.

Structures derived from Müllerian ducts include:

• Uterus
• Fallopian tubes
• Upper 2/3 of vagina

In MRKH:

• Uterus absent
• Upper vagina absent or shortened
• Ovaries normal

| Hormone | Level

| ------- | -----

| FSH | Normal

| LH | Normal

| Estrogen | Normal

This indicates normal hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis.

MRKH syndrome may be associated with:

| System | Abnormality

| ------ | -----------

| Renal | Renal agenesis

| Skeletal | Vertebral anomalies

| Cardiac | Rare congenital defects

Causes of Primary Amenorrhea with Normal Secondary Sexual Characters

| Cause | Key Feature

| ----- | -----------

| Mullerian agenesis (MRKH) | Absent uterus

| Androgen insensitivity | 46XY karyotype

| Imperforate hymen | Outflow obstruction

| Transverse vaginal septum | Vaginal obstruction

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old male patient presents with a swelling that has been slowly growing in the past 2 years. On examination, it was variable in consistency and fully mobile. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Parotid tumor

The given clinical scenario and image depict a likely case of parotid tumor, likely to be a pleomorphic adenoma.

Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common benign salivary gland tumor. The most commonly affected gland is the parotid gland. The superficial lobe is most commonly affected. It is also called as mixed tumor since it has both epithelial and mesenchymal components. It most commonly affects females around 40 years of age.

The common presenting feature is a painless swelling below, in front, or behind the ear. The involvement of the deep lobe leads to dumbbell tumor – swelling in both the neck and oral cavity.

Specific features:

• Slowly growing benign tumor
• Unicentric in origin
• Potentially malignant
• Possibility of protrusion of fringes of the tumor mass through the capsule
• Radioresistant
• Usually affects adults, females > males
• Painless swelling
• Well-defined margins
• Lobulated, firm, elastic-to-hard consistency
• Free from deeper structures
• No facial nerve involvement
• The deep lobe pushes tonsils and faucial pillars

Diagnosis is made by FNAC, which is considered the investigation of choice. Open biopsy contraindicated due to chances of injury to the facial nerve and seedling of the tumor

Surgery is the mainstay of treatment - Superficial parotidectomy (Patey's operation). Radiotherapy is considered in high-grade malignancies demonstrating extra-glandular disease, perineural invasion, direct invasion of surrounding tissue, or regional metastases.

Pathology:

Gross features:

• The tumors are rounded, well-demarcated, measuring <6 cm in greatest dimension.
• They are usually encapsulated, except in some areas such as the palate.
• The cut surface is gray-white with myxoid and blue translucent areas of the chondroid (cartilage-like) stroma.

Microscopic features:

• The epithelial elements resemble ductal cells or myoepithelial cells. They are arranged as ducts, acini, irregular tubules, strands, or sheets of cells.
• These epithelial elements are dispersed within a background of loose myxoid and hyaline tissue containing islands of cartilage and, rarely, foci of bone.

The image below shows pleomorphic adenoma of the salivary gland consisting of mixed epithelial (left) and mesenchymal cell components (right).

Dermoid cysts are slow-growing benign lesions. They are mostly seen on the scalp and skull. It is made of hair, teeth, cartilage, and skin glands. Other common sites are the forehead, postauricular, and lateral part of the eyebrow.

A sebaceous cyst is derived from hair follicle infundibulum or traumatic inclusion. The most common site of a sebaceous cyst is the postauricular sulcus or below and behind the ear lobule. Malignancy is rare.

Clinical features of a sebaceous cyst include:

• Benign swelling that is mobile, fluctuant, and fixed to the skin. It presents with a central punctum in about 70% of cases.
• It is generally an asymptomatic, non-tender swelling. It can be painful and red if inflamed.
• It may ooze out a foul-smelling, cheese-like discharge.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman who underwent dilatation and curettage for molar pregnancy 6 months ago presents with persistent symptoms of abdominal pain and distention. On further evaluation, the beta-hCG levels were persistently elevated and cannonball foci were found on the chest X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia

A woman with a history of dilatation & curettage for molar pregnancy complaining of abdominal pain, distention, cannonball foci, and persistently elevated beta HCG levels is likely having Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.

Based on the mentioned features in the question stem, the diagnosis is low risk gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN) of stage III.

Gestational trophoblastic diseases are histologically is divided into:

Hydatiform mole
Non-molar trophoblastic neoplasms

Villi present

Villi absent

Benign:

• Complete hydatidiform mole
• Partial hydatidiform mole

-

Malignant:

• Invasive mole

Malignant:

• Choriocarcinoma
• Placental site trophoblastic tumor
• Epithelioid trophoblastic
tumor

They typically develop along with or after a molar pregnancy. Rarely, it may develop after live birth, miscarriage, or medical termination of pregnancy.

Risk factors for malignant change are:

* Molar pregnancy -

* partial moles - 1-5% risk

* complete moles - 15-20% risk

* Patient's age ≥ 40 years or <20 years

* Parity ≥3

* Serum β hCG >1,00,000 IU/mL

* Uterine size >20 weeks

* Previous history of molar pregnancy

* Large theca lutein cysts >6 cm in diameter

Treatment of GTN:

* Low-risk GTN (FIGO Stages I-III: score <7): Single-agent chemotherapy with methotrexate (MTX) or Dactinomycin (less commonly used).

* 50 mg MTX is given IM on days 1, 3, 5, and 7 with folinic acid on alternate days.

* High-risk GTN (FIGO Stages II-III: score >7 and Stage IV): Multiple agent chemotherapies, with or without adjuvant surgery or radiotherapy. The preferred multiple agent chemotherapy regime is the EMACO regime:

* Etoposide

* Methotrexate

* Dactinomycin (actinomycin D)

* Cyclophosphamide

* Vincristine (Oncovin)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 21 year old woman is brought in a drowsy state from a PHC with complaints of fever, severe lower abdominal pain, and purulent vaginal discharge. Her friend revealed that she had had an unsafe abortion a week ago. On examination, her abdomen was distended, BP was 80/60 mmHg, PR was 140 bpm and RR was 36 /min. Which of the following is not a causative agent of her present condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Escherichia coli

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of toxic shock syndrome (TSS) following septic abortion. Escherichia coli can be detected in septic abortion but it is not a causative agent for TSS.

Organisms causing toxic shock syndrome in septic abortion are:

* Streptococcus pyogenes

* Clostridium perfringens

* Clostridium sordellii

Clinical features of septic abortion include:

* Fever with chills and rigors

* Abdominal or chest pain

* Diarrhoea and vomiting

* Renal angle tenderness

* Offensive purulent vaginal discharge.

Clinical grading of septic abortion:

* Grade I - infection localized in the uterus

* Grade II - infection spreads to parametrium, tubes, ovaries, or pelvic peritoneum

* Grade III - generalized peritonitis, endotoxic shock, jaundice, or acute renal failure

Empirical antibiotic therapy in septic abortion is started for the broadest microbial coverage. Piperacillin-tazobactam or carbapenem and clindamycin are given intravenously. Antibiotics can be changed once culture sensitivity reports are available.
questions.learning: Escherichia coli — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of toxic shock syndrome (TSS) following septic abortion. Escherichia coli can be detected in septic abortion but it is not a causative agent for TSS.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman with primary infertility is found to have bilateral tubal block on HSG. The next best step is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Laparoscopy with chromopertubation

HSG is a screening test for tubal patency.

• HSG findings must be confirmed --> by laparoscopy with chromopertubation.
• This allows direct visualization and dye testing for tubal patency.

IVF is considered only after confirmation, IUI and Letrozole are ineffective with bilateral block.

Methylene blue dye injected through cervix

↓

Dye passes through uterus

↓

Spillage from fimbrial end

↓

Confirms tubal patency

If no dye spill is seen, tubal obstruction is confirmed.
questions.learning: Laparoscopy with chromopertubation HSG is a screening test for tubal patency. • HSG findings must be confirmed --> by laparoscopy with chromopertubation. • This allows direct visualization and dye testing for tubal patency.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A middle aged patient presenting with change in her voice, anemia, recent hair loss and cold intolerance has been diagnosed with Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Which of the following antibody is commonly seen in such patients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anti thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibody

Hashimoto thyroiditis is an autoimmune destruction of the thyroid gland leading to hypothyroidism.

It is characterized by high titers of anti–thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies.

Anti-TPO antibodies mediate thyroid follicular cell damage via immune mechanisms.

Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) function:

• Oxidation of iodide
• Iodination of tyrosine
• Coupling → T3 & T4 formation

Anti-TPO antibodies:

• Attack TPO enzyme
• Impair hormone synthesis
• Cause gland destruction

➡ Hallmark of Hashimoto thyroiditis

TSIg and anti–TSH receptor antibodies are associated with Graves’ disease, not Hashimoto thyroiditis.
questions.learning: Anti thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibody Hashimoto thyroiditis is an autoimmune destruction of the thyroid gland leading to hypothyroidism. It is characterized by high titers of anti–thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 29-year-old pregnant woman at 32 weeks of gestation undergoes an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). Her fasting blood glucose is 110 mg/dL, and the 2-hour post-glucose value is 180 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Induce labor due to risk of fetal macrosomia
questions.explanation: The patient's OGTT results (fasting 110 mg/dl and 2-hour 180 mg/dl) are well above the diagnostic thresholds for Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM). In India, the DIPSI guidelines suggest that a fasting level or a 2-hour level is diagnostic. Because her levels are significantly elevated, particularly the fasting glucose, conservative management with diet alone is unlikely to be sufficient at 32 weeks. Admitting and starting insulin (Option C) is the most appropriate management to achieve rapid glycemic control and reduce the risk of maternal and fetal complications. Starting oral hypoglycemics (Option A) like metformin is an alternative, but insulin remains the gold standard in pregnancy for severe elevations. Reassurance (Option B) is inappropriate as untreated GDM leads to macrosomia and polyhydramnios. Induced labor (Option D) is not indicated at 32 weeks solely for GDM unless there are other severe complications. Prompt insulin therapy is the priority
questions.learning: The patient's OGTT results (fasting 110 mg/dl and 2-hour 180 mg/dl) are well above the diagnostic thresholds for Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM). In India, the DIPSI guidelines suggest that a fasting level or a 2-hour level is diagnostic.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Maternal antibodies that do not provide significant immunity in a neonate:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Polio

Maternal antibodies do not provide significant immunity to polio infection in a neonate.

Administering an oral polio vaccine (OPV) dose at birth can provide early mucosal protection, safeguarding against enteric pathogens before they can hinder the intestinal mucosal immune response. Furthermore, administering OPV during the period when infants are protected by maternal antibodies may help prevent vaccine-associated paralytic polio (VAPP).

All pregnant women should receive a tetanus toxoid, reduced diphtheria toxoid, and acellular pertussis (Tdap) vaccine during each pregnancy, as early in the 27–36-week-of-gestation window as possible. The maternal antibodies formed from Tdap will provide immunity against tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis in the newborn. Administering the Tdap vaccine earlier, between the 27th and 36th week of gestation, maximizes the transfer of passive antibodies to the infant (options A and C).

Infants less than 6 months are generally protected from measles by maternal antibodies (option D).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 65-year old patient visits his family practitioner for a yearly examination. On examination, his BP was 190/100 mm Hg. His pulse pressure was 90 mm Hg. What would have decreased resulting in this increase in pulse pressure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Arterial wall compliance

Pulse pressure increases with age due to decreased arterial wall compliance.

With advancing age, there is an increase in systolic blood pressure. Whilst diastolic blood pressure falls after 60 years of age due to increased arterial stiffness (decreased compliance). As a result of these two changes, pulse pressure increases (↑PP = ↑SBP - ↓DBP).
questions.learning: Arterial wall compliance Pulse pressure increases with age due to decreased arterial wall compliance. With advancing age, there is an increase in systolic blood pressure.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn presents with weak lower limb pulses and strong upper limb pulses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Coarctation of the Aorta (COA) is a congenital heart defect characterized by a narrowing of the aortic arch, most commonly just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery. This leads to high blood pressure and strong pulses in the upper extremities, contrasted with significantly lower pressure and weak or delayed pulses in the lower extremities (femoral pulses). Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA, Option A) presents with profound cyanosis in the newborn but uniform pulses. Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF, Option C) is a cyanotic heart disease presenting with "tet spells" but typically does not cause differential pulses. Ebstein anomaly (Option D) involves a malformed tricuspid valve leading to right-sided heart failure and cyanosis, but not a pulse differential between upper and lower limbs. Clinical diagnosis of COA is made by simultaneous palpation of the radial and femoral pulses (brachio-femoral delay) and is confirmed with echocardiography or CT angiography
questions.learning: Coarctation of the Aorta (COA) is a congenital heart defect characterized by a narrowing of the aortic arch, most commonly just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman is diagnosed with a uterine leiomyoma on ultrasound during evaluation for abnormal uterine bleeding. She is planned for surgical management with myomectomy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation prior to the procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. MRI pelvis

MRI pelvis is the best imaging modality for preoperative mapping of uterine fibroids, especially before myomectomy, as it accurately defines the number, size, location, and type of leiomyomas, helping plan the surgical approach and differentiate fibroids from adenomyosis.

Why not the other options?

• A. CT pelvis: Poor soft tissue characterization; not routinely used for fibroid evaluation.
• C. Hysterosalpingography (HSG): Used to assess the uterine cavity and tubal patency in infertility, not for preoperative fibroid mapping.
• D. Plain X-ray pelvis: Limited role; may show calcified fibroids but is not useful for surgical planning.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy was brought with the complaints of protrusion of the right eye with no h/o fever. CT Scan showed a well-defined mass in the orbit with an irregular border and adjacent bony destruction. Biopsy showed small, round cells which were positive for Desmin in Immunohistochemistry. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rhabdomyosarcoma

The clinical scenario of a patient with complaints of protrusion of eye with well-defined mass in the orbit and adjacent bony destruction on CT scan and biopsy showing small, round cells positive for Desmin favors rhabdomyosarcoma.

Cavernous hemangioma(option B) and orbital cellulitis(option C) usually are associated with fever, hence ruled out. Retinoblastoma(option A) is associated with Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes on microscopy, therefore its not correct.

Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common soft tissue sarcoma of childhood usually in the head and neck region, most common primary orbital malignancy in children. They are malignant tumors arising from voluntary muscle and produce a rapidly increasing proptosis. It extends in all directions. Diagnosis is done using biopsy in which cross-striations in the tumor cells are pathognomonic. Myoglobulin is a specific marker but it can also be positive for desmin.

Subtypes include embryonal(majority), alveolar, botryoid and pleomorphic.

Treatment includes combination of chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

• Two injections of vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and actinomycin D are given at weekly intervals before radiotherapy.
• Radiotherapy is given during which vincristine and cyclophosphamide are administered weekly.
• After radiotherapy, a combination of vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and doxorubicin is given for a year or longer in those patients in whom metastases were detected.

Other options:

Option A: Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular malignancy in children. It is associated with mutations in the RB1 gene at chromosome 13q14.  White pupillary reflex or leukocoria is the most common presenting feature, followed by a squint which is usually convergent. Histopathology of the tumor shows small round cells with large nuclei. Microscopic features includes Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes(highly specific of retinoblastoma), Homer-Wright rosettes, pseudorosettes, and fleurettes formation. Areas of necrosis and calcification can also be seen.

Option B: Cavernous hemangioma is the most common primary benign orbital tumor in adults. They are composed of large, dilated vascular channels; are more infiltrative; frequently involve deep structures; and do not spontaneously regress. On histologic examination, the mass is sharply delineated but unencapsulated with large, cavernous blood-filled vascular spaces, separated by connective tissue stroma.

Option C: Orbital cellulitis is the most common cause of unilateral proptosis in children. It refers to the acute infection of the contents of the orbit behind the orbital septum. Features include pain, lid edema, erythema, chemosis, and axial proptosis. Increased pain with movement of eyes and ophthalmoplegia(decreased ocular motility) is a classic symptom. With posterior exenteration cavernous sinus thrombosis, subdural empyema, and intracranial abscess develop.
questions.learning: Rhabdomyosarcoma — The clinical scenario of a patient with complaints of protrusion of eye with well-defined mass in the orbit and adjacent bony destruction on CT scan and biopsy showing small, round cells positive for Desmin favors rhabdomyosarcoma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which medication should be given to a 45-year- old woman with lung adenocarcinoma to prevent chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, considering she experienced these symptoms during prior treatment cycles?
questions.explanation: Palonosetron is a highly effective, second-generation 5-HT3 receptor antagonist specifically utilized for the prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV). It has a significantly longer half-life (approximately 40 hours) compared to first-generation agents like ondansetron, making it particularly useful for both acute and delayed vomiting phases. Metoclopramide (Option A) and Domperidone (Option C) are dopamine antagonists with prokinetic properties; while they can treat general nausea, they are less effective than 5-HT3 antagonists for the highly emetogenic stimulus of chemotherapy. Ropinirole (Option B) is a dopamine agonist used for Parkinson's disease and has no role in managing CINV. Therefore, because Palonosetron is part of the gold-standard antiemetic protocols for cancer patients, it is the most appropriate medication for this woman. Prevention is prioritized by administering these agents before chemotherapy begins. Consequently, palonosetron is the definitive pharmacological choice in this scenario
questions.learning: Palonosetron is a highly effective, second-generation 5-HT3 receptor antagonist specifically utilized for the prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Best method of diagnosis for Clostridium difficile?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Toxin gene detection by PCR

Nucleic acid amplification tests, including PCR assays, for C. difficile toxin A or B gene in stool have been approved for diagnostic purposes of Clostridium difficile infection due to high sensitivity, specificity and rapid turnaround time.

The diagnosis of CDI is based on a combination of clinical criteria:

(1) diarrhea (≥3 unformed stools per 24 h for ≥2 days) with no other recognized cause plus

(2) toxin A or B detected in the stool, toxin- producing C. difficile detected in the stool by PCR or culture, or pseudomembranes seen in the colon.

Other diagnostic methods include :

• Stool Culture in selective media
• Demonstrating Toxin by Hep-2 cell cultures
• Toxin gene identification by Enzyme immunoassay
• Colonscopy or sigmoidoscopy

Despite the array of tests available for C. difficile and its toxins, no single traditional test has high sensitivity, high specificity, and rapid turnaround.

Most laboratory tests for toxins, including enzyme immunoassays, lack sensitivity.

Nucleic acid amplification tests, including PCR assays, for C. difficile toxin A or B gene in stool have now been approved for diagnostic purposes and appear to be both rapid and sensitive while retaining high specificity.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a food adulteration disease?
questions.explanation: Fluorosis is not a food adulteration disease; rather, it is caused by the chronic ingestion of naturally occurring excess fluoride, primarily through contaminated drinking water. It leads to dental mottling and skeletal deformities. In contrast, Lathyrism (Option A) is a classic food adulteration disease caused by the consumption of Lathyrus sativus (Khesari dal) containing the neurotoxin -ODAP, which causes spastic paraparesis. Dropsy (Option C) results from mustard oil adulterated with Argemone mexicana seeds, leading to epidemic edema and heart failure. Aflatoxicosis (Option D) is caused by aflatoxins produced by Aspergillus species contaminating stored grains and nuts, which can lead to liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. While lathyrism, dropsy, and aflatoxicosis involve toxins added to or contaminating food supplies, fluorosis is an environmental intoxication
questions.learning: Fluorosis is not a food adulteration disease; rather, it is caused by the chronic ingestion of naturally occurring excess fluoride, primarily through contaminated drinking water.
